正德癸酉秋八月，天下當開科取士之期，順天府府尹臣𠭇、府丞臣珝具疏，請考試官主京畿鄉試。上命侍講學士臣一鵬、左中允兼修撰臣龍往簡拔之。

臣方承乏史館，纂修玉牒，聞命則驚惕而起，嘆曰：「玉牒之修，朝廷所以待天下宗藩，親親之道也；科目之設，
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the guiyou year of the Zhengde reign [1513], when examinations were due to be held throughout the realm to select scholars for office, your servants 𠭇 [?], Prefect of Shuntian, and Xu, Vice Prefect, submitted a memorial requesting Examiners to preside over the Provincial Examination of the capital region. His Majesty commanded your servants Yipeng, Expositor-in-Waiting, and Long, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent concurrently serving as Senior Compiler, to go and select the worthy candidates.

I was then serving, for want of someone more capable, in the Historiography Office, compiling the Imperial Genealogy. On hearing the command, I rose in alarm and apprehension, and sighed: “The compilation of the Imperial Genealogy is the means by which the court treats the imperial princes throughout the realm, following the Way of cherishing one’s kin; the establishment of the examination system…”

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
朝廷所以待天下賢才賢賢之道
也隨時緩急一惟
上命乃輟所謂纂修者即以求賢爲
重事翌日遂與臣龍
進辭于
廷退宴于府時同考試官學正臣
大綱臣大章臣慈教諭臣棠臣嶽訓
導臣震臣文榦臣碩臣衝皆禮聘
至自外郡監試官監察御史臣
瀛臣祺皆遴選至自内臺其他
百執事亦皆慎簡以充而提調
内外則臣庶臣珝也宴既畢遂
以是日入院而六館諸司及列
郡應試之士凡二千八百有竒

===
導臣震臣文榦臣碩臣衡皆禮聘
至自外郡監試官監察御史臣
瀛臣祺皆遴選至自内臺其他
百執事亦皆慎簡以充而提調
内外則臣廉臣翊也宴既畢遂
以是日入院而六館諸司及列
郡應試之士凡二千八百有奇
punctuated: 朝廷所以待天下賢才，賢賢之道也。隨時緩急，一惟上命，乃輟所謂纂修者，即以求賢爲重事。翌日，遂與臣龍進辭于廷，退宴于府。時同考試官學正臣大綱、臣大章、臣慈，教諭臣棠、臣嶽，訓導臣震、臣文榦、臣碩、臣衝，皆禮聘至自外郡；監試官監察御史臣瀛、臣祺，皆遴選至自内臺。其他百執事亦皆慎簡以充，而提調内外則臣庶、臣珝也。宴既畢，遂以是日入院，而六館諸司及列郡應試之士，凡二千八百有竒。
translation_en:
…is the court’s means of treating the worthy and talented throughout the realm—the way of honoring the worthy. As circumstances dictated the relative urgency of affairs, I followed solely His Majesty’s command. I therefore suspended the compilation mentioned above and made the search for worthy men my chief responsibility. The following day, your servant Long and I took our leave at court, then withdrew to a banquet at the prefectural offices.

At that time, the Associate Examiners—Confucian School Instructors Dagang, Dazhang, and Ci; County School Instructors Tang and Yue; and Assistant Instructors Zhen, Wen’gan, Shuo, and Chong, all servants of the throne—had arrived from outlying prefectures in response to formal invitations. The examination monitors, Investigating Censors Ying and Qi, likewise servants of the throne, had been selected and had arrived from the Censorate. All the other functionaries were also carefully selected to fill their posts. The Proctors responsible for affairs inside and outside the examination compound were your servants Shu and Xu.

When the banquet ended, we entered the examination compound that same day. The candidates from the Six Halls of the Directorate of Education, the various government offices, and the several prefectures numbered more than two thousand eight hundred…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
乃如故事三試之爰拔其尤得
百三十五人因錄其氏名幷文
之純者爲錄以
獻臣以職事宜爲序竊惟人才之
在天下其出而爲
國家用者類非一途然以
今日論之孰有重於科目者乎而
===

士與士之試于有司皆有不能

深則其造理有到與否其造理
有到與否則其措辭有高與下
文也者主乎理而達之辭者也
臣濫竽校文之任乃於

translation_en: …Then, following established practice, we examined them in three sessions and selected the most outstanding, obtaining 135 men. We accordingly recorded their names and compiled their finest compositions into a record for presentation to the throne. By virtue of my official duties, it falls to me, your servant, to write the preface. I humbly reflect that talented men throughout the realm enter the service of the state through more than one avenue. Yet, speaking of the present day, what avenue carries greater weight than the civil-service examinations? And what the examinations select is, indeed, judged through writing alone. Thus, both the officials who examine candidates and the candidates examined by those officials necessarily work within this framework. Yet men's learning may be shallow or profound, and accordingly their apprehension of principle may or may not be complete; according to whether their apprehension of principle is complete, their expression will be superior or inferior. Writing takes principle as its foundation and conveys it through words. I, your servant, unworthily entrusted with the task of evaluating compositions, thereupon, among …

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
京畿諸士之文得徧閱焉斐然成
章若皆有辭悠然趣味若皆有
理盖視天下為尤盛焉尤盛則
取之宜過於多而限於
制額則有弗得而盡然者亦惟窮
日夜殫心力務求其所謂高與
下者而甄别之其取其去一循
===
至公而不敢少以己意參焉以
仰副我
皇上求士之意此臣思竭駑鈍以求
逭其責者也雖然以文取士
朝廷立法然耳士之取重天下者
獨文乎哉昔孔子教人必兼文
行至論文學亦必以德行先之

章若皆有辭悠然趣味若皆有
理葢視天下爲尤盛焉尤盛則
取之宜過於多而限於
制額則有弗得而盡然者亦惟竊
日夜殫心力務求其所謂高與
下者而甄別之其取其去一循
至公而不敢少以己意參焉以
===
仰副我
皇上求士之意此臣思竭駑鈍以求
逭其責者也雖然以文取士
朝廷立法然耳士之取重天下者
獨文乎哉昔孔子教人必兼文
行至論文學亦必以德行先之
punctuated:
京畿諸士之文，得徧閱焉。斐然成章，若皆有辭；悠然趣味，若皆有理。盖視天下為尤盛焉。尤盛，則取之宜過於多，而限於制額，則有弗得而盡然者。亦惟窮日夜，殫心力，務求其所謂高與下者而甄别之。其取其去，一循至公，而不敢少以己意參焉，以仰副我皇上求士之意。此臣思竭駑鈍以求逭其責者也。
雖然，以文取士，朝廷立法然耳。士之取重天下者，獨文乎哉？昔孔子教人，必兼文行；至論文學，亦必以德行先之。
translation_en:
…I was able to read all the writings of the candidates from the metropolitan region. Their compositions were elegantly patterned, seemingly all possessing literary accomplishment; their lingering resonance and interest suggested that all possessed sound principle. Compared with those throughout the realm, these were exceptionally fine. Given such excellence, one ought to select an especially large number; yet the prescribed quota prevented this from being fully realized. I could only work day and night, exhausting my mental energies, striving to discern their relative merits and distinguish among them. In accepting or rejecting them, I followed complete impartiality, not daring to introduce the slightest personal preference, so as to fulfill His Majesty’s intention in seeking worthy men. In this way, your servant sought to exhaust his meager abilities and escape blame for failing in his duty.
Nevertheless, selecting men through their writing is simply the procedure established by the court. Is writing alone what earns a scholar the esteem of the realm? In former times, when Confucius taught others, he invariably combined literary learning with moral conduct. Even when discussing literary learning, he invariably placed virtue and conduct before it.

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖門所重盖如此諸士今以文
見録矣又將進而角天下士奉
廷對服官序寔自兹始盍使文行
彬彬實與華稱于以建偉績揚
休光蔚然成一代名臣而為天
下所取重乎夫是意也
朝廷所望於天下士者皆然況諸
===
===
士秀出
京畿固宜先天下而興者而可弗
知所重耶且臣輟纂修至此凡
以為
國家求賢也求而得人果如前所
云者則臣與有榮焉否則與有
愧焉臣用是懼乃敢輒附鄙意
alt_text:
聖門所重盖如此諸士今以文
見録矣又將進而角天下士奉
廷對服官序宦自茲始盍使文行
彬彬實與華稱于以建偉績揚
休光蔚然成一代名臣而爲天
下所取重乎夫是意也
朝廷所望於天下士者皆然况諸
===
京畿圖宦先天下而興者而可弗
知所重耶且臣輟纂修至此凡
士秀出
以爲
國家求賢也求而得人果如前所
云者則臣與有榮焉否則與有
愧焉臣用是懼乃敢輒附鄙意
punctuated: 聖門所重盖如此。諸士今以文見録矣，又將進而角天下士，奉廷對，服官序，寔自兹始。盍使文行彬彬，實與華稱，于以建偉績，揚休光，蔚然成一代名臣，而為天下所取重乎？夫是意也，朝廷所望於天下士者皆然，況諸士秀出京畿，固宜先天下而興者，而可弗知所重耶？且臣輟纂修至此，凡以為國家求賢也。求而得人，果如前所云者，則臣與有榮焉；否則與有愧焉。臣用是懼，乃敢輒附鄙意
translation_en:
…Such, indeed, were the priorities of the Sage’s school. You gentlemen have now been selected for your literary accomplishments. You will go on to compete with scholars from throughout the realm, respond to questions at court, and enter the ranks of official service: all this truly begins here. Why not bring your literary accomplishments and conduct into harmonious balance, making your substance match your outward refinement, so that you may achieve great deeds, spread your illustrious reputation, and rise to distinction as renowned ministers of your age, esteemed by all under Heaven? Such is what the court expects of scholars throughout the realm. How much more does this apply to you gentlemen, outstanding talents from the capital region, who surely ought to lead the realm in rising to the occasion! Can you fail to recognize what should be held most important?

Moreover, your servant suspended his compilation duties to come here solely to seek worthy men for the state. If those whom I seek and select indeed prove to be such men as I have described above, then I too shall share in their honor; otherwise, I shall share in their shame. This is what your servant fears, and thus I venture to append my humble thoughts…

翰林院侍講學士、奉訓大夫吳一鵬謹序。
translation_en:
…at the end, hoping to strive toward this together with the scholars of the metropolitan region, and also thereby to encourage scholars throughout the realm. This is indeed the sincerity of your servant’s humble, constant resolve to repay imperial favor.

Preface respectfully composed by Wu Yipeng, Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Instruction.

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
十室之邑必有忠信如丘者焉不如丘之
好學也
可以贊天地之化育則可以與天地參矣
夫君子所過者化所存者神上下與天地
同流豈曰小補之哉
易
謙亨天道下濟而光明地道卑而上行天
===
道虧盈而益謙地道變盈而流謙鬼神
害盈而福謙人道惡盈而好謙謙尊而
光卑而不可踰君子之終也
初九利用爲大作元吉无咎
是故天生神物聖人則之
人謀鬼謀百姓與能
書
同寅協恭和衷哉
從諫弗咈先民時若

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書
十室之邑，必有忠信如丘者焉，不如丘之好學也。
可以贊天地之化育，則可以與天地參矣。
夫君子所過者化，所存者神，上下與天地同流，豈曰小補之哉？

易
謙，亨。天道下濟而光明，地道卑而上行。天道虧盈而益謙，地道變盈而流謙，鬼神害盈而福謙，人道惡盈而好謙。謙，尊而光，卑而不可踰，君子之終也。
初九，利用爲大作，元吉，无咎。
是故天生神物，聖人則之。
人謀鬼謀，百姓與能。

書
同寅協恭，和衷哉！
從諫弗咈，先民時若。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books
“In a settlement of ten households, there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as I, Qiu, but none who equals my love of learning.”
“If one can assist the transforming and nourishing processes of Heaven and Earth, one can then stand alongside Heaven and Earth as a third.”
“Wherever the gentleman passes, people are transformed; wherever he abides, his influence is numinous. Above and below, he flows together with Heaven and Earth. How could one say that he offers only a small benefit?”

Book of Changes
“Modesty brings success. The Way of Heaven reaches downward, bringing light and clarity; the Way of Earth lies low, yet moves upward. The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and augments the modest; the Way of Earth alters the full and flows toward the lowly. Ghosts and spirits harm the full and bless the modest; the way of human beings is to dislike the full and favor the modest. Through modesty, those in high positions shine, while those in low positions cannot be surpassed. This is the gentleman’s ultimate attainment.”
“Initial Nine: It is favorable to undertake great works. Supreme good fortune; no blame.”
“Thus Heaven produces numinous objects, and the sages take them as models.”
“People deliberate, spirits deliberate, and the common people share in their efficacy.”

Book of Documents
“Be united in reverence and cooperative in respect, harmonious in your hearts!”
“Follow remonstrance without resisting it, and conform to the worthy men of old.”

不顯不承，無射於人斯。

春秋
蕭叔朝公。莊公二十三年。大夫宗婦覿，用幣。莊公二十四年。

在當時可知已抑可得而聞其槩乎往

punctuated:
曉然知臣虜之爲非，而遂奉我聖祖爲中國主。嗚呼，大哉皇言！何其感應神速若是哉！今去之百五十年，而中原父老尚有能莊誦而弗忘者，則在當時可知已。抑可得而聞其槩乎？往時漢伐秦，唐伐隋，宋受周禪，皆號以治易亂，然未聞檄諭天下者，何也？豈亦有之而今不傳乎？抑有不待於檄諭也？竊觀是檄所載，雖爲諭告一時臣民而發，要之帝王治天下之道，實不外此。我聖祖匪徒言之，實允蹈之，固以之定天下、訓萬世矣。豈非聖子神孫所當世世欽承而傳之無疆者乎？夫堯言萬世如見，而所謂燕薊者，即今京畿地也。諸生生長於斯，游歌於斯，諒必稔聞之矣。其敬述以對。

問：聖賢之道，措之而爲政事，發之而爲文章，未嘗無所本也。先儒有謂禮樂政事
translation_en:
…clearly understood that it was wrong to serve as subjects of the barbarians, and consequently acclaimed our sagely ancestor as ruler of China. Ah, how great were these imperial words! How could they have elicited so wondrously swift a response? Now, a hundred and fifty years later, there are still elders in the Central Plain who can solemnly recite them without forgetting; from this we may infer their effect at the time. Might we hear an account of their main purport? In former times, the Han attacked the Qin, the Tang attacked the Sui, and the Song received the Zhou’s abdication. All claimed to replace disorder with good government, yet we hear of no proclamations issued to instruct all under Heaven. Why is this? Were there such proclamations, but they have not survived? Or did those undertakings have no need of proclamations?

On examining the contents of this proclamation, we find that, although it was issued to instruct the subjects of that particular time, the essentials of the way emperors and kings govern all under Heaven are indeed encompassed within it. Our sagely ancestor did not merely speak these words: he truly put them into practice, using them to bring peace to all under Heaven and instruct ten thousand generations. Surely this is something his sagely sons and divine grandsons should reverently uphold, generation after generation, and transmit without end? The words of Yao remain vividly present through ten thousand generations, and the places called Yan and Ji are precisely the region surrounding the capital today. You students were born and raised here, and here you have wandered and sung in your studies; surely you must have heard these words often and know them well. Reverently recount them in your response.

Question: The Way of the sages and worthies, when put into practice, becomes affairs of government; when expressed in words, it becomes literary composition. Neither has ever been without a foundation. One earlier Confucian scholar said that rites, music, and affairs of government…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不可不出于一有謂文章道德不可使
出於二其亦各有所見乎三代之後世
未嘗無禮樂也何以謂之虛名禮樂不
可斯須去身而謂百年而後興者無乃
迂與諸葛亮治蜀汲汲以興復為事他
固未遑及也曰孔明庶幾禮樂其旨安
在漢有君嘗擬作大章矣所以任之者
果后夔其人乎唐有君嘗欲行周禮矣
其為輔相者果周公其人乎其治效竟
===
何如也六經之後世未嘗無文章也何
以謂之無益有德者必有言而謂文章
與時高下不亦遠與揚子雲於漢每每
以詞賦為工餘尚有可議也曰揚雄庶
幾於道其意何居唐有儒稱其師以為
得周公孔子之趣可矣而因文見道何
以猶有譏乎宋有儒贊其師以為得文
王孔子之傳似矣而終身行事何以尚
有病乎其議論果孰是也請詳著于篇

以繼有譏乎宋有儒贊其師以為得文
王孔子之傳似矣而終身行事何以尚
有病乎其議論果孰是也請詳著于篇
punctuated: 不可不出于一，有謂文章道德不可使出於二，其亦各有所見乎？三代之後，世未嘗無禮樂也，何以謂之虛名？禮樂不可斯須去身，而謂百年而後興者，無乃迂與？諸葛亮治蜀，汲汲以興復為事，他固未遑及也，曰「孔明庶幾禮樂」，其旨安在？漢有君嘗擬作大章矣，所以任之者，果后夔其人乎？唐有君嘗欲行周禮矣，其為輔相者，果周公其人乎？其治效竟何如也？六經之後，世未嘗無文章也，何以謂之無益？有德者必有言，而謂文章與時高下，不亦遠與？揚子雲於漢，每每以詞賦為工，餘尚有可議也，曰「揚雄庶幾於道」，其意何居？唐有儒稱其師，以為得周公孔子之趣可矣，而因文見道，何以猶有譏乎？宋有儒贊其師，以為得文王孔子之傳似矣，而終身行事，何以尚有病乎？其議論果孰是也？請詳著于篇。
translation_en:
…must issue from a single source. Another has said that literary writing and moral virtue must not be allowed to issue from two separate sources. Did each have particular insights? After the Three Dynasties, the world was never without rites and music; why, then, were they called empty names? Rites and music cannot be absent from one's person even for a moment; is it not far-fetched to say that they flourish only after a hundred years? When Zhuge Liang governed Shu, he devoted himself urgently to restoring the dynasty and indeed had no leisure to attend to other matters. Yet it was said, “Kongming came close to realizing rites and music.” Wherein lies the purport of this statement? A ruler of the Han once proposed to compose the Dazhang music. Was the person entrusted with it truly a Hou Kui? A ruler of the Tang once wished to put the Rites of Zhou into practice. Were those serving as his chief ministers truly men like the Duke of Zhou? What, ultimately, were the results of their government?

After the Six Classics, the world was never without literary writing; why, then, was it called useless? Those who possess virtue necessarily have something to say; is not the claim that literary writing rises and falls with the times far removed from this? Yang Ziyun of the Han repeatedly displayed his skill in verse and rhapsodies, while other aspects of his conduct remained open to criticism. Yet it was said, “Yang Xiong came close to the Way.” What was meant by this? A Confucian scholar of the Tang praised his teacher: it may be acceptable to say that he grasped the purport of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, but why was the claim that the Way could be discerned through his writing still criticized? A Confucian scholar of the Song extolled his teacher: it may seem plausible to say that he received the tradition of King Wen and Confucius, but why did his conduct throughout his life still invite criticism? Which of these judgments is actually correct? Please set out your views in detail in your essay.

軍細柳至遏乘輿然後令行而稱之為
===
真将軍者有輔相中興識兵畧達時令
而稱之為真漢相者有出刺豫州舉阿
縱隋政事而稱之為真刺史者有當國
儲之議立而不以利怵威懼存諸心而
稱之為真社稷臣者有因故主之歸欵
而不表獻其土地以求利而稱之為真
純臣者有議事延英破太平可樂之諛
辭而稱之為真宰相者有奉使雲中全
不辱命之節操而稱之為真忠臣者

觀所以潤身而及物者
問孔子謂君子疾沒世而名不稱孟子又
謂聲聞過情君子所恥則名固君子所
尚而亦不可無實盜名也以天下後世
公論難掩故也簡冊所載私相稱謂者
多矣姑舉其一二相類者試以問焉有
當春秋末軼讐襄子至擊其衣然後爲
快而稱之爲真義士者有當漢文時屯
軍細柳至過乘輿然後令行而稱之爲
===
真將軍者有輔相中興識兵畧達時令
而稱之爲真漢相者有出刺豫州舉阿
縱情政事而稱之爲真刺史者有當國
儲之議立而不以利怵威懼存諸心而
稱之爲真社稷臣者有因故主之歸款
而不表獻其土地以求利而稱之爲真
純臣者有議事延英破太平可樂之諛
辭而稱之爲真宰相者有奉使雲中全
持臣衔命之節操而稱之爲真忠臣者
punctuated:
觀所以潤身而及物者。

問：孔子謂君子疾沒世而名不稱，孟子又謂聲聞過情，君子所耻，則名固君子所尚，而亦不可無實盜名，正以天下後世公論難掩故也。簡冊所載，私相稱謂者多矣。姑舉其一二相類者，試以問焉。有當春秋末，報讐襄子，至擊其衣，然後為快，而稱之為真義士者；有當漢文時，屯軍細柳，至遏乘輿，然後令行，而稱之為真将軍者；有輔相中興，識兵畧、達時令，而稱之為真漢相者；有出刺豫州，舉阿縱隋政事，而稱之為真刺史者；有當國儲之議立，而不以利怵、威懼存諸心，而稱之為真社稷臣者；有因故主之歸欵，而不表獻其土地以求利，而稱之為真純臣者；有議事延英，破太平可樂之諛辭，而稱之為真宰相者；有奉使雲中，全不辱命之節操，而稱之為真忠臣者；
translation_en:
…to see how they cultivate their own persons and extend their influence to others.

Question: Confucius said that the gentleman is troubled lest his name go unmentioned after his death. Mencius also said that a reputation exceeding the reality is something a gentleman finds shameful. Thus, although reputation is indeed prized by the gentleman, he must not steal a name for himself without the substance to support it, precisely because the public judgment of the world and of later generations is difficult to suppress. The historical records contain many instances of people bestowing such descriptions upon one another in a private capacity. Let us select a few comparable instances and put them to you as a question.

There was one who, at the end of the Spring and Autumn period, sought vengeance against Xiangzi and was satisfied only after striking his clothing; he was called a true man of righteousness. There was one who, in the time of Emperor Wen of Han, stationed his army at Xiliu and enforced his orders even to the point of halting the imperial carriage; he was called a true general. There was one who assisted the restoration of the dynasty as chief minister, understood military strategy, and was versed in the ordinances governing seasonal activities; he was called a true Han chancellor. There was one who went out to serve as Regional Inspector of Yuzhou and conducted affairs of government [the phrase 舉阿縱隋 is unclear]; he was called a true Regional Inspector. There was one who, when the establishment of an heir apparent was being debated, allowed neither the temptation of advantage nor fear of coercion to enter his heart; he was called a true minister of the altars of soil and grain. There was one who, upon his former ruler’s submission, did not seek advantage by presenting a memorial offering up that ruler’s territory; he was called a truly pure minister. There was one who, while discussing affairs in Yanying Hall, refuted the flattering claim that peace prevailed and could simply be enjoyed; he was called a true chief minister. There was one who, sent on a mission to Yunzhong, preserved his integrity by bringing no dishonor upon his commission; he was called a truly loyal minister…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
有身居宰輔論事有先見而稱之爲真
聖人者有身任言責直聲動四方而稱
之爲真御史者有建儲草詔筆不輕下
而稱之爲真學士者有經筵進講一時
聳聽而稱之爲真侍講者有三人貢獻
不市上恩而總稱之爲真良吏者有一
人竒偉見重於時而兼稱之爲真宰相
真男子者凡此皆君子美稱或出於一
時之褒嘉或得之後世之追論而真之
===
===
爲言又非形似彷彿之謂以今觀之信
乎其難也已抑不知之數人者果足以
當是名而無愧歟抑有名浮其實者存
其間也願明以告我且觀尚友之志毋
諉之曰不暇
問夫人幼而學之壯而欲行之此古今不
易之理也三代以上其人之見于事功
澤被當時芳流後世者未有不本於學
術漢以来乃有不盡然者姑舉數子相
alt_text:
有身居宰輔論事有先見而稱之爲眞
聖人者有身任言責直聲動四方而稱
之爲眞御史者有建儲草詔筆不輕下
而稱之爲眞學士者有經筵進講一時
聳聽而稱之爲眞侍講者有三人貢獻
不市上恩而總稱之爲眞良吏者有一
人奇偉見重於時而兼稱之爲眞宰相
眞男子者凡此皆君子美稱或出於一
時之褒嘉或得之後世之追論而眞之
===
爲言又非形似彷彿之謂以今觀之信
乎其難也已抑不知之數人者果足以
當是名而無愧歟抑有名浮其實者存
其間也願明以告我且觀尚友之志毋
諉之曰不暇
問夫人幼而學之壯而欲行之此古今不
易之理也三代以上其人之見于事功
澤被當時芳流後世者夲有不本於學
術漢以来乃有不盡然者姑舉數子相
punctuated:
有身居宰輔，論事有先見，而稱之爲真聖人者；有身任言責，直聲動四方，而稱之爲真御史者；有建儲草詔，筆不輕下，而稱之爲真學士者；有經筵進講，一時聳聽，而稱之爲真侍講者；有三人貢獻，不市上恩，而總稱之爲真良吏者；有一人竒偉，見重於時，而兼稱之爲真宰相、真男子者。凡此皆君子美稱，或出於一時之褒嘉，或得之後世之追論，而真之爲言，又非形似彷彿之謂。以今觀之，信乎其難也已！抑不知之數人者，果足以當是名而無愧歟？抑有名浮其實者存其間也？願明以告我，且觀尚友之志，毋諉之曰不暇。

問：夫人幼而學之，壯而欲行之，此古今不易之理也。三代以上，其人之見于事功，澤被當時，芳流後世者，未有不本於學術。漢以来，乃有不盡然者。姑舉數子相
translation_en:
There was one who occupied the highest ministerial office and showed foresight in discussing affairs, and was called a true sage; one entrusted with the duty of remonstrance whose reputation for forthrightness resounded throughout the realm, and who was called a true censor; one who, when drafting an edict establishing the heir apparent, would not lightly set brush to paper, and was called a true academician; one whose exposition at the Classics Colloquium commanded the attention of all present, and who was called a true expositor-in-waiting; three who presented tribute without seeking to purchase the sovereign’s favor, and who were collectively called truly good officials; and one whose extraordinary qualities won the esteem of his contemporaries, and who was called both a true chief minister and a true man. All these are laudatory designations for exemplary men. Some arose from praise bestowed in their own time; others were acquired through the retrospective judgments of later generations. Yet the word “true” does not signify merely an outward resemblance or approximation. Looking at it now, how difficult indeed it is to merit such a designation! But I wonder whether these men really deserved these names without shame, or whether some among them possessed reputations exceeding their actual merits. Please explain this clearly to me, so that I may also see your aspiration to befriend the worthy of antiquity. Do not excuse yourself by saying that you have no time.

Question: People study when young and wish to put their learning into practice when mature: this is a principle unchanged from antiquity to the present. During the Three Dynasties and earlier, those who distinguished themselves through practical achievements, whose beneficence reached their contemporaries and whose good name endured in later generations, invariably grounded their accomplishments in learning. Since the Han, however, this has not always been so. Let us provisionally take several men and together …

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
與論其世可乎重厚少文者木強之人
耳何以能副大事之屬卒建社稷之功
不學無術者匹夫之類耳何以能受託
孤之詔以成伊周之業或謂其人之似
光而顛沛之中飲博自如摧強敵於談
笑之頃或謂其人之似勃而危疑之際
不動聲色措國家於泰山之安不知其
為學術者果亦各有所類故其設施若
合符節抑其天資偶合有不在於學術
===
耶或謂之有儒者氣象或謂之非知學
不能當時未見其果何所學而為帝師
為謀臣其建立卓然為一代之冠而明
經對策立談封侯者顧曲學阿世無救
於海内虛耗之弊有其學止於論語一
部者有以論語終身誦之者當時未聞
其别有所學而任天下之重得大臣之
體其相業炳然非後世可及而博學強
記致位宰輔者乃變亂成法使天下喪

為學術者果亦各有所類故其設施若
合符節抑其天資偶合有不在於學術
===

不能當時未見其果何所學而為帝師
為謀臣其建立卓然為一代之冠而明
經對策立談封侯者顧曲學阿世無救
於海內虛耗之弊有其學止於論語一
部者有以論語終身誦之者當時未聞
其別有所學而任天下之重得大臣之
體其相業炳然非後世可及而博學強
記致位宰輔者乃變亂成法使天下與
punctuated: 與論其世，可乎？重厚少文者，木強之人耳，何以能副大事之屬，卒建社稷之功？不學無術者，匹夫之類耳，何以能受託孤之詔，以成伊周之業？或謂其人之似光，而顛沛之中飲博自如，摧強敵於談笑之頃；或謂其人之似勃，而危疑之際不動聲色，措國家於泰山之安。不知其為學術者，果亦各有所類，故其設施若合符節，抑其天資偶合，有不在於學術耶？或謂之有儒者氣象，或謂之非知學不能，當時未見其果何所學，而為帝師，為謀臣，其建立卓然，為一代之冠。而明經對策、立談封侯者，顧曲學阿世，無救於海内虛耗之弊。有其學止於《論語》一部者，有以《論語》終身誦之者，當時未聞其别有所學，而任天下之重，得大臣之體，其相業炳然，非後世可及。而博學強記、致位宰輔者，乃變亂成法，使天下喪
translation_en:
…and discuss the age in which they lived together—may we do so? A man who was grave and dignified but little versed in letters was merely a blunt, unbending fellow; how could he fulfill the great charge entrusted to him and ultimately render meritorious service to the state? A man without learning or scholarly method was merely an ordinary fellow; how could he receive an imperial edict entrusting an orphaned ruler to his care and accomplish deeds like those of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou? One man was said to resemble Guang, yet amid adversity he drank and gambled as freely as ever, crushing powerful enemies in the space of a laughing conversation. Another was said to resemble Bo, yet amid danger and uncertainty he betrayed nothing in his voice or expression, making the state as secure as Mount Tai. Did their learning indeed resemble that of their respective counterparts, so that their measures matched like the two halves of a tally? Or did their natural endowments happen to coincide, independently of learning?

One was said to possess the bearing of a Confucian scholar; of another it was said that without understanding learning he could not have achieved what he did. At the time, it was not apparent what they had actually studied, yet they became a teacher to the emperor and a counseling minister, their outstanding achievements foremost in their age. Yet one who mastered the Classics and answered policy questions, gaining enfeoffment as a marquis through a single conversation, instead distorted learning to curry favor with his age and did nothing to remedy the depletion and exhaustion of the realm. There was one whose learning extended only to the single book of the Analects, and another who recited the Analects throughout his life. At the time, no one heard that they had studied anything else, yet they shouldered responsibility for all under Heaven and embodied the proper bearing of great ministers. Their achievements as chief ministers shone brilliantly, beyond the reach of later generations. Yet one whose extensive learning and powerful memory brought him to the position of chief minister proceeded to disrupt established institutions and caused all under Heaven to lose…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其樂生之心豈其學有所得固不在於
徒博抑學術有邪正而見諸躬行者自
有所不能揜乎試爲我言之
問天下親民之職大而藩臬小而郡縣皆
是也誠得其人則民受其福不得其人
則民受其殃而天下治忽繫之盖其職
不可不慎擇如此顧民事浩繁類非一
人可獨治者故其下各有僚属以分理
之必其彼此得人之盛然後力同心協
===
事克有濟否則掣肘相妨下石相擠其
不僨厥事者幾希宋儒西山真文忠公
有見於此故其帥長沙時嘗具咨目示
其僚属謂欲各以四事自勉而爲民去
其十害其意至矣所謂四事十害者亦
可得而聞乎豈其間亦有先後乎古之
良吏如龔黄卓魯之流號稱善治民者
其亦用此道乎抑外此别有他道也方
今任藩臬郡縣者多出科目之英

不僨厥事者幾希宋儒西山真文忠公
有見於此故其帥長沙時嘗具咨目示

良吏如龔黄卓魯之流號稱善治民者
其亦用此道乎抑外此别有他道也方
今任藩臬郡縣者多出科目之英
punctuated:
其樂生之心。豈其學有所得，固不在於徒博？抑學術有邪正，而見諸躬行者，自有所不能揜乎？試爲我言之。

問：天下親民之職，大而藩臬，小而郡縣，皆是也。誠得其人，則民受其福；不得其人，則民受其殃，而天下治忽繫之。盖其職不可不慎擇如此。顧民事浩繁，類非一人可獨治者，故其下各有僚属以分理之。必其彼此得人之盛，然後力同心協，事克有濟。否則掣肘相妨，下石相擠，其不僨厥事者幾希。宋儒西山真文忠公有見於此，故其帥長沙時，嘗具咨目示其僚属，謂欲各以四事自勉，而爲民去其十害，其意至矣。所謂四事十害者，亦可得而聞乎？豈其間亦有先後乎？古之良吏，如龔、黄、卓、魯之流，號稱善治民者，其亦用此道乎？抑外此别有他道也？方今任藩臬郡縣者，多出科目之英
translation_en:
…their joy in living. Could it be that what these men gained through learning did not depend upon mere breadth of knowledge? Or is it that learning has deviant and orthodox forms, whose manifestations in personal conduct inevitably reveal what cannot be concealed? Explain this for me.

Question: Offices directly concerned with governing the people range from provincial administration and surveillance commissions at the higher level to prefectures and counties at the lower. If truly suitable men are appointed, the people receive blessings; if unsuitable men are appointed, the people suffer calamities. The order or disorder of the realm depends upon this. Such is the care required in selecting men for these offices. Yet the people's affairs are so numerous and complex that, generally, no single person can manage them alone. Hence each official has subordinate staff to share their administration. Only when suitable men fill both the superior and subordinate positions can they unite their efforts and purposes and bring affairs to a successful conclusion. Otherwise, they obstruct and thwart one another, casting stones at those who have fallen and pushing one another aside; rarely will they avoid ruining their work.

The Song Confucian scholar Master Zhen, known as Xishan and posthumously honored as Wenzhong, perceived this. Thus, when governing Changsha, he once drew up written instructions for his subordinate staff, stating that he wished each to strive to fulfill four duties and to remove ten harms for the people. His intention was most admirable. May we hear what these four duties and ten harms were? Was there also an order of priority among them? Did the good officials of antiquity, such as Gong, Huang, Zhuo, and Lu, renowned for their skill in governing the people, also employ this method? Or did they have some other method beyond it? Today, those serving in provincial administration and surveillance commissions, prefectures, and counties are mostly drawn from the outstanding men of the examination system…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
朝廷所以責成斯民所以仰望最先且重其
有率其僚属勉四事去十害能心西山
之心者乎果有之則天下之治成矣此
當宁所欲聞者將於歲首述職公黜陟示勸懲
焉願一陳之以為
今日
聖政之助
alt_text:
朝廷所以責成斯民所以仰望㝡先且重其
有率其僚屬勉四事去十害能心西山
之心者乎果有之則天下之治成矣此
當宁所欲聞者將於歲首述職公黜陟示勸懲
焉願一陳之以爲
今日
聖政之助
punctuated: 朝廷所以責成、斯民所以仰望，最先且重。其有率其僚属勉四事、去十害，能心西山之心者乎？果有之，則天下之治成矣。此當宁所欲聞者。將於歲首述職，公黜陟，示勸懲焉。願一陳之，以為今日聖政之助。
translation_en: …The responsibilities the court entrusts to them and the hopes the people place in them are of the highest priority and greatest weight. Are there any who lead their subordinate officials in striving to fulfill the four commitments and eliminate the ten abuses, and who can take Xishan’s concerns as their own? If indeed there are, good government throughout the realm will be achieved. This is what the sovereign wishes to hear. At the beginning of the year, when officials report on their service, dismissals and promotions will be decided impartially, thereby encouraging the worthy and admonishing the unworthy. Please set forth your views fully, to assist the sage governance of the present day.

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
十室之邑必有忠信如丘者焉不如丘之
好學也
吕璋
同考試官訓導林批美質至道難易正在
十室好學上見作者體認不真往往信筆漫言姑取
成篇而已獨此篇能説出聖人勉人為學之意讀之
令人暢然信非穉筆可到也高薦何疑
===
同考試官教諭高批是題士子類能下筆
但詞多誇非聖人謙己誨人意理足文整且筆力老
健如此篇者其最優者歟宜刻以式來學
同考試官學正余批論語一題作者於十
室上類疊陳語於忠信上強析為對到不如處却涉
自誇便不似夫子口氣此篇能以典雅之詞講出夫
子謙人本意非平素潜心本領者不能故特錄之
考試官左中允劉批詞理俱到
考試官侍講學士吳批是善言聖人之言者

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“In a hamlet of ten households, there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as I, Qiu; but he will not equal my love of learning.”

Lü Zhang

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Assistant Instructor: The relative ease of possessing fine natural qualities and difficulty of attaining the highest Way are revealed precisely in the phrases “ten households” and “love of learning.” Writers fail to grasp this truly and often let their brushes wander into loose statements, seeking merely to complete an essay. This essay alone succeeds in expressing the sage’s intention to encourage others to learn. Reading it brings a sense of clarity and satisfaction; such an achievement is certainly beyond an immature writer. What doubt can there be about recommending it highly!

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor: Candidates generally manage to write on this topic, but their language is often boastful and fails to convey the sage’s intention of speaking humbly of himself and instructing others. An essay such as this, with ample reasoning, orderly composition, and a mature and vigorous style, must surely rank among the very best! It should be printed to serve as a model for future students.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Instructor: On this topic from the Analects, writers generally pile up stock phrases when discussing “ten households,” forcibly separate “loyalty” and “trustworthiness” to form a parallel pair, and, upon reaching “will not equal,” lapse into self-praise. They thus cease to sound like the Master. This essay uses refined and elegant language to bring out the Master’s original intention of speaking humbly to others [?]. This could not be achieved without a foundation in sustained, concentrated study; therefore it has been specially selected for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: Both expression and reasoning fully achieve their purpose.

Comment by Examiner Wu, Expositor-in-Waiting: Here is someone skilled at expressing the sage’s words.

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖人論人得乎美質也易聞乎至道也難盖美
質易得而好學以聞道則難也聖人即已而較
之人焉其勉人之意何至哉想其意若曰人當
以至道而自彊不可以美質而自恃如有恃焉
則去道遠矣彼十室之邑邑之小者也忠信之
質質之美者也丘非所謂忠信者歟試以其邑
言之一隅相望其地可謂狹矣然而篤實之資
毎特稟於其間者則誠聞之不可以其地之狹
而遂謂無是人也數家攸聚其人可謂少矣然
===
而敦朴之懿恒秀出於其地者則信有之不可
以其人之少而遂謂無是質也十室之邑豈不
有忠信如丘者乎有則有矣然如丘之好學者
則甚鮮焉誠以生質之美天之所以賦於人也
學問之功人之所以求乎道也丘豈敢有所恃
而倦於學耶盖吾慕道之心已定於忠信自得
之後故發憤忘食至於終日乾乾焉求以探義
理之精微者融而會之使與吾心而相孚盖庶
幾美質之不負耳彼十室之邑果有如丘之不

punctuated: 聖人論人，得乎美質也易，聞乎至道也難。盖美質易得，而好學以聞道則難也。聖人即已而較之人焉，其勉人之意何至哉！想其意若曰：人當以至道而自彊，不可以美質而自恃。如有恃焉，則去道遠矣。彼十室之邑，邑之小者也；忠信之質，質之美者也。丘非所謂忠信者歟？試以其邑言之，一隅相望，其地可謂狹矣。然而篤實之資，毎特稟於其間者，則誠聞之。不可以其地之狹，而遂謂無是人也。數家攸聚，其人可謂少矣。然而敦朴之懿，恒秀出於其地者，則信有之。不可以其人之少，而遂謂無是質也。十室之邑，豈不有忠信如丘者乎？有則有矣，然如丘之好學者，則甚鮮焉。誠以生質之美，天之所以賦於人也；學問之功，人之所以求乎道也。丘豈敢有所恃而倦於學耶？盖吾慕道之心，已定於忠信自得之後，故發憤忘食，至於終日乾乾焉。求以探義理之精微者，融而會之，使與吾心而相孚，盖庶幾美質之不負耳。彼十室之邑，果有如丘之不
translation_en:
In discussing people, the sage held that it is easy to possess fine natural qualities but difficult to hear the highest Way. For fine qualities are readily found, whereas loving learning so as to hear the Way is difficult. The sage took himself as a point of comparison with others: how profound was his intention to encourage them!

We may imagine his meaning as follows: People ought to strive to improve themselves in pursuit of the highest Way; they must not rely complacently upon fine natural qualities. If they do, they will be far from the Way. A settlement of ten households is a small settlement; dutifulness and trustworthiness are fine qualities. Am I, Qiu, not someone who may be called dutiful and trustworthy? Consider such a settlement: its households stand within sight of one another in a single corner, so its territory may indeed be called confined. Yet we certainly hear of people there who are exceptionally endowed with an earnest and sincere disposition. We cannot therefore say that no such people exist merely because its territory is confined. Only a few families gather there, so its population may indeed be called small. Yet people distinguished by the excellence of their simple honesty assuredly do emerge there. We cannot therefore say that no such qualities exist merely because its people are few. In a settlement of ten households, surely there are people as dutiful and trustworthy as I, Qiu? There certainly are; yet those who love learning as I do are exceedingly rare.

This is truly because the excellence of one's native disposition is what Heaven bestows upon people, while the work of learning is how people seek the Way. How would I, Qiu, dare rely complacently upon anything and grow weary of learning? Once dutifulness and trustworthiness had become my own, my heart was firmly set upon longing for the Way. Thus, in my determination, I forget to eat, exerting myself tirelessly throughout the day. I seek to probe the subtle depths of moral principle, integrating them into a comprehensive understanding and bringing them into accord with my heart. This is merely to hope that I may not fail the fine qualities with which I am endowed. In that settlement of ten households, is there really someone who, like Qiu, would not…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
敢自恃者乎求道之力倍加於吾心向慕之餘
故好古敏求至於惟日孜孜焉于以玩物理之
著見者研而精之使與吾身而爲一蓋庶幾至
道之可聞耳彼忠信之人抑有如丘之能知自
彊者乎學問在我我所當盡忠信在我我則不
知此丘之始與人同而終與人異也吁夫子言
此豈真矜己以誇人哉無非勉人爲學而欲其
同歸于道焉耳是即與人爲善之心歟嗟夫學
之於人大矣以夫子生知而亦未嘗不好學況
===
其他哉夫子嘗曰吾十有五而志於學又曰我
非生而知之者好古敏以求之者也其倦倦於
學如此豈非謙己誨人而欲人知所從事乎奈
之何人不知好學之爲務也噫學而不厭聖之
所以益聖困而不學愚之所以益愚然則有志
學道者其尚猛省夫子之言哉
可以贊天地之化育則可以與天地參矣

敢自恃者乎？求道之力，倍加於吾心向慕之餘，故好古敏求，至於惟日孜孜焉。于以玩物理之著見者，研而精之，使與吾身而爲一，蓋庶幾至道之可聞耳。彼忠信之人，抑有如丘之能知自彊者乎？學問在我，我所當盡；忠信在我，我則不知。此丘之始與人同，而終與人異也。吁！夫子言此，豈真矜己以誇人哉？無非勉人爲學，而欲其同歸于道焉耳。是即與人爲善之心歟？嗟夫！學之於人大矣！以夫子生知，而亦未嘗不好學，況其他哉？夫子嘗曰：「吾十有五而志於學。」又曰：「我非生而知之者，好古，敏以求之者也。」其倦倦於學如此，豈非謙己誨人，而欲人知所從事乎？奈之何人不知好學之爲務也？噫！學而不厭，聖之所以益聖；困而不學，愚之所以益愚。然則有志學道者，其尚猛省夫子之言哉！

可以贊天地之化育，則可以與天地參矣。

translation_en:
…dare to rely on themselves? My efforts to seek the Way are redoubled beyond my heart’s yearning for it. Thus I love antiquity and diligently seek understanding, applying myself tirelessly each day. I contemplate the manifest principles of things, investigating and refining my understanding of them until they become one with my person, hoping thereby to hear the ultimate Way. Among those loyal and trustworthy people, are there any who, like me, Qiu, know to exert themselves? Learning lies within my power, and I must pursue it to the utmost; as for the loyalty and trustworthiness within me, I take no account of them. This is how I, Qiu, begin like others but ultimately differ from them.

Ah! When the Master said this, was he truly vaunting himself to impress others? He was simply encouraging people to learn, wishing them all to arrive together at the Way. Is this not the heart that helps others to do good? Alas! How great is the importance of learning for human beings! Even the Master, who possessed knowledge from birth, never ceased to love learning; how much more should others! The Master once said, “At fifteen, I set my heart on learning.” He also said, “I am not one who was born with knowledge; I love antiquity and diligently seek it.” With such devotion to learning [?], was he not humbling himself to instruct others, wishing them to know where to direct their efforts? Why, then, do people fail to recognize loving learning as their task? Ah! Learning without weariness is how the sage becomes ever more sagely; encountering difficulty yet failing to learn is how the foolish become ever more foolish. Those resolved to study the Way should therefore earnestly awaken to the Master’s words!

“If one can assist the transforming and nurturing work of Heaven and Earth, one can then form a triad with Heaven and Earth.”

In their treatment of the two terms “forming a triad” and “assisting,” candidates in the examination mostly repeat conventional expressions and err by placing undue weight on one side. They do not understand that the respective activities of Heaven and humanity inherently have their own bounds. This script alone develops the meaning fully: its language is not redundant, yet its reasoning is complete. Its author has evidently gained insight from reading the Doctrine of the Mean. I submit that utmost sincerity can bring the work of cosmic creation to completion and stand alongside it in rank. Vast indeed is cosmic creation, and difficult it is to stand beside it! Yet if the achievement of utmost sincerity in fully realizing nature can assist the transforming and nourishing processes, what cause for misgiving can there be in joining Heaven and Earth to form a triad? Chapter twenty-two of the Doctrine of the Mean elucidates the Way of Heaven in this manner through the process of proceeding from sincerity to understanding. This means that when Heaven and Earth produce the sage, they invariably intend him to assist them; and in his relation to Heaven and Earth, the sage invariably embodies their purpose.

Thus, the nature possessed by human beings contains what Heaven and Earth endow them with to make them human. Human beings cannot fully realize it themselves. If there were no sage at this point, what would become of them? The nature possessed by things contains what Heaven and Earth endow them with to make them things. Things cannot fully realize it themselves. If there were no sage at this point, what would become of them? title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
道而後可以爲人則於化育乎人者不有以贊
而成之耶盡人之性且以盡物之性使之各遂
其生而後可以爲物則於化育乎物者不有以
贊而全之耶如是則其參天地也不亦宜乎何
則人非天地不生生人而賦之性固天地之分
也而盡人之性不與焉兹不在於聖人乎物非
天地不育育物而賦之性固天地之限也而盡
物之性不與焉兹可責之他人乎故天位乎上
地與之偶宜無復與倫矣而聖人贊之以成其
===
功是有天不可以無聖人也則聖人與天等爾
獨地乎哉地位乎下天與之對宜無復能肖矣
而聖人贊之以全其用是有地不可以無聖人
也則聖人與地均爾獨天乎哉謂之曰與天地
參信乎上則有天下則有地中則有聖人可以
並立而爲三也吁至誠盡性之功其大如此子
思言天道而有以及之其亦深達天人之妙者
歟考之禮其論參天地者不一而足有曰聖人
參於天地有曰天子與天地參有曰三王之德

獨地乎哉地位乎下天與之對宜無復能肖矣
而聖人贊之以全其用是有地不可以無聖人
也則聖人與地均爾獨天乎哉謂之曰與天地

思言天道而有以及之其亦深達天人之妙者

…the Way, and only then can they fully be human: does this not assist and bring to completion Heaven and Earth’s transformation and nurture of human beings? Having fully realized human nature, the sage also fully realizes the nature of other things, enabling each to fulfill its life and thus fully become what it is: does this not assist and bring to fulfillment Heaven and Earth’s transformation and nurture of things? If so, is it not fitting that the sage should form a triad with Heaven and Earth? Why is this? Without Heaven and Earth, human beings would not be born. To give birth to human beings and endow them with their nature is indeed the allotted task of Heaven and Earth; yet fully realizing human nature is not included in it. Does this not rest with the sage? Without Heaven and Earth, things would not be nurtured. To nurture things and endow them with their nature is indeed the limit of Heaven and Earth’s role; yet fully realizing the nature of things is not included in it. Can anyone else be charged with this responsibility? Thus Heaven occupies the position above, with Earth as its counterpart, and it would seem that nothing else could rank alongside it. Yet the sage assists it in completing its work. This means that, where there is Heaven, the sage cannot be dispensed with. The sage therefore stands equal to Heaven; is Earth alone its equal? Earth occupies the position below, with Heaven facing it, and it would seem that nothing else could match it. Yet the sage assists it in bringing its operation to fulfillment. This means that, where there is Earth, the sage cannot be dispensed with. The sage therefore stands equal to Earth; is Heaven alone its equal? How true it is to say that the sage forms a triad with Heaven and Earth! Above is Heaven, below is Earth, and between them is the sage: they can stand together as three.

Was he not one who deeply understood the subtle workings of Heaven and humanity? Examining the Book of Rites, we find more than one discussion of forming a triad with Heaven and Earth. translation_en:
…participate with Heaven and Earth. Here, however, he says: “Utmost sincerity participates with Heaven and Earth.” Although this expression occurs repeatedly, with a different referent each time, all these statements concern virtue and government. What is called virtue must reach its culmination in utmost sincerity and the full realization of one's nature; what is called government must reach its culmination in assisting the transforming and nourishing processes of Heaven and Earth. Thus, what makes the sage a sage can scarcely admit of any further addition, and the workings of Heaven and humanity are complete, lacking nothing. We can also discern, beyond the explicit words, the subtle truth that principle is one while its particular manifestations differ. Ah! Is this not what makes Zisi who he is!

“Wherever the gentleman passes, transformation follows; wherever he abides, his influence is numinous. Above and below, he flows together with Heaven and Earth. How could one call this a mere minor contribution?”
Wu Jing

Associate Examiner Chen, Assistant Instructor, comments: “Transformation wherever he passes and numinous influence wherever he abides both refer to the virtue and achievements of the true king. Writers generally manage to discuss transformation wherever he passes, but when they reach numinous influence wherever he abides, they fall far short in their understanding. This essay analyzes the matter clearly, and its force of writing adequately brings out the meaning. It should be recorded as a model.”

Associate Examiner Yu, Assistant Instructor, comments: “To flow together with Heaven and Earth, rather than merely make the minor contributions of a hegemon: this is precisely where the greatness of the kingly Way lies. Students generally discuss these phrases separately and praise them. This paper alone grasps this meaning, while its language and tone are spacious and unhurried, showing no traces of effort. It aptly portrays the greatness of the kingly Way. How could we fail to select it!”

Examiner Liu, Left Assistant Mentor, comments: “This, too, is an essay that discusses the kingly Way well.”

Examiner Wu, Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “It shows an intimate understanding of Zhu Xi's commentary.”

text:
大賢論王道有同於造化自異於覇功盖莫大
於造化也而王者之道與之同焉豈覇者可得
而並論哉孟子論王道之所以大者如此何則
君子者以德言則聖人以位言則王者也其道
若之何而大耶誠以身之所過特其一時經歷
云耳而人自無不化焉聲光所被而得於觀感
者幡然而自新足跡所加而得於見聞者翕然
以不變其所過者何如其化也心之所存特其
一念主宰云耳而神自不可測焉精神方爾運
===
用而彼之歌帝力者已自作而自息心思方爾
籌畫而彼之順帝則者即不識而不知其所存
者何如其神也如是則其德業可謂盛矣果將
何以擬之哉彼資始萬物而無所不覆天之於
物然也君子舉一世而甄陶之至大無外是即
天之物無不覆者矣上不與天之化而同運乎
資生萬物而無所不載地之於物然也君子舉
天下而陶鑄之至廣無垠是即地之物無不載
者矣下不與地之化而並行乎王道同於天地

translation_en:
The great worthy, in discussing the kingly Way, holds that it is like the creative transformations of nature and inherently different from the achievements of a hegemon. For nothing is greater than those creative transformations, and the Way of a true king accords with them. How could a hegemon possibly be discussed on equal terms? Such is Mengzi’s account of what makes the kingly Way great. Why is this so? The gentleman, considered in terms of virtue, is a sage; considered in terms of position, he is a king. In what way is his Way great?

Where his person passes is merely the place through which he happens to travel for a time, yet the people are all spontaneously transformed. Those reached by his voice and radiance, who gain something through observing him and being moved by him, turn about and renew themselves. Those reached by his footsteps, who gain something through seeing and hearing him, are united in remaining unchanged [?]. How transforming is his passage! What he holds within his mind is merely the governing intention of a single thought, yet its spiritual efficacy is unfathomable. Just as he puts his spiritual energies into operation, those who sing of the emperor’s power already work and rest of their own accord. Just as his mind devises its plans, those who follow the emperor’s standards do so without recognition or awareness. How spiritually efficacious is what he holds within! Thus his virtue and achievements may be called abundant indeed. With what, then, can they be compared?

To provide all things with their beginnings and leave nothing uncovered: such is Heaven’s relation to things. The gentleman takes an entire age and molds it, his greatness so complete that nothing lies outside it. This is precisely like Heaven’s leaving nothing uncovered. Above, does he not move in concert with Heaven’s transforming activity? To provide all things with life and leave nothing unsupported: such is Earth’s relation to things. The gentleman takes all under Heaven and molds and casts it, his breadth so complete that it has no bounds. This is precisely like Earth’s leaving nothing unsupported. Below, does he not proceed together with Earth’s transforming activity? The kingly Way accords with Heaven and Earth…

有如此者。視彼霸者之於其民，屑屑焉違道以干譽，煦煦焉徇情以市恩，要其所就，不過小小補塞其罅漏而已，豈可與同日而語耶？信乎，王道之大，非霸功所能彷彿其萬一也！孟子論王霸之殊，至此盖瞭然矣。大抵時至戰國，功利之說勝，而義理之學微。其肆為縱横捭闔者，日交騖於天下，抑孰知王道之當行哉？孟子慨然有志帝王之治，故每以尊王賤霸為言。惜乎時不能用，而世道竟不可復！然百世之下，吾人皆知王霸義利之辨，而治天下者尚有賴焉，其功不可誣也。君子謂其繼孔子而得道統之傳，觀此益信。

易

謙亨。天道下濟而光明，地道卑而上行。天道虧盈而益謙，地道變盈而流謙，鬼神害盈而福謙，人道惡盈而好謙。謙，尊而光，卑而不可踰，君子之終也。

劉鎮
translation_en:
…such is the way of the true king. Consider how a hegemon treats his people: fussily departing from the Way to seek praise, offering petty kindnesses and indulging their wishes to purchase their gratitude. In the end, his accomplishments amount merely to patching a few gaps and leaks. How could the two be spoken of in the same breath? Truly, so great is the kingly Way that a hegemon’s achievements cannot approximate even one ten-thousandth of it! At this point, Mencius’s discussion has surely made the distinction between true kings and hegemons clear.

By the Warring States period, doctrines of achievement and profit generally prevailed, while learning devoted to righteousness and moral principle had declined. Those who freely practiced the arts of diplomatic alliances and political manipulation daily competed throughout the realm. Who among them understood that the kingly Way ought to be put into practice? Deeply moved, Mencius aspired to the government of the ancient emperors and kings, and therefore repeatedly spoke of honoring true kings and disparaging hegemons. Alas, his age could not put his teachings into practice, and the proper order of the world was never restored! Yet a hundred generations later, we all understand the distinctions between true kings and hegemons, and between righteousness and profit; those who govern the realm still have his teachings to rely upon. His contribution cannot be denied. Learned gentlemen say that he succeeded Confucius and received the transmission of the lineage of the Way. Looking at this, we believe it all the more.

Book of Changes

“Modesty brings success. The Way of Heaven extends its aid downward and is radiant; the Way of Earth occupies a low position yet moves upward. The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and augments the modest; the Way of Earth transforms the full and lets its bounty flow to the modest. Spirits harm the full and bless the modest. The way of human beings is to dislike the full and favor the modest. Through modesty, those in honored positions shine, while those in lowly positions cannot be surpassed. This is the culmination attained by the gentleman.”

Liu Zhen 劉鎮

人之所行齟齬者多亨通者寡而何謙之得其
亨也曷不觀諸天地乎蓋輕清成象天本位於
上也重濁成形地本位於下也天以其氣下交
於地而其化育之功煥乎光明而不可掩地以
其職卑處乾後而其交感之氣勃然上行而不
可遏下與地交天之謙也而其道光明亨可見

同考試官訓導于批：「裒多益寡，稱物平施，謙之法也。此作蓋以此意施之筆下，所謂約能使侈，繁能不亂者，作手也。」
考試官左中允劉批：「迥出衆作。」
考試官侍講學士吳批：「勻整可誦。」
聖人傳彖，既明謙必有亨之義，復明謙必有終之義。蓋人之得亨與有其終，要必有所自也，而能謙者兼而有之，此君子所以貴於謙歟！昔文王繫謙曰：「亨，君子有終。」吾夫子彖傳釋之，蓋謂人之所行，齟齬者多，亨通者寡，而何謙之得其亨也？曷不觀諸天地乎？蓋輕清成象，天本位於上也；重濁成形，地本位於下也。天以其氣下交於地，而其化育之功煥乎光明而不可掩；地以其職卑處乾後，而其交感之氣勃然上行而不可遏。下與地交，天之謙也，而其道光明，亨可見
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Chen, an Instructor, comments: “The topic itself is easy to understand. But when one seeks to give matching treatments to the explanations of ‘success’ and ‘having a proper end,’ their lengths are difficult to balance, and writers are often hampered by this. This essay develops its ideas by following the text and is thoroughly orderly. It deserves inclusion.”
Associate Examiner Yu, an Instructor, comments: “‘Reduce what is excessive and augment what is deficient; weigh things and distribute impartially’: this is the method of modesty. This essay appears to apply that principle in its writing. Its author is an accomplished writer of the kind described as ‘able to make the concise expansive and the elaborate free of disorder.’”
Examiner Liu, Left Assistant Adviser, comments: “Far surpasses the other essays.”
Examiner Wu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Balanced and orderly, and worthy of recitation.”
In his Commentary on the Judgments, the Sage first elucidated why modesty must bring success and then elucidated why modesty must bring a proper end. For a person’s attaining success and reaching a proper end must surely have a source; one who can be modest possesses both. Is this why the noble man prizes modesty? In former times, King Wen appended to the hexagram Modesty the words: ‘Success. The noble man has a proper end.’ Our Master explained these in the Commentary on the Judgments. His meaning was that, in human undertakings, setbacks are many and successes few. Why, then, does modesty bring success? Why not look to Heaven and Earth? The light and clear form celestial images: Heaven’s original position is above. The heavy and turbid take material form: Earth’s original position is below. Heaven sends its vital energy downward to unite with Earth, and its work of transforming and nurturing shines with a brilliance that cannot be concealed. Earth, in fulfilling its office, humbly takes its place after Qian, the Creative, and its vital energy of reciprocal response rises vigorously and cannot be checked. To descend and unite with Earth is Heaven’s modesty; its Way is radiant, and its success can be seen…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
矣卑處乾後地之謙也而其道上行亨可知矣
謙必有亨盖如此夫莫難得者亨通也而天地
以謙得之况於人而可不謙哉若乃人之所行
有始者易克終者難又何謙之得其終也曷不
觀諸天地神人乎盖盈而滿者乃所以招損也
謙而虚者乃所以受益也天地之道其於盈者
既虧之變之矣而獨於謙則益且流焉鬼神與
人其於盈者既害之惡之矣而獨於謙則福且
好焉故君子以謙抑為尚而得於天人之所祐
===
則在尊位也徳盛而彌光始雖屈矣不有以伸
於後乎以盈滿為戒而不為天人之所廢則在
下位也徳崇而難及終則揚矣不由於初之抑
乎謙必有終盖如此夫莫難得者有終也而君
子以謙致之况衆人而可不謙哉吁聖人於釋
謙亨則若兩言而有餘於釋有終則又累言而
不足于以見謙固能亨而亨尤貴於有終也其
所以勸勉吾人者至矣抑文王周公繫卦與爻
惟謙占辭最美聖人傳彖與象亦惟謙賛辭為

translation_en:
… is thus apparent. To dwell humbly behind Qian, Heaven, is Earth's modesty; yet its Way moves upward, and its success can be understood. Such is the reason modesty must bring success. Nothing is harder to attain than success, yet Heaven and Earth attain it through modesty. How much less, then, can human beings dispense with modesty?

As for human conduct, making a beginning is easy, but carrying it through to the end is difficult. Why, then, does modesty enable one to attain a good end? Why not look to Heaven, Earth, spirits, and human beings? Fullness and self-satisfaction invite loss; modesty and emptiness allow one to receive benefit. In their operation, Heaven and Earth diminish and alter what is full, whereas they augment the modest and cause abundance to flow toward them. Spirits and human beings injure and dislike what is full, whereas they bless and favor the modest.

Thus the gentleman esteems modesty and self-restraint and receives the protection of Heaven and humankind. When he occupies an honored position, his virtue flourishes and shines ever more brightly. Though initially bent down, does he not thereby find scope to stand upright afterward? He guards against self-satisfaction and is therefore not cast aside by Heaven and humankind. When he occupies a lowly position, his virtue is lofty and difficult to equal. That he is exalted in the end—is this not due to his initial humility? Such is the reason modesty must bring a good end. Nothing is harder to attain than a good end, yet the gentleman achieves it through modesty. How much less, then, can ordinary people dispense with modesty?

Ah! When the Sage explains how modesty brings success, it seems that two statements more than suffice; when he explains how it brings a good end, even repeated statements seem insufficient. From this we see that modesty assuredly enables success, but that what is especially precious in success is bringing it to a good end. His encouragement and exhortation to us could go no further!

Moreover, when King Wen and the Duke of Zhou appended statements to the hexagrams and their lines, only those for Modesty were most auspicious in their prognostications. And when the Sage composed the Commentaries on the Judgments and the Images, likewise only for Modesty were his words of praise …

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
盛而獨異於他卦者何哉盖謙者人之美德而
天地神人之所與者悉萃於謙此謙之所以獨
異也夫以大禹之勤儉而猶不矜伐有周公之
才美而猶不敢驕其亨而有終者歟此其聖德
之盛所以垂諸天下後世愈久而愈光也嗚呼
休哉
是故天生神物聖人則之

盛，而獨異於他卦者何哉？盖謙者，人之美德，而天地神人之所與者悉萃於謙，此謙之所以獨異也。夫以大禹之勤儉，而猶不矜伐；有周公之才美，而猶不敢驕，其亨而有終者歟？此其聖德之盛，所以垂諸天下後世，愈久而愈光也。嗚呼，休哉！

考試官侍講學士吳批：「明健。」
translation_en:
…so abundant, uniquely distinguishing it from the other hexagrams—why is this? Humility is a fine human virtue, and everything approved by Heaven, Earth, spirits, and human beings gathers within it. This is what makes Humility unique. Even with his diligence and frugality, Yu the Great did not boast of his achievements; even with his gifts and excellence, the Duke of Zhou did not dare to be arrogant. Were these not men who prospered and brought matters to a successful conclusion? Such was the abundance of their sagely virtue that, transmitted throughout the world and to later generations, it shone ever more brightly as time passed. Ah, how splendid!

“Therefore Heaven produces numinous things, and the sages take them as models.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Assistant Instructor: “On this topic of milfoil and tortoise shells, the candidates in the examination compound have almost all followed worn-out formulas, making their essays tiresome to read. Some even speak only of milfoil. This essay alone remains true to the original meaning while offering fresh ideas and vigorous language. Its treatment of Heaven and humanity is nearly exhaustive. It deserves selection.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Assistant Instructor: “In discussing why milfoil and tortoise shells are numinous and why the sages take them as models, the writer draws fresh meanings from established interpretations throughout. His language bristles with incisiveness, setting him apart from others. At the end he further refutes the claim that milfoil divination is inferior and tortoise-shell divination superior, showing particular insight. In the Book of Changes examination section, how many fingers could one bend in counting papers like this?”

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Secretariat Rectifier: “The writing is subtle and nuanced, with much to savor.”

Comment by Examiner Wu, Academician Lecturer-in-Waiting: “Clear and vigorous.”

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
造化有以肇卜筮之器聖人因以立卜筮之法
盖天生蓍龜其爲物也神矣聖人從而則之豈
不立卜筮之法於天下哉大傳十一章專言卜
筮及此若曰易之爲易果何爲而作哉而蓍之
與龜則其所本之一也彼其植而爲衆卉之異
者爲蓍是蓍也天以生之而其莖長丈其叢滿
百以具圓神之德一天之和氣所融乎動而爲
介族之靈者爲龜是龜也天以生之而五行中
具八卦外列以含黙藏之智一天之禎祥所鍾
===
乎蓍生矣而豈偶然哉天將有意於立筮以前
斯民之用也龜生矣而豈徒然哉天將有意於
立卜以開斯人之先也於是聖人者出上明天
道而有以發造化之祕下察民故而有以通天
下之情則夫蓍也用之四十有九于以假分揲
掛扐之四營或成卦焉或成爻焉而所以前民
用者於是乎存則夫龜也鑽之七十有二于以
著雨霽蒙驛克之五兆或爲陰焉或爲陽焉而
所以開民先者於是乎在泰筮之法立而用靜

造化有以肇卜筮之器，聖人因以立卜筮之法。

盖天生蓍龜，其爲物也神矣。聖人從而則之，豈不立卜筮之法於天下哉？大傳十一章專言卜筮，及此若曰：易之爲易，果何爲而作哉？而蓍之與龜，則其所本之一也。彼其植而爲衆卉之異者爲蓍。是蓍也，天以生之，而其莖長丈，其叢滿百，以具圓神之德，一天之和氣所融乎！動而爲介族之靈者爲龜。是龜也，天以生之，而五行中具，八卦外列，以含黙藏之智，一天之禎祥所鍾乎！蓍生矣，而豈偶然哉？天將有意於立筮，以前斯民之用也。龜生矣，而豈徒然哉？天將有意於立卜，以開斯人之先也。於是聖人者出，上明天道，而有以發造化之祕；下察民故，而有以通天下之情。則夫蓍也，用之四十有九，于以假分揲掛扐之四營，或成卦焉，或成爻焉，而所以前民用者於是乎存。則夫龜也，鑽之七十有二，于以著雨霽蒙驛克之五兆，或爲陰焉，或爲陽焉，而所以開民先者於是乎在。泰筮之法立，而用靜
translation_en:
The workings of creation brought forth the instruments of turtle-shell and milfoil divination; the sages accordingly established the methods of divination.

Heaven produces milfoil and turtles, and these beings possess numinous powers. When the sages followed them and took them as models, did they not thereby establish methods of divination throughout the world? Chapter Eleven of the Great Commentary deals specifically with divination. At this point it seems to say: for what purpose, indeed, was the Book of Changes made what it is? Milfoil and turtles constitute one of its foundations. That which grows rooted in the soil and stands apart from all other plants is milfoil. Heaven produces this milfoil with stalks a zhang in length and a full hundred stems in each clump, endowing it with the virtue of roundness and numinous efficacy: surely it is wholly formed by Heaven’s harmonious vital breath! That which moves and is the most spiritually potent among shelled creatures is the turtle. Heaven produces this turtle with the Five Phases complete within and the Eight Trigrams arrayed without, so that it harbors a wisdom concealed in silence: surely Heaven’s auspicious influences are wholly concentrated in it!

Can the production of milfoil be accidental? Heaven must intend the establishment of milfoil divination to guide the people’s undertakings in advance. Can the production of turtles be purposeless? Heaven must intend the establishment of turtle-shell divination to give people foreknowledge. Then the sages arose. Above, they understood the Way of Heaven and could reveal the secrets of creation; below, they examined human affairs and could comprehend the circumstances of all under Heaven. Taking milfoil as their model, they used forty-nine stalks and employed the four operations of dividing, counting off, suspending, and placing the remainders between the fingers. These formed hexagrams or individual lines, and therein lay the means of guiding the people’s undertakings in advance. Taking the turtle as their model, they drilled seventy-two hollows to disclose the five kinds of crack兆: rain, clearing, clouding, dispersal [?], and crossing. These were either yin or yang, and therein lay the means of giving the people foreknowledge. Once the method of great milfoil divination [?] was established, those remaining still …

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
用作者有所資吉凶悔吝已昭然而莫揜矣是
雖蓍有以兆之聖人先物之智可少哉蓍之神
固聖人之神也泰龜之法行而人謀鬼謀者有
所頼吉凶得失已瞭然而無疑矣是雖龜有以
啓之聖人創物之功可忘哉龜之神固聖人之
神也夫以蓍龜之神其原出於天其制裁於聖
人者如此此卜筮之用所以爲大而聖人作易
之功所由見也歟雖然易之用固以蓍龜爲大
然非象數與辭之周則枯莖敗甲其何以通天
===
下之志定天下之業哉故卜筮占也象數理也
二者並行不悖而易之道始全矣夫以蓍龜有
關於易者如此世之人顧以筮短龜長議之而
從違於其間何其不知易之甚耶
書
從諫弗咈先民時若
同考試官訓導周 批 伊尹輔嗣王只此二
言已含蓄許多惓惓忠愛之意是作詞氣和緩意味

啓之聖人創物之功可忘哉龜之神固聖人之
神也夫以蓍龜之神其原出於天其制裁於聖
人者如此此卜筮之用所以爲大而聖人作易
之功所由見也歟雖然易之用固以蓍龜爲大
然非象數與辭之周則枯莖敗甲其何以通天

二者並行不悖而易之道始全矣夫以蓍龜有
關於易者如此世之人顧以筮短龜長議之而

punctuated:
用作者有所資，吉凶悔吝已昭然而莫揜矣。是雖蓍有以兆之，聖人先物之智可少哉？蓍之神，固聖人之神也。泰龜之法行，而人謀鬼謀者有所頼，吉凶得失已瞭然而無疑矣。是雖龜有以啓之，聖人創物之功可忘哉？龜之神，固聖人之神也。夫以蓍龜之神，其原出於天，其制裁於聖人者如此，此卜筮之用所以爲大，而聖人作易之功所由見也歟！雖然，易之用固以蓍龜爲大，然非象數與辭之周，則枯莖敗甲，其何以通天下之志、定天下之業哉？故卜筮，占也；象數，理也。二者並行不悖，而易之道始全矣。夫以蓍龜有關於易者如此，世之人顧以筮短龜長議之，而從違於其間，何其不知易之甚耶？

translation_en:
…those undertaking action have something to draw upon, and good fortune, misfortune, regret, and humiliation are already plainly revealed, with nothing concealed. Although it is the milfoil that gives these signs, can the sages’ wisdom in anticipating events be slighted? The spiritual efficacy of milfoil is indeed the spiritual efficacy of the sages. When the method of the great tortoise [?] is put into practice, those consulting men and spirits have something to rely upon; good and ill fortune, gain and loss, are already clear and beyond doubt. Although it is the tortoise that reveals them, can the sages’ achievement in devising this practice be forgotten? The spiritual efficacy of the tortoise is indeed the spiritual efficacy of the sages.

The spiritual efficacy of milfoil and tortoise thus originates in Heaven and is given regulated form by the sages. Is this not why the use of divination by tortoise shell and milfoil is so momentous, and why the sages’ achievement in making the Book of Changes becomes manifest? Nevertheless, although milfoil and tortoise are central to the use of the Changes, without the completeness of its images, numbers, and statements, how could withered stalks and decayed shells comprehend the intentions of all under Heaven and settle their undertakings? Divination by tortoise shell and milfoil concerns prognostication; images and numbers concern principle. Only when these two operate together without conflict is the Way of the Changes complete. Given this relationship of milfoil and tortoise to the Changes, how profoundly ignorant of the Changes are those who nevertheless argue that milfoil divination is inferior and tortoise divination superior, and accept or reject them accordingly!

納忠言而不逆，任舊臣而不違，先王之修人紀然也。盖忠言不可逆，舊臣不可違也。兼盡是道者，孰有過於先王也哉？昔太甲嗣位之初，伊尹以成湯修人紀者訓之，謂夫人紀之修，先王所以為聖；修紀之實，吾王在所當知。是故世之忠諫者，盡言不諱，多勿欺而犯之辭；鯁直不阿，無面從退言之弊。或援古以證今之失，或戒後以懲前之非。其剴切易至於見拒也，是孰能容耶？惟我先王於是言也，則知其為圖治之良規，即委心而聽受之，雖貴而在朝者，不以其勢逼而見猜；取其為保邦之至計，即虛己而延納之，雖賤而在野者，不以其跡疎而見忤。諤諤之論，咈
translation_en:
…of lingering depth; moreover, it brings out what Yi Yin left unspoken. Might its author, too, aspire to such loyalty and loving concern?

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: The language is measured and ample, and the writing mature and vigorous. It conveys Yi Yin’s loyalty and loving concern so vividly that one can readily imagine them. A work of classical scholarship such as this fully deserves inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Rectifier: It reaches points that others cannot express.

Comment by Examiner Wu, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: This is writing of real consequence.

To accept loyal words without resisting them, and to employ longstanding ministers without going against them: such was the former king’s way of ordering human relationships. For loyal words must not be resisted, nor longstanding ministers opposed. Who ever fulfilled both these principles more completely than the former king? In the past, when Tai Jia first succeeded to the throne, Yi Yin instructed him through the example of how Cheng Tang had ordered human relationships. His meaning was this: ordering human relationships was what made the former king a sage; the actual means of ordering them are something our king ought to understand.

Thus, those in the world who remonstrate loyally speak their minds fully and without concealment. Their words often exemplify the principle of never deceiving their ruler, even when they must confront him. Upright and unbending, they avoid the fault of assenting to his face and criticizing him after withdrawing. Some invoke antiquity to demonstrate present failings; others warn about the future to correct past errors. Their pointed earnestness readily causes them to be rebuffed. Who can tolerate such men?

Our former king alone recognized such words as sound guidance for achieving good government, and entrusted his heart to hearing and accepting them. Even when their speakers were men of high rank at court, he did not suspect them because their power pressed close upon his own. He valued their words as the best plans for safeguarding the realm, and humbly welcomed and accepted them. Even when their speakers were men of low station outside office, he did not take offense because they stood remote from him. As for forthright arguments, to oppose them [?]…

之惟恐不足恢恢之量容之常若有餘盖導之
而使言則有矣未有聞其言而弗納也夫於其
難容者而能容之則忠言之在當時者何有不
日至乎人之耆舊者齒尊德隆為生民之倚賴
位高望重為治道之指南老成焉而類迂闊質
朴焉而若遲鈍其年耄易至於見疎也又孰能
親耶惟我先王於是人也則念其練達也深于
以信如蓍龜而敬順之不遑雖近而一朝一夕
恒置於左右嘉其閲歷也久于以待如神明而
===

如所言惟循其舊立之規心如其貌不替乎初
待之敬盖聞之而輒從則有矣未有從之後而

punctuated: 之惟恐不足，恢恢之量，容之常若有餘。盖導之而使言則有矣，未有聞其言而弗納也。夫於其難容者而能容之，則忠言之在當時者，何有不日至乎？人之耆舊者，齒尊德隆，為生民之倚賴；位高望重，為治道之指南。老成焉而類迂闊，質朴焉而若遲鈍，其年耄易至於見疎也，又孰能親耶？惟我先王於是人也，則念其練達也深，于以信如蓍龜，而敬順之不遑；雖近而一朝一夕，恒置於左右。嘉其閲歷也久，于以待如神明，而尊信之惟謹；雖小而一話一言，亦取為法程。行如所言，惟循其舊立之規；心如其貌，不替乎初待之敬。盖聞之而輒從則有矣，未有從之後而復悖也。夫於其當親者而能親之，則舊臣之在當時者，何敢不盡心乎？是則不逆忠言，以廣容人之量；不遠舊臣，以盡優老之誠。先王之修人紀如此，可謂誠於樂善者矣，吾王可不念之哉？繼之太甲，庸罔念聞，背棄師保，其於所謂納忠言、順舊臣者，盖不能無慚德焉。伊尹先見其徵
translation_en:
… fearing only that this was insufficient [?]; with his vast generosity of spirit, he always seemed to have more than enough capacity to accommodate them. Indeed, he encouraged them to speak; never did he hear their words and refuse to accept them. If he could accommodate those whom it was difficult to accommodate, how could loyal counsel in those days fail to reach him daily?

As for venerable elders, their advanced age and lofty virtue made them a support for the people; their high standing and great prestige made them guides in the art of government. Yet their maturity might seem impractical, and their simplicity might appear slow-witted. Their great age made them liable to be kept at a distance: who, then, could keep them close? Our former king alone, considering such men, reflected upon the depth of their experience and understanding. He trusted them as he would the divining milfoil and tortoise shell, and was tireless in respecting and heeding them. Even for so brief a span as a single morning or evening, he always kept them at his side. Esteeming their long experience, he treated them like divine spirits and scrupulously honored and trusted them. Even something as small as a single remark or word he adopted as a standard. His actions accorded with his words, following the rules they had established of old; his inward feelings matched his outward demeanor, never diminishing the respect with which he had first treated them. Indeed, he followed their advice whenever he heard it; never did he follow it and afterward turn against it. If he could keep close those whom he ought to keep close, how would the longstanding ministers of that time dare to withhold their wholehearted service?

Thus he did not reject loyal counsel, thereby enlarging his capacity to accommodate others; he did not distance himself from longstanding ministers, thereby fully expressing his sincerity in honoring the aged. Such was the former king’s cultivation of the bonds of human relations. He may truly be called sincere in delighting in goodness. Can our king fail to reflect upon this? Tai Jia, who succeeded him, failed to ponder what he heard and turned his back on his preceptors and guardians. With regard to what is called accepting loyal counsel and heeding longstanding ministers, his conduct could hardly have been free of cause for shame. Yi Yin foresaw the signs of this…

translation_en:
…Thus he earnestly admonished him with these words, seeking to stir him to change his course: his loyalty was utmost. Thereafter, the king sustained his virtue to the end, shining gloriously in the historical records. Although Heaven’s Mandate resting upon Shang seemed secretly to guide him, this was also because Yi Yin’s instruction and admonition came at the outset. Mencius said, “Only a great man can rectify what is wrong in the ruler’s heart.” Was he not speaking of Yi Yin? Those who serve as great ministers in later ages should take him as their model.

“Do not say that you cannot accomplish it; only exert your heart to the full. Do not say that the people are few; only attend carefully to your duties.”
By Wang Rui.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Assistant Instructor: The meaning of King Kang’s admonition to the Duke of Bi is expounded almost exhaustively. The discussion of the heart and of duties is particularly insightful. This is no carelessly composed work; it should be selected.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: This essay singles out the two words “heart” and “duties” to illuminate the essentials of safeguarding and governing. This is precisely King Kang’s meaning. Moreover, its language is dignified and its principles correct; it thoroughly captures the form of a formal investiture charge. An excellent composition: accept it.

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Mentor: The reasoning is lucid and the writing vigorous.

Comment by Examiner Wu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: The beginning and end correspond well; the writing has force.

When a worthy king commissions a great minister, the minister should plan for what is difficult and not neglect what is easy. The essentials of safeguarding and governing lie simply in giving full expression to sincerity, inwardly and outwardly. If he regards his responsibilities merely in terms of difficulty or ease and forgets the duties incumbent upon him, how can he transform the people of Yin and discharge his office? Formerly, King Kang commissioned the Duke of Bi to safeguard and govern Chengzhou. At the close of the chapter, he sighed and admonished him…

毖於始而利口之餘風未殄君陳和於中而怙
侈之放心未閑予何人哉而有是任也其弗能

===
不及慮千里之憂紆籌於几席之下百世之患
决策於旦暮之間何者為淑何者為慝而權度
之不差如是則剛如是則柔而酌量之必審如
此則心無不盡而成周可治矣尚何難之足畏
哉視之太輕而忽其易則以為不足為矣如民
何公此行也其勿曰一人莫非其臣今則蕞爾
殷民已化周公之毖尺地莫非其有今則遷於
洛邑已被君陳之和彼何人斯而有他志也其
無足虞矣乎自我言之亦惟慎厥事焉耳盖事

之如此謂夫成周之事既付我公所以保釐之
者豈言語所能盡邪彼視之太重而畏其難則
有所不敢爲矣如治何公斯往也其勿曰周公
毖於始而利口之餘風未殄君陳和於中而怙
侈之放心未閑予何人哉而有是任也其弗能
勝矣乎自我觀之亦惟既厥心焉耳蓋心者爲
治之本而主乎其內也心有不既則事爲徒法
其可哉必也有弗謀焉謀則精粗俱到謀人之
所不能謀有弗慮焉慮則巨細不遺慮人之所
===
不及慮千里之憂紆籌於几席之下百世之患
決策於旦暮之間何者爲淑何者爲慝而權度

無足虞矣乎自我言之亦惟愼厥事焉耳蓋事
punctuated: 之如此，謂夫成周之事既付我公，所以保釐之者，豈言語所能盡邪？彼視之太重而畏其難，則有所不敢為矣，如治何？公斯往也，其勿曰：「周公毖於始，而利口之餘風未殄；君陳和於中，而怙侈之放心未閑。予何人哉，而有是任也？其弗能勝矣乎？」自我觀之，亦惟既厥心焉耳。盖心者，為治之本而主乎其内也。心有不既，則事為徒法，其可哉？必也有弗謀焉，謀則精粗俱到，謀人之所不能謀；有弗慮焉，慮則巨細不遺，慮人之所不及慮。千里之憂，紆籌於几席之下；百世之患，决策於旦暮之間。何者為淑，何者為慝，而權度之不差；如是則剛，如是則柔，而酌量之必審。如此則心無不盡，而成周可治矣，尚何難之足畏哉？視之太輕而忽其易，則以為不足為矣，如民何？公此行也，其勿曰：「一人莫非其臣，今則蕞爾殷民已化周公之毖；尺地莫非其有，今則遷於洛邑已被君陳之和。彼何人斯，而有他志也？其無足虞矣乎？」自我言之，亦惟慎厥事焉耳。盖事
translation_en:
…admonished him in this way, meaning: “The affairs of Chengzhou have now been entrusted to you, my duke. How could words fully express all that is required to preserve order and govern there?” If one regards the task as too weighty and fears its difficulty, there will be things one dares not undertake. What, then, becomes of government? As you go, my duke, do not say: “The Duke of Zhou exercised vigilance at the outset, yet the lingering habit of glib speech has not been extinguished; Jun Chen fostered harmony in the intervening period, yet the unrestrained hearts of those clinging to extravagance have not been checked. Who am I to bear this responsibility? Surely I cannot discharge it!” As I see it, it is simply a matter of applying your heart to the utmost. For the heart is the foundation of government and governs its inward aspect. If the heart is not fully applied, administrative affairs become mere rules. How could that suffice? There may be matters one does not plan for, but whenever one plans, one must encompass both the subtle and the broad, planning what others cannot plan. There may be matters one does not consider, but whenever one considers, one must omit neither the great nor the small, considering what others fail to consider. For troubles a thousand li away, work out plans at your desk; for dangers a hundred generations hence, decide upon measures within the span of a day. Weigh without error what is good and what is evil; judge carefully when to be firm and when to be gentle. In this way the heart is applied to the fullest, and Chengzhou can be governed. What difficulty would then warrant fear?

If one regards the task too lightly and neglects it because it seems easy, one will think it unworthy of undertaking. What, then, becomes of the people? As you make this journey, my duke, do not say: “There is not a single person who is not the king’s subject; now this small remnant of the Yin people has already been transformed by the Duke of Zhou’s vigilance. There is not a foot of land that is not his possession; now, having been moved to Luoyi, they have already benefited from Jun Chen’s harmonious rule. Who are these people, that they should harbor other intentions? Surely there is nothing in them to fear!” For my part, it is simply a matter of attending carefully to one’s duties. For administrative affairs…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者爲治之具而行乎其外也事有不慎則心爲
徒善其可哉必也將有安焉則謹其割裂之施
而不過於嚴將有理焉則慎其潤澤之及而不
傷乎縱品式已脩而猶恐其或弛規模既備而
猶懼其或疎表宅里殊井疆所以彰善而癉惡
者必欲其當申郊圻慎封守所以防微而杜漸
者必欲其周如此則事無不慎而殷民可化矣
尚何易之可忽哉吁心既則事之慎者以成事
慎則心之既者不失而慎于始和于中者亦庶
===
乎克成于終矣康王以是而命畢公其戒勉之
意何其深且切歟抑論之武王一戎衣而有天
下克殷如此其易成康繼體至於世歷三紀殷
民猶未率從如此其難何也盖紂之暴虐生民
如在水火故就拯之者爲甚急耳天下既定良
心復萌則又思先王之德而不忍棄此周人號
爲頑民而三后相繼於洛畢命諸篇所以作也
然非殷民之頑亦無以見周室之仁而錮陰沍
寒卒消融於春風和氣其長治久安衍八百年

translation_en:
…are the instruments of government, through which the heart finds outward expression. If affairs are handled without due care, the heart possesses merely good intentions: how could that suffice? To bring peace, one must carefully apply measures that cut away abuses, without becoming excessively harsh; to establish order, one must carefully extend ameliorating benefits, without lapsing into indulgence. Even when standards and procedures have been put in order, one must still fear that they may grow lax; even when the framework is complete, one must still fear that it may contain omissions. Distinguishing dwellings and neighborhoods, and differentiating fields and boundaries—the means of honoring goodness and condemning wickedness—must be done appropriately. Reaffirming the suburban boundaries and carefully guarding the borders—the means of preventing trouble while it is slight and checking its growth—must be done comprehensively. In this way, no affair will lack careful attention, and the people of Yin can be transformed. How, then, could anything be neglected because it seems easy?

Ah! When the heart is fully devoted, careful attention to affairs achieves its purpose; when affairs receive careful attention, the heart’s full devotion is preserved. Thus, what began with vigilance and continued with harmony may also be brought to a successful conclusion. King Kang charged the Duke of Bi in these terms: how profound and earnest was his intention to admonish and encourage him!

Consider further: King Wu donned his battle dress once and gained all under Heaven—so easy was the conquest of Yin. Kings Cheng and Kang succeeded to the throne, yet even after three twelve-year cycles had elapsed, the people of Yin still had not submitted—so difficult was it. Why? Under Zhou’s cruel tyranny, the people had been as though amid flood and fire, and so they hastened urgently to those who would rescue them. Once the realm was settled, however, their innate goodness stirred again: they remembered the virtue of their former kings and could not bear to abandon them. These were the people whom the Zhou called obstinate; this explains why three lords served successively at Luo and why such chapters as “The Charge to Bi” were composed. Yet without the obstinacy of Yin’s people, there would have been no means of revealing the benevolence of the house of Zhou. The entrenched gloom and bitter cold finally melted in the spring breeze and its genial warmth, and their enduring order and lasting peace extended an eight-hundred-year…

…there was indeed a reason why their dynastic fortune endured so long!

Book of Poetry

“Like flying, like soaring wings; like the Jiang, like the Han; like a mountain’s luxuriant growth, like a river’s flow. Unbroken and orderly, unfathomable and invincible.”

Liu Ke 劉珂

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Assistant Instructor: Most candidates can discuss the grandeur of military might, but they do not know where the banks of the Huai are [?]. Moreover, their explanations repeat themselves from beginning to end and give little satisfaction. This paper’s analysis is clear and orderly; it sweeps away every stale expression. Its concluding words are especially rich in lingering significance. Admirable! Admirable!

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor: The wording of this topic recurs repeatedly, but its meanings differ in each instance, making analysis difficult for writers. For lucid discrimination, apt language, and clear reasoning, no essay matches this one. We have therefore singled it out for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner She, Instructor: In writing on this topic from the Greater Odes, candidates in the examination hall failed to consider that the topic itself already contains six instances of “like.” Their explanations then added still more comparisons, piling them up in tedious profusion and making the essays tiresome to read. This essay alone examines each word closely, with clear reasoning and vigorous language. It can serve as a model for writers of essays on the meaning of the Classics; hence its inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Rectifier: “The Poetry is orthodox yet luxuriant.” This composition possesses those qualities.

Comment by Examiner Wu, Expositor-in-Waiting: The exposition is clear and clean.

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
詩人於周王之師必極言其兵威之盛也盖王
師無敵於天下也詩人舉其兵威而極言之所
以昭一時之盛也歟是詩美宣王自將以伐淮
北之夷其意謂夫外夷猾夏固天討之所當加
兵威極盛又王師之所當尚我宣王之伐淮夷
也其師何如其盛哉想其以所將之師陳淮浦
之上彼至疾者莫飛翰若也我師所至速於應
變威武自爾其奮揚敏於趨事王靈不覺其震
蕩其疾不如飛如翰乎至衆者莫江漢過也我
===
師所在武騎桓桓遠近布濩於原野武夫赳赳
前後充斥於周行其衆不如江如漢乎其靜而
少斂歟持重不浮隨時而止有如山之苞焉屹
乎其不可動誰得而撼之其動而大舉歟奮勇
並進以時而行有如川之流焉沛乎其不可禦
誰得而撓之跂而望焉部伍聨屬首尾之相顧
者無虧其不可絶者盖緜緜然也即而觀焉行
隊整肅左右之司局者有定其不可亂者盖翼
翼然也神謀睿筭默運於帷幄之中敵欲投間

punctuated:
詩人於周王之師，必極言其兵威之盛也，盖王師無敵於天下也。詩人舉其兵威而極言之，所以昭一時之盛也歟？

是詩美宣王自將以伐淮北之夷。其意謂夫外夷猾夏，固天討之所當加；兵威極盛，又王師之所當尚。我宣王之伐淮夷也，其師何如其盛哉！想其以所將之師陳淮浦之上，彼至疾者莫飛翰若也。我師所至，速於應變，威武自爾其奮揚；敏於趨事，王靈不覺其震蕩。其疾不如飛如翰乎？至衆者莫江漢過也。我師所在，武騎桓桓，遠近布濩於原野；武夫赳赳，前後充斥於周行。其衆不如江如漢乎？其靜而少斂歟，持重不浮，隨時而止，有如山之苞焉，屹乎其不可動，誰得而撼之？其動而大舉歟，奮勇並進，以時而行，有如川之流焉，沛乎其不可禦，誰得而撓之？跂而望焉，部伍聨屬，首尾之相顧者無虧，其不可絶者盖緜緜然也。即而觀焉，行隊整肅，左右之司局者有定，其不可亂者盖翼翼然也。神謀睿筭，默運於帷幄之中，敵欲投間
translation_en:
When the poet speaks of the army of the king of Zhou, he invariably describes its martial might in the strongest terms, for the royal army has no equal under Heaven. Does the poet not thus extol its martial might to make manifest the glory of that age?

This poem praises King Xuan for personally commanding the campaign against the Yi peoples north of the Huai River. Its meaning is that when the outlying Yi peoples bring disorder to the central lands, Heaven’s punishment must indeed be inflicted upon them; and overwhelming martial might is also what the royal army should prize. How magnificent was the army with which our King Xuan attacked the Huai Yi! Imagine the troops under his command drawn up along the banks of the Huai. Nothing is swifter than flying wings. Wherever our army arrives, it responds swiftly to changing circumstances, its martial power naturally rising into vigorous action; it hastens promptly to its tasks, the king’s numinous might spreading its tremors imperceptibly. Is its swiftness not like flight, like wings? Nothing surpasses the Yangzi and Han rivers in abundance. Wherever our army is stationed, its valiant cavalry spreads across the plains, near and far; its stalwart warriors fill the great roads, before and behind. Are its numbers not like the Yangzi, like the Han? When it rests and draws itself in a little, it is steady and unhurried, halting as the occasion requires, like the massive bulk of a mountain: towering and immovable, who could shake it? When it moves and advances in force, its men press forward together with surging courage, marching when the time is right, like a river’s flow: rushing irresistibly onward, who could check it? Rise on tiptoe and look into the distance: its units are linked together, with nothing lacking in the mutual support of front and rear. This unbroken continuity is indeed what is meant by being ceaselessly connected. Approach and observe: its ranks are orderly and disciplined, and those responsible for their stations on left and right have fixed assignments. This resistance to disorder is indeed what is meant by being perfectly arrayed. Inspired plans and sagacious calculations are silently set in motion within the command tent; should the enemy seek to exploit an opening…
