punctuated: 與論其世，可乎？重厚少文者，木強之人耳，何以能副大事之屬，卒建社稷之功？不學無術者，匹夫之類耳，何以能受託孤之詔，以成伊周之業？或謂其人之似光，而顛沛之中飲博自如，摧強敵於談笑之頃；或謂其人之似勃，而危疑之際不動聲色，措國家於泰山之安。不知其為學術者，果亦各有所類，故其設施若合符節，抑其天資偶合，有不在於學術耶？或謂之有儒者氣象，或謂之非知學不能，當時未見其果何所學，而為帝師，為謀臣，其建立卓然，為一代之冠。而明經對策、立談封侯者，顧曲學阿世，無救於海內虛耗之弊。有其學止於《論語》一部者，有以《論語》終身誦之者，當時未聞其別有所學，而任天下之重，得大臣之體，其相業炳然，非後世可及。而博學強記、致位宰輔者，乃變亂成法，使天下喪
translation_en: …and discuss with you the times in which they lived: may we do so? A man described as grave and substantial but lacking in refinement was merely a blunt, unbending fellow. How could he fulfill the trust placed in him in great affairs and ultimately render meritorious service to the altars of soil and grain? A man without learning or cultivated abilities was merely an ordinary fellow. How could he receive an imperial edict entrusting an orphaned ruler to his care and accomplish deeds like those of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou? One man was said to resemble Guang, yet amid upheaval he drank and gambled as calmly as ever, crushing powerful enemies in the space of a casual conversation. Another was said to resemble Bo, yet amid danger and uncertainty he betrayed no agitation in voice or expression and made the state as secure as Mount Tai. Were their respective kinds of learning indeed similar, so that their measures corresponded like the two halves of a tally? Or did their natural endowments happen to coincide, with something at work that did not depend upon learning? One was said to possess the bearing of a Confucian scholar; of another it was said that he could not have accomplished what he did without understanding learning. In their own day, it was not apparent what they had actually studied, yet they served as imperial teachers and counselors, and their outstanding achievements ranked foremost in their age. Yet a man who elucidated the Classics, answered policy questions, and was enfeoffed as a marquis after a single audience distorted learning to curry favor with his age and did nothing to remedy the depletion of resources throughout the realm. There was one whose learning extended only to the single book of the Analects, and another who recited the Analects throughout his life. In their own day, they were not known to have studied anything else, yet they shouldered responsibility for the realm and exemplified the proper bearing of great ministers. Their achievements as chief councilors shone brilliantly, beyond the reach of later generations. Yet a man of extensive learning and powerful memory who rose to the position of chief councilor disrupted established institutions and caused all under Heaven to lose…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其樂生之心豈其學有所得固不在於
徒博抑學術有邪正而見諸躬行者自
有所不能揜乎試為我言之
問天下親民之職大而藩臬小而郡縣皆
是也誠得其人則民受其福不得其人
則民受其殃而天下治忽繫之盖其職
不可不慎擇如此顧民事浩繁類非一
人可獨治者故其下各有僚属以分理
之必其彼此得人之盛然後力同心協
===
事克有濟否則掣肘相妨下石相擠其
不僨厥事者幾希宋儒西山真文忠公
有見於此故其帥長沙時嘗具咨目示
其僚属謂欲各以四事自勉而為民去
其十害其意至矣所謂四事十害者亦
可得而聞乎豈其間亦有先後乎古之
良吏如龔黃卓魯之流號稱善治民者
其亦用此道乎抑外此别有他道也方
今任藩臬郡縣者多出科目之英

則民受其殃而天下治忽繫之蓋其職

人可獨治者故其下各有僚屬以分理
之必其彼此得人之盛然後力同心協
===
事克有濟否則掣肘相妨下石相擠其
不僨厥事者幾希宋儒西山真文忠公
有見於此故其帥長沙時嘗具咨目示

其十害其意至矣所謂四事十害者亦
可得而聞乎豈其間亦有先後乎古之
良吏如龔黄卓魯之流號稱善治民者
其亦用此道乎抑外此別有他道也方
今任藩臬郡縣者多出科目之英
punctuated:
其樂生之心。豈其學有所得，固不在於徒博，抑學術有邪正，而見諸躬行者自有所不能揜乎？試為我言之。

問：天下親民之職，大而藩臬，小而郡縣，皆是也。誠得其人，則民受其福；不得其人，則民受其殃，而天下治忽繫之。盖其職不可不慎擇如此。顧民事浩繁，類非一人可獨治者，故其下各有僚属以分理之。必其彼此得人之盛，然後力同心協，事克有濟；否則掣肘相妨，下石相擠，其不僨厥事者幾希。宋儒西山真文忠公有見於此，故其帥長沙時，嘗具咨目示其僚属，謂欲各以四事自勉，而為民去其十害，其意至矣。所謂四事十害者，亦可得而聞乎？豈其間亦有先後乎？古之良吏，如龔黃卓魯之流，號稱善治民者，其亦用此道乎？抑外此别有他道也？方今任藩臬郡縣者，多出科目之英
translation_en:
…their joy in living. Was it that what they gained from learning did not, after all, depend on mere breadth of knowledge? Or does learning have orthodox and heterodox forms, whose manifestations in personal conduct inevitably reveal what cannot be concealed? Explain this for me.

Question: Offices directly concerned with governing the people range from the higher posts in provincial administration and surveillance to the lower posts in prefectures and counties. If suitable men are indeed appointed, the people enjoy the benefits; if unsuitable men are appointed, the people suffer the harm. Order and disorder throughout the realm depend upon this. Such is the necessity of choosing carefully those who hold these offices. Yet the people's affairs are so numerous and complex that they generally cannot be managed by one man alone. Thus each official has subordinate colleagues among whom responsibility is divided. Only when suitable men fill both superior and subordinate posts can they unite their efforts and purposes and bring affairs to a successful conclusion. Otherwise, they hamper and obstruct one another, casting stones at those already fallen and pushing one another aside; seldom will they avoid ruining their work. The Song Confucian Master Zhen of Xishan, posthumously titled Wenzhong, understood this. Thus, when governing Changsha, he once drew up written instructions for his subordinate colleagues, saying that he wished each to strive to fulfill four duties and to eliminate ten harms for the people. His intention was most commendable. May we hear what these four duties and ten harms were? Was there also an order of priority among them? Did the good officials of antiquity, such as Gong, Huang, Zhuo, and Lu, who were renowned for governing the people well, also follow this method? Or did they have some other method beyond it? Today, those holding posts in provincial administration and surveillance, prefectures, and counties are mostly drawn from the outstanding men of the examination system…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
朝廷所以責成斯民所以仰望最先且重其
有率其僚属勉四事去十害能心西山
之心者乎果有之則天下之治成矣此
當宁所欲聞者將於是首述職公黜陟示勸懲
焉願一陳之以為
今日
聖政之助
alt_text:
朝廷所以責成斯民所以仰望㝡先且重其
有率其僚屬勉四事去十害能心西山
之心者乎果有之則天下之治成矣此
當宁所欲聞者將於歲首述職公黜陟示勸懲
焉願一陳之以爲
今日
聖政之助
punctuated: 朝廷所以責成、斯民所以仰望，最先且重。其有率其僚属勉四事、去十害，能心西山之心者乎？果有之，則天下之治成矣。此當宁所欲聞者，將於是首述職、公黜陟、示勸懲焉。願一陳之，以為今日聖政之助。
translation_en: … The court’s demands upon them for results, and the people’s expectations of them, are foremost and weighty. Are there any who lead their subordinate officials in striving to fulfill the four duties and eliminate the ten harms, making Xishan’s concerns their own? If indeed there are, then good government throughout the realm will be achieved. This is what His Majesty wishes to hear. On this basis, he will give priority to reports on the discharge of official duties [?], make demotions and promotions impartially, and provide encouragement and admonition. Please set forth your views, to aid the sage governance of the present day.

text:
第壹場
四書
十室之邑必有忠信如丘者焉不如丘之
好學也
呂璋
同考試官訓導林批美質至道難易正在
十室好學上見作者體認不真往往信筆漫言姑取
成篇而已獨此篇能說出聖人勉人為學之意讀之
令人惕然信非穉筆可到也高薦何疑
===
同考試官教諭高批是題士子類能下筆
但詞多誇非聖人謙己誨人意理足文整且筆力老
健如此篇者其最優者歟宜刻以式来學
同考試官學正余批論語一題作者於十
室上類疊陳語於忠信上強析為對到不如處却涉
自誇便不似夫子口氣此篇能以典雅之詞講出夫
子誨人本意非平素潜心本領者不能故特錄之
考試官左中允劉批詞理俱到
考試官侍講學士吳批是善言聖人之言者

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

「十室之邑，必有忠信如丘者焉，不如丘之好學也。」

呂璋

同考試官訓導林批：「美質、至道難易，正在『十室』『好學』上見。作者體認不真，往往信筆漫言，姑取成篇而已。獨此篇能說出聖人勉人為學之意，讀之令人惕然，信非穉筆可到也。高薦何疑！」

同考試官教諭高批：「是題士子類能下筆，但詞多誇，非聖人謙己誨人意。理足文整，且筆力老健如此篇者，其最優者歟！宜刻以式来學。」

同考試官學正余批：「論語一題，作者於『十室』上類疊陳語，於『忠信』上強析為對，到『不如』處却涉自誇，便不似夫子口氣。此篇能以典雅之詞講出夫子誨人本意，非平素潜心本領者不能，故特錄之。」

考試官左中允劉批：「詞理俱到。」

考試官侍講學士吳批：「是善言聖人之言者。」
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Even in a hamlet of ten households, there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as I, Qiu; yet he will not equal my love of learning.”

Lü Zhang

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Assistant Instructor: “The relative ease of possessing fine natural qualities and the difficulty of attaining the ultimate Way are revealed precisely in ‘ten households’ and ‘love of learning.’ Writers who fail to grasp this accurately often let their brushes wander and write loosely, merely seeking to finish an essay. This essay alone succeeds in expressing the sage’s intention to encourage others to learn. Reading it makes one sharply attentive. Such writing is surely beyond an immature hand. What doubt can there be about recommending it highly!”

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor: “Most candidates can write something on this topic, but their language is often boastful and fails to convey the sage’s intention to speak humbly of himself and instruct others. With reasoning so ample, composition so orderly, and a brush so mature and vigorous, is this essay not among the very best? It should be printed to serve as a model for future students.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Instructor: “On this topic from the Analects, writers generally pile up stale expressions when treating ‘ten households’ and force ‘loyalty and trustworthiness’ apart to construct parallel phrases. When they reach ‘will not equal,’ they lapse into self-praise and cease to sound like the Master. This essay uses refined and dignified language to express the Master’s original intention to instruct others. Only someone who has habitually devoted himself to the fundamentals could accomplish this; therefore, I have specially selected it for inclusion.”

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Mentor: “Both expression and reasoning are fully accomplished.”

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖人論人得乎美質也易聞乎至道也難蓋美
質易得而好學以聞道則難也聖人即已而較
之人焉其勉人之意何至哉想其意若曰人當
以至道而自彊不可以美質而自恃如有恃焉
則去道遠矣彼十室之邑邑之小者也忠信之
質質之美者也丘非所謂忠信者歟試以其邑
言之一隅相望其地可謂狹矣然而篤實之資
毎特稟於其間者則誠聞之不可以其地之狹
而遂謂無是人也數家攸聚其人可謂少矣然
===
而敦朴之懿恒秀出於其地者則信有之不可
以其人之少而遂謂無是質也十室之邑豈不
有忠信如丘者乎有則有矣然如丘之好學者
則甚鮮焉誠以生質之美天之所以賦於人也
學問之功人之所以求乎道也丘豈敢有所恃
而倦於學耶蓋吾慕道之心已定於忠信自得
之後故發憤忘食至於終日乾乾焉于以探義
理之精微者融而會之使與吾心而相孚蓋庶
幾美質之不負耳彼十室之邑果有如丘之不

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
敢自恃者乎求道之力倍加於吾心向慕之餘
故好古敏求至於惟日孜孜焉于以玩物理之
著見者研而精之使與吾身而爲一蓋庶幾至
道之可聞耳彼忠信之人抑有如丘之能知自
彊者乎學問在我我所當盡忠信在我我則不
知此丘之始與人同而終與人異也吁夫子言
此豈眞矜已以誇人哉無非勉人爲學而欲其
同歸于道焉耳是即與人爲善之心歟嗟夫學
之於人大矣以夫子生知而亦未嘗不好學況
===
其他哉夫子嘗曰吾十有五而志於學又曰我
非生而知之者好古敏以求之者也其惓惓於
學如此豈非謙已誨人而欲人知所從事乎奈
之何人不知好學之爲務也噫學而不厭聖之
所以益聖困而不學愚之所以益愚然則有志
學道者其尚猛省夫子之言哉
可以贊天地之化育則可以與天地參矣

translation_en:
…dare not rely on their own qualities, as I, Qiu, do? My efforts to seek the Way redouble as my heart yearns toward it. Thus I love antiquity and diligently seek understanding, applying myself tirelessly each day. I contemplate the manifest principles of things, investigating and refining my understanding of them until they become one with my own person, hoping thereby to come to hear the supreme Way. Among those who are loyal and trustworthy, are there any who know how to exert themselves as I do? Learning lies within my power, and I must pursue it to the utmost; as for the loyalty and trustworthiness within me, I take no account of them. This is why I, Qiu, begin the same as others but end by differing from them.

Ah! In saying this, could the Master really have been vaunting himself to impress others? He was simply encouraging others to learn, wishing them all to arrive together at the Way. Was this not his desire to join others in doing good? Alas, how great is the importance of learning for human beings! Even the Master, though born with knowledge, never failed to love learning. How much more, then, should others! The Master once said, “At fifteen I set my heart on learning.” He also said, “I am not one born with knowledge; I love antiquity and am diligent in seeking it.” So devoted was he to learning: was this not a way of humbling himself and instructing others, wishing them to know where to direct their efforts? Why, then, do people fail to recognize that loving learning is their proper task? Ah! Learning without weariness is how the sage becomes ever more sagely; being beset by difficulties yet failing to learn is how the foolish become ever more foolish. Let those resolved to learn the Way earnestly reflect upon the Master’s words!

“If one can assist in the transforming and nourishing work of Heaven and Earth, one can then form a triad with Heaven and Earth.”

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
道而後可以爲人則於化育乎人者不有以贊
而成之耶盡人之性且以盡物之性使之各遂
其生而後可以爲物則於化育乎物者不有以
贊而全之耶如是則其參天地也不亦宜乎何
則人非天地不生生人而賦之性固天地之分
也而盡人之性不與焉茲不在於聖人乎物非
天地不育育物而賦之性固天地之限也而盡
物之性不與焉茲可責之他人乎故天位乎上
地與之偶宜無復與倫矣而聖人贊之以成其
===
功是有天不可以無聖人也則聖人與天等爾
獨地乎哉地位乎下天與之對宜無復能肖矣
而聖人贊之以全其用是有地不可以無聖人
也則聖人與地均爾獨天乎哉謂之曰與天地
參信乎上則有天下則有地中則有聖人可以
並立而爲三也吁至誠盡性之功其大如此子
思言天道而有以及之其亦深達天人之妙者
歟考之禮其論參天地者不一而足有曰聖人
參於天地有曰天子與天地參有曰三王之德

translation_en:
…the Way, and only then can they fully become human. In the transformation and nurture of human beings, does the sage not thereby assist and bring the process to completion? Having fully realized human nature, he also fully realizes the nature of things, enabling each to fulfill its life and only then fully become what it is. In the transformation and nurture of things, does he not thereby assist and bring the process to perfection? If so, is it not fitting that he should form a triad with Heaven and Earth? Why is this? Without Heaven and Earth, human beings would not be born. To produce human beings and endow them with their nature is indeed the allotted task of Heaven and Earth; yet fully realizing human nature is not included in it. Does this not rest with the sage? Without Heaven and Earth, things would not be nurtured. To nurture things and endow them with their nature is indeed the limit of Heaven and Earth’s task; yet fully realizing the nature of things is not included in it. Can this responsibility be demanded of anyone else?

Thus Heaven occupies its place above, with Earth as its partner; one might suppose that nothing else could rank alongside it. Yet the sage assists it in completing its achievement. This means that, where there is Heaven, the sage cannot be dispensed with. The sage therefore stands equal to Heaven—could Earth alone do so? Earth occupies its place below, with Heaven as its counterpart; one might suppose that nothing else could match it. Yet the sage assists it in bringing its operation to fulfillment. This means that, where there is Earth, the sage cannot be dispensed with. The sage therefore stands equal to Earth—could Heaven alone do so? How true it is to say that he “forms a triad with Heaven and Earth”! Above is Heaven, below is Earth, and between them is the sage: they can stand together as three.

Ah! Such is the greatness of the achievement of utmost sincerity in fully realizing nature! 參於天地。於此則曰：「至誠與天地參。」雖其言屢出，而各有所指，然皆不外乎德與政也。其所謂德，又必以至誠盡性爲極；所謂政，又必以賛化育爲極。則聖人所以聖者，殆不可復加，而天人所爲全備無缺，理一分殊之妙，見於言外者，亦可識矣。噫！此其所以爲子思乎！

translation_en:
…participates with Heaven and Earth. Here, however, he says: “Utmost sincerity participates with Heaven and Earth.” Although this expression occurs repeatedly, each occurrence has its own referent; nevertheless, all concern virtue and government. What is called virtue must culminate in utmost sincerity and the full realization of one’s nature; what is called government must culminate in assisting the transforming and nourishing processes of creation. Thus, what makes the sage a sage can scarcely be carried any further, and the workings of Heaven and humanity are complete, lacking nothing. The subtlety of principle being one while its particular manifestations differ can also be discerned beyond the words themselves. Ah! Is this not what makes Zisi who he is?
“Wherever the gentleman passes, transformation follows; wherever he abides, his influence is spirit-like. Above and below, he flows together with Heaven and Earth. How could this be called merely a small contribution?”
Wu Jing
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Assistant Instructor: Transformation wherever he passes and spirit-like influence wherever he abides both refer to the virtue and achievements of a true king. Writers can generally discuss the former, but when it comes to the latter, they fall decidedly short in their understanding. This essay offers a clear analysis, and its literary power is sufficient to bring out the meaning. It should be recorded as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Assistant Instructor: Flowing together with Heaven and Earth, rather than making the small contribution of a hegemon—this is precisely where the greatness of the Kingly Way lies. Students generally discuss its aspects separately and praise them. This script alone grasps this meaning; its language and tone are unhurried and ample, revealing no trace of effort. It describes the greatness of the Kingly Way well: how could we fail to select it?
Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Assistant Mentor: This, too, is someone who speaks well of the Kingly Way.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Expositor-in-waiting: He is able to enter into the meaning of Zhu Xi’s commentary.

於造化也而王者之道與之同焉豈覇者可得
而並論哉孟子論王道之所以大者如此何則
君子者以德言則聖人以位言則王者也其道
若之何而大耶誠以身之所過特其一時經歷
云耳而人自無不化焉聲光所被而得於觀感
者幡然而自新足跡所加而得於見聞者翕然

translation_en: The great worthy explains that the Kingly Way shares in the creative transformations of nature and is inherently distinct from the achievements of a hegemon. For nothing is greater than nature’s creative transformations, and the way of a true king accords with them. How could a hegemon be discussed on equal terms with him? Such is Mencius’s account of what makes the Kingly Way great. Why is this so? The noble man, considered in terms of virtue, is a sage; considered in terms of position, he is a true king. How, then, is his way great? Wherever he passes in person, he merely spends a moment passing through, yet the people are naturally transformed, without exception. Those reached by his voice and radiance, who benefit from observing him and being moved by his example, turn about and renew themselves; those reached by his footsteps, who benefit from what they see and hear, remain unchanged in unison [?]. How profound is the transformation wherever he passes! What he holds within his heart is merely the directing force of a single thought, yet its spiritual efficacy is naturally unfathomable. Just as his spiritual energies begin to operate, those who sing of imperial power already work and rest of their own accord; just as his mind begins to devise plans, those who follow the imperial pattern do so without conscious recognition or knowledge. How wondrous is the spiritual efficacy of what he holds within! Thus his virtue and accomplishments may be called abundant indeed. With what, then, can they be compared? Giving all things their beginning and leaving nothing uncovered: such is Heaven’s relation to things. The noble man takes an entire age and fashions it, so great that nothing lies outside his scope. This is precisely like Heaven, which leaves nothing uncovered. Above, does he not operate in concert with Heaven’s transforming activity? Giving all things life and leaving nothing unsupported: such is Earth’s relation to things. The noble man takes all under Heaven and molds it, so expansive that his scope has no bounds. This is precisely like Earth, which leaves nothing unsupported. Below, does he not proceed in concert with Earth’s transforming activity? The Kingly Way accords with Heaven and Earth…

有如此者，視彼霸者之於其民，屑屑焉違道以干譽，煦煦焉狥情以市恩，要其所就，不過小小補塞其罅漏而已，豈可與同日而語耶？信乎，王道之大，非霸功所能彷彿其萬一也。孟子論王霸之殊，至此盖瞭然矣。大抵時至戰國，功利之說勝，而義理之學微，其肆為縱横捭闔者，日交騖於天下，抑孰知王道之當行哉？孟子慨然有志帝王之治，故每以尊王賤霸為言。惜乎時不能用，而世道竟不可復。然百世之下，吾人皆知王霸義利之辨，而治天下者尚有頼焉，其功不可誣也。君子謂其繼孔子而得道統之傳，觀此益信。

易

謙，亨。天道下濟而光明，地道卑而上行。天道虧盈而益謙，地道變盈而流謙，鬼神害盈而福謙，人道惡盈而好謙。謙，尊而光，卑而不可踰，君子之終也。

劉鎮
translation_en:
…in this way. Consider, by contrast, how the hegemons treat their people: fussily violating the Way to seek acclaim, dispensing petty kindnesses and yielding to people's feelings to purchase their favor. In the end, their achievements amount to no more than minor repairs to plug the gaps. How could the two be mentioned in the same breath? Truly, the greatness of the Kingly Way is such that the achievements of hegemons cannot approach even one ten-thousandth of it. At this point, Mengzi's discussion has made the distinction between true kings and hegemons entirely clear. By the Warring States period, doctrines of achievement and profit had generally prevailed, while the learning of moral principle had declined. Those who gave free rein to schemes of vertical and horizontal alliances and diplomatic manipulation competed daily throughout the realm. Who among them understood that the Kingly Way ought to be practiced? Mengzi, deeply moved, aspired to the government of the ancient emperors and kings. Thus he repeatedly spoke of honoring true kings and disparaging hegemons. Regrettably, his age could not put his teachings into practice, and the world ultimately could not be restored to the proper course. Yet a hundred generations later, we all understand the distinctions between kingship and hegemony, righteousness and profit, and those who govern the realm still have his teachings to rely upon. His contribution cannot be denied. Learned gentlemen say that he succeeded Kongzi and received the transmission of the succession of the Way. Considering this makes that claim still more convincing.

Book of Changes

“Modesty: success. The Way of Heaven extends downward in aid and shines brightly; the Way of Earth is lowly, yet moves upward. The Way of Heaven diminishes fullness and augments modesty; the Way of Earth alters fullness and channels its bounty toward modesty. Ghosts and spirits harm the full and bless the modest; the way of human beings is to dislike fullness and favor modesty. Through modesty, those in high station shine, and those in low station cannot be surpassed. This is the noble man's consummation.”

Liu Zhen

===
之義蓋人之得亨與有其終要必有所自也而
能謙者兼而有之此君子所以貴於謙歟昔文

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, an Instructor: The topic itself is readily understood. But when one tries to give parallel treatment to the explanations of “success” and “having an ending,” it is difficult to balance their lengths, and many writers are hampered by this. This essay develops its ideas in accordance with the text and is thoroughly orderly. It deserves inclusion in the record.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, an Instructor: “Diminishing what is excessive and augmenting what is deficient, weighing things and distributing impartially”—this is the method of modesty. This essay seems to apply that principle in its writing. Here is what is meant by being concise yet capable of amplitude, and elaborate yet free from disorder: this is an accomplished writer.
Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Mentor: Far surpasses the other essays.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting: Balanced and orderly, and worthy of recitation.
In his Commentary on the Judgment, the sage first elucidated why modesty must bring success, and then elucidated why modesty must bring a successful ending. For a person’s attaining success and bringing matters to their proper conclusion must have a source; one who can be modest possesses both. Is this why the gentleman prizes modesty? Formerly, King Wen appended to the hexagram Modesty the words: “Success. The gentleman has an ending.” Our Master explained these words in his Commentary on the Judgment. His meaning was that, in human undertakings, frustration is frequent and smooth success rare. Why, then, does modesty attain success? Why not look to Heaven and Earth? The light and clear take on celestial configurations: Heaven’s proper position is above. The heavy and turbid take on concrete form: Earth’s proper position is below. Heaven sends its vital force downward to interact with Earth, and its work of transforming and nurturing shines with a brilliance that cannot be concealed. Earth, in fulfilling its office, humbly takes its place after Qian, the Creative, and its vital force of reciprocal response rises vigorously upward, beyond obstruction. To descend and interact with Earth is Heaven’s modesty; its Way is therefore radiant, and its success can be seen…

text:
矣卑處乾後地之謙也而其道上行亨可知矣
謙必有亨盖如此夫莫難得者亨通也而天地
以謙得之况於人而可不謙哉若乃人之所行
有始者易克終者難又何謙之得其終也曷不
觀諸天地神人乎盖盈而滿者乃所以招損也
謙而虚者乃所以受益也天地之道其於盈者
既虧之變之矣而獨於謙則益且流焉鬼神與
人其於盈者既害之惡之矣而獨於謙則福且
好焉故君子以謙抑為尚而得於天人之所祐
===
則在尊位也德盛而彌光始雖屈矣不有以伸
於後乎以盈滿為戒而不為天人之所廢則在
下位也德崇而難及終則揚矣不由於初之抑
乎謙必有終盖如此夫莫難得者有終也而君
子以謙致之况衆人而可不謙哉吁聖人於釋
謙亨則若兩言而有餘於釋有終則又累言而
不足于以見謙固能亨而亨尤貴於有終也其
所以勸勉吾人者至矣抑文王周公繫卦與爻
惟謙占辭最美聖人傳彖與象亦惟謙賛辭為

…Taking a lowly place behind Qian, the Creative, is Earth’s humility; yet its way moves upward, so its success can be understood. Such is the reason humility must bring success. Nothing is harder to obtain than success, yet Heaven and Earth obtain it through humility. How much less, then, can human beings dispense with humility?

As for human conduct, beginning is easy, but carrying through to the end is difficult. Why, then, does humility enable one to reach a worthy end? Why not consider Heaven, Earth, spirits, and human beings? Being full and overflowing invites loss; being humble and empty allows one to receive benefit. In their ways, Heaven and Earth diminish and alter what is full, but augment what is humble and cause abundance to flow to it. Spirits and human beings harm and hate what is full, but bless and favor what is humble. Thus the gentleman prizes humility and restraint and receives the protection of Heaven and human beings. When he occupies an exalted position, his abundant virtue shines all the more brightly. Though initially bowed down, does he not thereby gain the means to rise afterward? He guards against fullness and complacency and is not cast aside by Heaven and human beings. When he occupies a lowly position, his lofty virtue is difficult to equal. That he is exalted in the end—does this not arise from his initial self-restraint? Such is the reason humility must bring a worthy end. Nothing is harder to obtain than a worthy end, yet the gentleman achieves it through humility. How much less, then, can ordinary people dispense with humility?

…so abundant, uniquely distinguishing it from the other hexagrams—why is this? Humility is a beautiful human virtue, and everything that Heaven, Earth, spirits, and human beings approve converges in humility. This is what makes humility unique. Despite his diligence and frugality, Yu the Great still did not boast of his achievements; despite possessing such admirable talents, the Duke of Zhou still did not dare to be arrogant. Were they not men who prospered and carried matters through to the end? Such was the greatness of their sagely virtue: handed down throughout the world and to later generations, it shines ever more brightly with the passage of time. Ah, how splendid!

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
造化有以肇卜筮之器聖人因以立卜筮之法
盖天生蓍龜其爲物也神矣聖人從而則之豈
不立卜筮之法於天下哉大傳十一章專言卜
筮及此若曰易之爲易果何爲而作哉而蓍之
與龜則其所本之一也彼其植而爲衆卉之異
者爲蓍是蓍也天以生之而其莖長丈其叢滿
百以具圓神之德一天之和氣所毓乎動而爲
介族之靈者爲龜是龜也天以生之而五行中
具八卦外列以含默藏之智一天之禎祥所鍾
===
乎蓍生矣而豈偶然哉天將有意於立筮以前
斯民之用也龜生矣而豈徒然哉天將有意於
立卜以開斯人之先也於是聖人者出上明天
道而有以發造化之祕下察民故而有以通天
下之情則夫蓍也用之四十有九于以假分揲
掛扐之四營或成卦焉或成爻焉而所以前民
用者於是乎存則夫龜也鑽之七十有二于以
著雨霽蒙驛克之五兆或爲陰焉或爲陽焉而
所以開民先者於是乎在泰筮之法立而用靜

造化有以肇卜筮之器，聖人因以立卜筮之法。

盖天生蓍龜，其爲物也神矣。聖人從而則之，豈不立卜筮之法於天下哉？大傳十一章專言卜筮，及此若曰：易之爲易，果何爲而作哉？而蓍之與龜，則其所本之一也。彼其植而爲衆卉之異者爲蓍。是蓍也，天以生之，而其莖長丈，其叢滿百，以具圓神之德，一天之和氣所毓乎？動而爲介族之靈者爲龜。是龜也，天以生之，而五行中具，八卦外列，以含默藏之智，一天之禎祥所鍾乎？蓍生矣，而豈偶然哉？天將有意於立筮，以前斯民之用也。龜生矣，而豈徒然哉？天將有意於立卜，以開斯人之先也。於是聖人者出，上明天道，而有以發造化之祕；下察民故，而有以通天下之情。則夫蓍也，用之四十有九，于以假分揲掛扐之四營，或成卦焉，或成爻焉，而所以前民用者於是乎存。則夫龜也，鑽之七十有二，于以著雨霽蒙驛克之五兆，或爲陰焉，或爲陽焉，而所以開民先者於是乎在。泰筮之法立，而用靜
translation_en:
The workings of creation brought forth the instruments of shell and milfoil divination; the sages, building upon these, established the methods of divination.

Heaven produced milfoil and tortoises, things endowed with spiritual efficacy. Following them and taking them as models, did the sages not establish methods of divination throughout the world? Chapter Eleven of the Great Commentary deals specifically with divination. At this point it seems to say: for what purpose, indeed, was the Changes made what it is? Milfoil and tortoises are among its foundations. Among growing plants, milfoil stands apart from all other herbs. Heaven produced this milfoil with stalks a zhang in length and a hundred stems to a clump, endowing it with the virtue of rounded spiritual responsiveness. Is it not nurtured entirely by Heaven’s harmonious vital energy? Among moving creatures, the tortoise is the spiritually potent member of the shelled kind. Heaven produced this tortoise with the Five Phases complete within and the Eight Trigrams arrayed without, embodying wisdom silently concealed. Is it not a concentration of Heaven’s auspicious influences?

Could the production of milfoil have been accidental? Heaven intended to establish milfoil divination to guide the people’s undertakings in advance. Could the production of tortoises have been without purpose? Heaven intended to establish shell divination to give people foreknowledge. Then the sages arose. Above, they understood the Way of Heaven and thereby disclosed the secrets of creation; below, they examined human affairs and thereby comprehended the circumstances of all under Heaven. Taking milfoil as their model, they used forty-nine stalks and employed the four operations of dividing, counting, setting aside, and holding the remainders between the fingers, forming hexagrams or individual lines. Herein lay the means of guiding the people’s undertakings in advance. Taking the tortoise as their model, they bored seventy-two holes in its shell, thereby revealing the five kinds of cracks: rain, clearing skies, cloudiness, discontinuity, and crossing. These might be yin or yang; herein lay the means of giving the people foreknowledge. Once the method of great milfoil divination [?] was established, those employing it in stillness …

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
用作者有所資吉凶悔吝已昭然而莫揜矣是
雖蓍有以兆之聖人先物之智可少哉蓍之神
固聖人之神也泰龜之法行而人謀鬼謀者有
所頼吉凶得失已瞭然而無疑矣是雖龜有以
啓之聖人創物之功可忘哉龜之神固聖人之
神也夫以蓍龜之神其原出於天其制裁於聖
人者如此此卜筮之用所以爲大而聖人作易
之功所由見也歟雖然易之用固以蓍龜爲大
然非象數與辭之周則枯莖敗甲其何以通天
===
下之志定天下之業哉故卜筮占也象數理也
二者並行不悖而易之道始全矣夫以蓍龜有
關於易者如此世之人顧以筮短龜長議之而
從違於其間何其不知易之甚耶

translation_en:
…those who act have something to rely upon, and good fortune, misfortune, regret, and humiliation are already plainly revealed, with nothing concealed. Although the milfoil provides these indications, can the sage’s wisdom in anticipating things be belittled? The spiritual efficacy of milfoil is indeed the spiritual efficacy of the sage. When the method of great tortoise divination [?] is put into practice, those who consult human beings and spirits have something to rely upon; good fortune and misfortune, gain and loss, are already clear and beyond doubt. Although the tortoise discloses these things, can the sage’s achievement in establishing institutions be forgotten? The spiritual efficacy of the tortoise is indeed the spiritual efficacy of the sage.

Thus the spiritual efficacy of milfoil and tortoise originates in Heaven, while its regulation rests with the sage. Is this not why the uses of divination are so great, and how the sage’s achievement in making the Book of Changes becomes manifest? Nevertheless, although milfoil and tortoise are central to the use of the Changes, without the completeness of its images, numbers, and statements, how could withered stalks and decaying shells give access to the intentions of all under Heaven and settle the undertakings of all under Heaven? Divination by tortoise and milfoil concerns prognostication; images and numbers concern principle. Only when the two operate together without contradiction is the Way of the Changes complete. Given this relationship between milfoil, tortoise, and the Changes, how profoundly ignorant of the Changes are those who nevertheless argue that milfoil divination is inferior and tortoise divination superior, accepting one and rejecting the other!

納忠言而不逆，任舊臣而不違，先王之修人紀然也。盖忠言不可逆，舊臣不可違也。無盡是道者，孰有過於先王也哉？昔太甲嗣位之初，伊尹以成湯修人紀者訓之，謂夫人紀之修，先王所以為聖；修紀之實，吾王在所當知。是故世之忠諫者，盡言不諱，多勿欺而犯之辭；鯁直不阿，無面從退言之弊。或援古以證今之失，或戒後以懲前之非，其剴切易至於見拒也，是孰能容耶？惟我先王於是言也，則知其為圖治之良規，即委心而聽受之，雖貴而在朝者，不以其勢逼而見猜；取其為保邦之至計，即虛己而延納之，雖賤而在野者，不以其跡疎而見忤。諤諤之論□

…and enduring in its resonance. It also brings out what Yi Yin left unexpressed. Might its author likewise aspire to such loyalty and loving concern?
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: The language is composed and ample, and the writing mature and vigorous. It portrays Yi Yin’s loyalty and loving concern so vividly that one can readily imagine them. A work of classical scholarship such as this well deserves inclusion in the record.
Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Companion: It articulates what others cannot express.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: This is writing of real consequence.
To accept loyal words without resisting them, and to employ longstanding ministers without going against them: this was how the former king cultivated the norms of human relationships. Loyal words must not be resisted, and longstanding ministers must not be opposed. Who could have surpassed the former king in fully realizing this Way [?]? Formerly, when Tai Jia first succeeded to the throne, Yi Yin instructed him through the example of Cheng Tang’s cultivation of human relationships. He meant that cultivating these norms was what made the former king a sage, and that our king ought to understand the practical substance of their cultivation.
Thus, those in the world who remonstrate loyally speak fully and without concealment. Their words frequently exemplify the principle of never deceiving their ruler, even at the cost of offending him. Forthright and unbending, they avoid the fault of agreeing to his face and criticizing him after withdrawing. Some invoke antiquity to demonstrate present failings; others warn about what lies ahead to correct earlier errors. Their incisiveness readily leads to their rejection. Who can accommodate such men?
Our former king alone recognized these words as sound guidance for achieving good government and therefore listened to and accepted them wholeheartedly. Even when their speakers were eminent men at court, he did not suspect them because their power pressed close upon his own. He valued their words as the best counsel for preserving the state and therefore received and welcomed them with humility. Even when their speakers were men of humble station outside office, he did not take offense at them because they were remote from him. Forthright arguments [illegible character]…

text:
之惟恐不足恢恢之量容之常若有餘盖導之
而使言則有矣未有聞其言而弗納也夫於其
難容者而能容之則忠言之在當時者何有不
日至乎人之耆舊者齒尊德隆為生民之倚賴
位高望重為治道之指南老成焉而類迂闊質
朴焉而若遲鈍其年耄易至於見疎也又孰能
親耶惟我先王於是人也則念其練達也深于
以信如蓍龜而敬順之不遑雖近而一朝一夕
恒置於左右嘉其閱歷也久于以待如神明而
===
遵信之惟謹雖小而一話一言亦取為法程行
如所言惟循其舊立之規心如其貌不替乎初
待之敬盖聞之而輒從則有矣未有從之後而
復悖也夫於其當親者而能親之則舊臣之在
當時者何敢不盡心乎是則不逆忠言以廣容
人之量不違舊臣以盡優老之誠先王之修人
紀如此可謂誠於樂善者矣吾王可不念之哉

之，惟恐不足；恢恢之量，容之常若有餘。盖導之而使言則有矣，未有聞其言而弗納也。夫於其難容者而能容之，則忠言之在當時者，何有不日至乎？人之耆舊者，齒尊德隆，為生民之倚賴；位高望重，為治道之指南。老成焉而類迂闊，質朴焉而若遲鈍，其年耄易至於見疎也，又孰能親耶？惟我先王於是人也，則念其練達也深，于以信如蓍龜，而敬順之不遑，雖近而一朝一夕，恒置於左右；嘉其閱歷也久，于以待如神明，而遵信之惟謹，雖小而一話一言，亦取為法程。行如所言，惟循其舊立之規；心如其貌，不替乎初待之敬。盖聞之而輒從則有矣，未有從之後而復悖也。夫於其當親者而能親之，則舊臣之在當時者，何敢不盡心乎？是則不逆忠言，以廣容人之量；不違舊臣，以盡優老之誠。先王之修人紀如此，可謂誠於樂善者矣。吾王可不念之哉？

translation_en:
…them, fearing only that it was insufficient; his capacious generosity always seemed to have room to spare in accommodating them. He did indeed encourage them to speak; never did he hear their words and refuse to accept them. If he could accommodate those whom it was difficult to accommodate, how could loyal counsel in his time fail to arrive daily?
Those who are elders of long service, venerable in years and eminent in virtue, are a support upon whom the people depend; high in position and weighty in reputation, they are guides to the way of governance. Yet their seasoned judgment may seem impractical, and their plain sincerity may appear slow-witted. Their advanced age readily causes them to be kept at a distance. Who, then, can keep them close? Our former king, however, considered the depth of their experience and understanding, trusting them like divining milfoil and tortoise shells and showing tireless respect and deference. Even for so brief a span as a single morning or evening, he constantly kept them beside him. He esteemed their long experience, treating them like divine intelligences and taking the greatest care to follow and trust them. Even something as small as a single remark or word he adopted as a standard. His actions accorded with their words, following the rules they had long established; his inward feelings matched his outward demeanor, never diminishing the respect with which he had first treated them. He did indeed follow their advice whenever he heard it; never did he follow it only to go against it afterward. If he could keep close those whom he ought to keep close, how could the veteran ministers of his time dare not devote themselves wholeheartedly?
Thus, by not rejecting loyal counsel, he enlarged his capacity to accommodate others; by not going against veteran ministers, he fully expressed his sincerity in honoring the aged. Such was the former king’s cultivation of the proper human relationships. He may truly be called sincere in delighting in goodness. Can our king fail to reflect upon this?
As for Tai Jia [?], he failed to reflect upon what he heard and abandoned his preceptors and guardians. In respect of what is called accepting loyal counsel and heeding veteran ministers, he could hardly have been without cause for shame at his conduct. Yi Yin discerned the first subtle signs of this beforehand…

…Thus he earnestly addressed these words to him, seeking to stir him to change his course: his loyalty was utmost indeed. Thereafter, the king maintained his virtue to the end, shining gloriously in the historical records. Although Heaven’s mandate resting upon Shang seemed to guide him unseen, this also resulted from Yi Yin’s instruction and admonition at the outset. Mencius said, “Only a great man can correct what is wrong in the ruler’s heart.” Was he not speaking of Yi Yin? Those who serve as great ministers in later generations should take him as their model.
“Do not say that you cannot accomplish it; only exert your heart to the utmost. Do not say that the people are few; only attend carefully to your duties.”
Wang Chong
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Assistant Instructor: The meaning of King Kang’s address to the Duke of Bi is expounded almost exhaustively. The discussion of the heart and of duties is especially perceptive. Its merit lies in aptness rather than novelty. It should be accepted.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: This paper elucidates the essentials of protecting and governing through the two words ‘heart’ and ‘duties’ alone. This is precisely King Kang’s meaning. Moreover, its language is dignified and its principles correct; it thoroughly captures the form of a written royal charge. An excellent composition: accept it.
Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Mentor: The reasoning is lucid, and the writing’s spirit abundant.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: The beginning and end correspond with one another; the writing has strength.
When a worthy king commissions a great minister, the minister should plan for what is difficult and not neglect what is easy. For the essentials of protecting and governing lie simply in giving full expression to sincerity, inwardly and outwardly. If he regards his charge in terms of difficulty or ease and forgets the duties incumbent upon him, how can he transform the people of Yin and discharge his office? Formerly, King Kang commissioned the Duke of Bi to protect and govern Chengzhou. At the close of the chapter, he sighed and admonished…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之如此謂夫成周之事既付我公所以保釐之
者豈言語所能盡邪彼視之太重而畏其難則
有所不敢為矣如治何公斯往也其勿曰周公
毖於始而利口之餘風未殄君陳和於中而怙
侈之放心未閑予何人哉而有是任也其弗能
勝矣乎自我觀之亦惟既厥心焉耳盖心者為
治之本而主乎其内也心有不既則事為徒法
其可哉必也有弗謀焉謀則精粗俱到謀人之
所不能謀有弗慮焉慮則巨細不遺慮人之所
===
不及慮千里之憂紆籌於几席之下百世之患
决策於旦暮之間何者為淑何者為慝而權度
之不差如是則剛如是則柔而酌量之必審如
此則心無不盡而成周可治矣尚何難之足畏
哉視之太輕而忽其易則以為不足為矣如民
何公此行也其勿曰一人莫非其臣今則蕞爾
殷民已化周公之毖尺地莫非其有今則遷於
洛邑已被君陳之和彼何人斯而有他志也其
無足虞矣乎自我言之亦惟慎厥事焉耳盖事

punctuated: 之如此，謂夫成周之事既付我公，所以保釐之者，豈言語所能盡邪？彼視之太重而畏其難，則有所不敢為矣，如治何？公斯往也，其勿曰：「周公毖於始，而利口之餘風未殄；君陳和於中，而怙侈之放心未閑。予何人哉，而有是任也？其弗能勝矣乎？」自我觀之，亦惟既厥心焉耳。盖心者，為治之本而主乎其内也。心有不既，則事為徒法，其可哉？必也有弗謀焉，謀則精粗俱到，謀人之所不能謀；有弗慮焉，慮則巨細不遺，慮人之所不及慮。千里之憂，紆籌於几席之下；百世之患，决策於旦暮之間。何者為淑，何者為慝，而權度之不差；如是則剛，如是則柔，而酌量之必審。如此則心無不盡，而成周可治矣，尚何難之足畏哉？視之太輕而忽其易，則以為不足為矣，如民何？公此行也，其勿曰：「一人莫非其臣，今則蕞爾殷民，已化周公之毖；尺地莫非其有，今則遷於洛邑，已被君陳之和。彼何人斯，而有他志也？其無足虞矣乎？」自我言之，亦惟慎厥事焉耳。盖事
translation_en:
…admonished him in this way, meaning: “The affairs of Chengzhou have now been entrusted to you, my duke. How could words exhaust all that is involved in preserving its peace and governing it? If you regard the task as too weighty and fear its difficulty, there will be things you dare not undertake. What, then, will become of government? As you go, my duke, do not say: ‘The Duke of Zhou exercised vigilance at the outset, yet the lingering habit of glib speech has not been extinguished; Jun Chen brought harmony in the intervening period, yet unrestrained hearts, clinging to extravagance, have not been checked. Who am I to bear this responsibility? Surely I cannot discharge it?’ From my perspective, you need only devote your whole heart to it.

“The heart is the foundation of government and governs what lies within. If the heart is not fully engaged, administrative measures become mere rules. How could that suffice? You may refrain from planning, but once you plan, attend to both the fine points and the broad outlines, planning what others cannot plan. You may refrain from deliberating, but once you deliberate, overlook neither great matters nor small, considering what others fail to consider. For troubles a thousand li away, work out your plans at your desk; for dangers extending over a hundred generations, determine your measures within the span of a day. Weigh without error what is good and what is evil; judge with care which circumstances call for firmness and which for gentleness. In this way, your heart will be fully engaged, and Chengzhou can be governed. What difficulty will then be worth fearing?

“If you regard the task too lightly and neglect it because it seems easy, you will think it unworthy of your efforts. What, then, will become of the people? On this journey, my duke, do not say: ‘There is not a single person who is not the king’s subject; now this small remnant of the Yin people has already been transformed by the Duke of Zhou’s vigilance. There is not a foot of land that is not the king’s possession; now, having been moved to Luoyi, they have already received the benefits of Jun Chen’s harmonious rule. Who are they to harbor other intentions? Surely there is nothing to worry about?’ As I would put it, you need only attend carefully to your duties. For administrative affairs…”

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者為治之具而行乎其外也事有不慎則心為
徒善其可哉必也將有安焉則謹其割裂之施
而不過於嚴將有理焉則慎其潤澤之及而不
傷乎縱品式已脩而猶恐其或弛規模既備而
猶懼其或疎表宅里殊井疆所以彰善而癉惡
者必欲其當申郊圻慎封守所以防微而杜漸
者必欲其周如此則事無不慎而殷民可化矣
尚何易之可忽哉吁心既則事之慎者以成事
慎則心之既者不失而慎于始和于中者亦庶
===
乎克成于終矣康王以是而命畢公其戒勉之
意何其深且切歟抑論之武王一戎衣而有天
下克殷如此其易成康繼體至於世歷三紀殷
民猶未率從如此其難何也盖紂之暴虐生民
如在水火故就拯之者為甚急耳天下既定良
心復萌則又思先王之德而不忍棄此周人號
為強民而三后相繼於洛畢命諸篇所以作也
然非殷民之頑亦無以見周室之仁而錮陰沍
寒卒消融於春風和氣其長治久安衍八百年

punctuated: 者，為治之具而行乎其外也。事有不慎，則心為徒善，其可哉？必也將有安焉，則謹其割裂之施，而不過於嚴；將有理焉，則慎其潤澤之及，而不傷乎縱。品式已脩，而猶恐其或弛；規模既備，而猶懼其或疎。表宅里，殊井疆，所以彰善而癉惡者，必欲其當；申郊圻，慎封守，所以防微而杜漸者，必欲其周。如此，則事無不慎，而殷民可化矣，尚何易之可忽哉？吁！心既，則事之慎者以成；事慎，則心之既者不失。而慎于始、和于中者，亦庶乎克成于終矣。康王以是而命畢公，其戒勉之意何其深且切歟！抑論之，武王一戎衣而有天下，克殷如此其易；成康繼體，至於世歷三紀，殷民猶未率從，如此其難，何也？盖紂之暴虐，生民如在水火，故就拯之者為甚急耳。天下既定，良心復萌，則又思先王之德而不忍棄。此周人號為強民，而三后相繼於洛，《畢命》諸篇所以作也。然非殷民之頑，亦無以見周室之仁，而錮陰沍寒卒消融於春風和氣，其長治久安衍八百年
translation_en:
…affairs are the instruments of government, carried out in the external realm. If affairs are handled without care, the heart’s goodness remains ineffectual. How could that be acceptable? If the aim is to bring peace, one must carefully apply measures of division and separation, without being excessively severe; if the aim is to establish order, one must carefully extend beneficent nurture, without lapsing into indulgence. Though standards and regulations have been put in order, one must still fear that they may grow lax; though the framework is complete, one must still fear that it may have gaps. In marking out dwellings and neighborhoods and distinguishing field boundaries—the means of honoring goodness and condemning evil—one must insist on fitting measures. In defining the suburban boundaries and attending carefully to the defense of the borders—the means of guarding against the slightest danger and preventing its growth—one must insist on thorough provision. In this way, no affair will be handled without care, and the people of Yin can be transformed. How, then, could anything be neglected as easy?

Ah! When the heart is fully devoted, affairs undertaken with care reach completion; when affairs are handled carefully, the heart’s full devotion is not lost. Thus, what was begun with caution and continued with harmony may also be brought to a successful conclusion. King Kang charged the Duke of Bi in these terms: how profound and earnest was his intention to admonish and encourage him!

Consider further: King Wu donned his military robes once and possessed All under Heaven—so easy was the conquest of Yin. Kings Cheng and Kang succeeded to the throne, yet even after three cycles of twelve years the people of Yin had still not submitted—so difficult was it. Why? Under Zhou’s cruel tyranny, the people lived as though amid water and fire, and so they hastened with the utmost urgency to whoever would rescue them. Once All under Heaven was settled, their innate good heart stirred again, and they remembered the virtue of their former kings and could not bear to abandon them. This is why the Zhou called them an intractable people, why three sovereigns successively concerned themselves with Luo, and why such chapters as “The Charge to Bi” were composed. Yet without the obstinacy of the people of Yin, there would have been no means of revealing the benevolence of the house of Zhou. The entrenched gloom and freezing cold finally melted in the spring breeze and its gentle warmth, and its enduring order and lasting peace extended for eight hundred years…

Book of Odes

“Like flight, like soaring; like the Jiang, like the Han; like the firm mass of a mountain, like the flow of a river; unbroken and orderly, unfathomable and unconquerable.”

Liu Ke

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Assistant Instructor: Most candidates can speak of the grandeur of military might, but they do not understand its setting on the banks of the Huai [?]. Moreover, their explanations repeat themselves from beginning to end and offer little satisfaction. This script’s analysis is clear and orderly; it sweeps away every stale expression. The concluding words are particularly rich in lingering meaning. Admirable! Admirable!

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor: The wording of this topic recurs, yet its meanings differ in each instance, making it difficult for writers to distinguish them. For lucid discrimination, apt language, and clear reasoning, no essay equals this one. I have therefore singled it out for presentation.

Comment by Associate Examiner She, Instructor: In treating this topic from the Greater Odes, writers in the examination hall fail to consider that the passage already contains six instances of “like.” In their explanations they proceed to add further comparisons, piling them up in tedious profusion until one tires of reading. This essay alone carefully distinguishes each word, with clear reasoning and vigorous language. It can serve as a model for writers of essays on the meaning of the Classics; hence its inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Vice Mentor: “The Odes are correct and yet ornate.” This composition possesses those qualities.

Comment by Examiner Wu, Expositor-in-Waiting: The exposition is clear and clean.

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
詩人於周王之師必極言其兵威之盛也盖王
師無敵於天下也詩人舉其兵威而極言之所
以昭一時之盛也歟是詩美宣王自將以伐淮
北之夷其意謂夫外夷猾夏固天討之所當加
兵威極盛又王師之所當尚我宣王之伐淮夷
也其師何如其盛哉想其以所將之師陳淮浦
之上彼至疾者莫飛翰若也我師所至速於應
變威武自爾其奮揚敏於趨事王靈不覺其震
蕩其疾不如飛如翰乎至衆者莫江漢過也我
===
師所在武騎桓桓遠近布濩於原野武夫赳赳
前後充斥於周行其衆不如江如漢乎其靜而
止歛歟持重不浮隨時而止有如山之苞焉屹
乎其不可動誰得而撼之其動而大舉歟奮勇
並進以時而行有如川之流焉沛乎其不可禦
誰得而撓之跂而望焉部伍聯屬首尾之相顧
者無虧其不可絕者盖緜緜然也即而觀焉行
隊整肅左右之司局者有定其不可亂者盖翼
翼然也神謀睿筭默運於帷幄之中敵欲投間

punctuated: 詩人於周王之師，必極言其兵威之盛也。盖王師無敵於天下也，詩人舉其兵威而極言之，所以昭一時之盛也歟？是詩美宣王自將以伐淮北之夷，其意謂夫外夷猾夏，固天討之所當加；兵威極盛，又王師之所當尚。我宣王之伐淮夷也，其師何如其盛哉！想其以所將之師陳淮浦之上，彼至疾者莫飛翰若也。我師所至，速於應變，威武自爾其奮揚；敏於趨事，王靈不覺其震蕩。其疾不如飛如翰乎？至衆者莫江漢過也。我師所在，武騎桓桓，遠近布濩於原野；武夫赳赳，前後充斥於周行。其衆不如江如漢乎？其靜而止歛歟，持重不浮，隨時而止，有如山之苞焉，屹乎其不可動，誰得而撼之？其動而大舉歟，奮勇並進，以時而行，有如川之流焉，沛乎其不可禦，誰得而撓之？跂而望焉，部伍聯屬，首尾之相顧者無虧，其不可絕者盖緜緜然也；即而觀焉，行隊整肅，左右之司局者有定，其不可亂者盖翼翼然也。神謀睿筭，默運於帷幄之中，敵欲投間
translation_en:
When the poet speaks of the Zhou king’s army, he necessarily describes its military might in the strongest terms. For the royal army has no equal under Heaven. Is not the poet’s fullest description of its military might intended to display the grandeur of that age? This poem praises King Xuan for personally commanding the campaign against the Yi peoples north of the Huai River. Its meaning is that when foreign peoples disturb the Chinese realm, Heaven’s punishment must indeed be inflicted upon them; and overwhelming military might is also what the royal army should prize. When our King Xuan campaigned against the Huai Yi, how magnificent was his army!

Imagine the troops under his command drawn up along the banks of the Huai. Nothing is swifter than flight, than wings. Wherever our army goes, it responds swiftly to changing circumstances, its martial majesty naturally rising high; it hastens promptly to its tasks, and the king’s numinous power spreads its tremors imperceptibly. Is its swiftness not like flight, like wings? In abundance, nothing surpasses the Yangzi and Han rivers. Wherever our army is stationed, mighty cavalry spread across the plains, near and far; valiant warriors fill the great roads, before and behind. Are its multitudes not like the Yangzi, like the Han? When it rests and holds itself in check, it is steady and free of rashness, halting as circumstances require, like the solid mass of a mountain. Towering and immovable, who could shake it? When it moves and advances in force, its troops press forward together with resolute courage, moving at the proper time, like a river’s flow. Surging irresistibly, who could obstruct it? Stand on tiptoe and look into the distance: its units are linked together, front and rear supporting one another without a gap. Its unbroken continuity is indeed ceaseless. Approach and observe: its ranks are orderly and disciplined, with those on the left and right assigned fixed duties and stations. Its resistance to disorder is indeed a matter of meticulous order. Inspired plans and sagacious calculations are silently set in motion within the command tent; should the enemy seek to exploit an opening…

同考試官教諭高 批：顯承無射四字，不可分截，傳觧明矣。學者顧不之察，何耶？是篇見理的َ，行
translation_en:
…they would naturally be unable to put their stratagems into practice. How could they fathom it? With stout armor and sharp weapons, victory is secured at a gesture of command. Should the enemy seek battle, none could withstand its cutting edge. How could they overcome it? With the army commanded by King Xuan displaying military might of such fullness, how could any of the Huai Yi fail to submit when he marched against them?
Further, those who possess All under Heaven have employed both civil and military means since antiquity. Yet there is a proper way to repel hostile peoples: must the ruler act in person before distant peoples can be brought to submission? King Xuan’s campaign against them surely arose from necessity; it was not the reckless exhaustion of military force seen in later ages. In composing “The Jiang and Han Rivers” (Jiang Han) and “Ever Martial” (Chang Wu), the poets concluded the one by urging him toward civil virtue and the other by directing him toward the Kingly Way. Their intentions can be understood. May those who possess All under Heaven seek guidance in this.
“Are they not illustrious, are they not honored? People never weary of them.”
Associate Examiner Lin, Assistant Instructor, comments: The three divisions—being illustrious, being honored, and never being wearied of—are clear in themselves. Reverence and harmony, holding fast to virtue, responding to those above, and hastening in service: not one of these can be omitted. Writers seize upon one and discard another, offering a confusion of unsettled interpretations. This essay apprehends the principle with precision and expresses it with meticulous care. It is outstanding in its interpretation of the hymn.
Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor, comments: The four characters for “illustrious,” “honored,” and “never weary” must not be split apart; the commentary makes this clear. Why, then, do students fail to perceive it? This essay’s understanding of the principle is exact [?], and its writing …

…the writing flows freely. Is this not someone deeply grounded in the fundamentals?
Associate Examiner Yu, Instructor, comments: Considering the meaning of the commentary, it is correct to take the three expressions “manifest indeed,” “upheld indeed,” and “never wearied of” as jointly encompassing the four preceding lines, though each conveys its meaning indirectly and subtly. Although “manifest indeed” pertains to solemn harmony and holding fast to virtue, and “upheld indeed” pertains to responding to the spirit and hastening in service, their meanings also overlap. “Never wearied of,” however, still embraces them all. With meanings recurring and expressions overlapping, the passage is extremely difficult to handle. Only in this essay have I seen such polished completeness and meticulous composition, fully bringing out every subtlety of the praise of virtue. I have selected it for inclusion.
Examiner Liu, Left Rectifier, comments: Only someone with exceptional literary power could have written this.
Examiner Wu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: A difficult topic, skillfully brought under control.
When the people of Zhou sacrificed to their former kings, they invariably praised in turn the fullness of their virtue. For the virtue of the former kings was not easily described in words. Without the sacrifice in the Pure Temple, could that which made their virtue so abundant have become visible? Formerly, when the Duke of Zhou had completed Luoyi and received the feudal lords in audience, he then led them in sacrificing to King Wen. At this point their sacrificial song seems to say: Without praising virtue, sacrifice cannot fully express a filial son’s sincerity; unless virtue resides in people, the greatness of the former king cannot be seen. Thus, what is manifest in an earlier age often becomes obscure in a later one. Our former king was assuredly illustrious in his day, but how could anyone know that his glory would remain undimmed through the passage of time? Look within the Pure Temple: those assisting at the sacrifice are illustrious assistants, and those performing its duties are the many officers. Solemn and harmonious in their ranks, they splendidly display the fullness of his virtue; holding fast to his cultivated virtue, they richly embody its accumulated abundance. His glory, manifest in their response to his spirit, is as it was when manifest in the western lands; his radiance, shining through their swift service, is as it was when shining throughout the four quarters. title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
與逝吾何辨焉盖其德之在人而不可掩如此
豈不顯矣乎承於始者易怠於終維我先王向
固承矣孰知其久而弗怠乎觀其洛邑之烝顯
相則肅雝也多士則秉德也對越於恍惚之交
精神自爾其流通駿奔於焄蒿之感欲色自爾
其如見有神斯尊即其左右趨之也有主斯奉
即其六師及之也其存與亡吾何擇焉盖其德
之在人而不容已如此豈不承矣乎無射於昔
者恒替於今維我先王昔固無射矣抑孰知其
===
久而弗替乎觀夫肅雝有顯相秉德有多士何
者而非愛慕之人在天則對越在廟則駿奔何
往而非敬崇之地西土怙冒洽於肌膚宛然其
可見四方攸同淪於骨髓斷然其不誣其遠與
近吾又何知焉盖其德之在人而不能忘如此
信乎其無射於人矣吁詩人頌文王之德之盛
如此可謂善言德行而深知聖人者歟考之鬼
神之德使天下之人齊明盛服以承祭祀武王
周公之祭亦與天下共之耳如是則無射於人

translation_en:
…and his passing—what distinction can I make between them? Such is the way his virtue abides among the people and cannot be concealed. Is it not manifest indeed? Those who offer reverent service at the beginning easily grow negligent at the end. Our former king certainly received such service before; but how do we know that it continued long without negligence? Consider the winter sacrifice at Luoyi: the illustrious assistants are reverent and harmonious, and the many officers uphold his virtue. As they commune with him in the dim, elusive encounter, their spirits naturally communicate with his. As they hasten about, moved by the rising sacrificial vapors, his desires and countenance seem naturally present to their sight [?]. There is a spirit, and so they honor him, hastening to his side; there is a lord, and so they serve him, his six armies attending him [?]. What distinction can I make between his presence and his absence? Such is the way his virtue abides among the people and will not allow their service to cease. Does he not indeed receive reverent service?

What inspired no weariness in the past often declines in the present. Our former king certainly inspired no weariness in the past; but how do we know that this endured long without decline? Consider the illustrious assistants, reverent and harmonious, and the many officers who uphold his virtue: which of them is not a person filled with love and longing? In heaven they commune with him; in the temple they hasten about in his service. Where is there any place without reverence and veneration for him? The protection he afforded the western lands has permeated their very flesh and skin, as though plainly visible; the allegiance of the four quarters has sunk into their bones and marrow, assuredly no falsehood. What difference, then, can I perceive between far and near? Such is the way his virtue abides among the people and cannot be forgotten. Truly, people never weary of him!

Ah! The poet extols the abundance of King Wen’s virtue in this manner. May he not be called one who speaks well of virtuous conduct and deeply understands the sage? Examine this in light of the potency of ghosts and spirits: they cause the people of the world to purify themselves and put on splendid robes to perform sacrifices. The sacrifices of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, too, were simply shared with all under Heaven. Thus, people never weary of him…

text:
不朝者乃有蕭叔来朝而見譏者何哉盖朝禮
也朝非其所則非禮矣使蕭也走車馬於曲阜
之邦薦玉帛於周公之廟則禮得其所孰得而
譏者今来朝之地則于穀焉誠以犧象不出門
嘉樂不野合而穀本齊地是豈魯之廟乎于是
云朝則威儀雖盛而草莽之間非所以為燕享
之地禮度雖周而封疆之外非所以展賓主之

栗棗脩以告虔則禮當其物孰得而議者今宗
婦来覿則用幣焉誠以夫婦人倫之本朝廷風
化之原而幣為男用是豈女之贄乎乃是而亂
則案帛之將雖恭敬之特隆而廢男女之大倫
punctuated:
不朝者，乃有蕭叔来朝而見譏者，何哉？盖朝，禮也；朝非其所，則非禮矣。使蕭也走車馬於曲阜之邦，薦玉帛於周公之廟，則禮得其所，孰得而譏者？今来朝之地則于穀焉。誠以犧象不出門，嘉樂不野合，而穀本齊地，是豈魯之廟乎？于是云朝，則威儀雖盛，而草莽之間非所以為燕享之地；禮度雖周，而封疆之外非所以展賓主之誠。締好於途，殊乖先王之制；委禮于野，有愆小國之儀。雖曰朝之，不若不朝之為愈也。噫！人而無禮，詩有明戒。使蕭也知是意而自沮焉，則《相鼠》之刺不其可免乎？《春秋》所以譏之者如此。
若乃夫人既至，宗婦未有来覿而無贄者，乃有用幣成禮而見譏者，何哉？盖覿，禮也；覿非其物，則非禮矣。使魯也大夫玉帛禽鳥以章物，宗婦榛栗棗脩以告虔，則禮當其物，孰得而譏者？今宗婦来覿則用幣焉。誠以夫婦人倫之本，朝廷風化之原，而幣為男用，是豈女之贄乎？乃是而覿，則束帛之將雖亦敬之特隆，而廢男女之大倫
translation_en:
…never pay a court visit throughout their lives. Yet Xiao Shu came to pay a court visit and was censured. Why? A court visit is a rite; but if conducted in an improper place, it violates ritual propriety. Had the ruler of Xiao driven his carriages and horses to Qufu and presented jade and silk at the temple of the Duke of Zhou, the rite would have had its proper setting. Who could then have censured him? Yet the place where he came to pay his visit was Gu. Indeed, the ox-shaped and elephant-shaped wine vessels do not pass beyond the gate, and ceremonial music is not performed in the open countryside. Gu was originally territory of Qi: how could it be Lu’s ancestral temple? To call what took place there a court visit means that, however splendid the ceremonial deportment, the wilderness was no place for ritual banquets; however complete the ritual observances, a place beyond the borders was no setting for expressing the sincerity of host and guest. To establish friendly relations on the road departed utterly from the institutions of the former kings; to consign ritual to the open fields transgressed the ceremonial obligations of a small state. Though called a court visit, it would have been better not to make it. Alas! Against being a person without ritual propriety, the Book of Odes gives an explicit warning. Had the ruler of Xiao understood this meaning and restrained himself, could he not have escaped the reproach of “Look at the Rat” (Xiang shu)? Such was the reason for the censure in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
As for the ruler’s wife, once she had arrived, the wives of the ruling clan never came to have an audience without presentation gifts. Yet they were censured for completing the rite with silk. Why? An audience is a rite; but if its gifts are improper, it violates ritual propriety. Had Lu’s grandees used jade, silk, and birds to display the distinctions embodied in their gifts, and the wives of the ruling clan used hazelnuts, chestnuts, dates, and dried meat to express their reverence, the gifts would have suited the rite. Who could then have censured them? Yet when the wives of the ruling clan came for their audience, they used silk. Indeed, husband and wife form the foundation of human relationships, and the court is the source of moral transformation. Silk is for men to use: how could it be a woman’s presentation gift? To have an audience with such gifts meant that, although the offering of bundles of silk expressed an exceptional degree of respect, it abolished the fundamental distinction between men and women…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
厥篚之陳雖昭禮之異數而混夫婦於無别紛
更故典致褻宗婦之儀創立新規求悅夫人之
意雖曰覿之不若不覿之爲勝也噫夫婦有别
古有格言使魯也以此道而自克焉則牝雞之
凶何自而起乎春秋所以譏之者又如此是則
嘉禮兩有所失春秋兩有所譏聖筆之於蕭魯
也其嚴矣哉抑蕭叔朝穀宗婦用幣律之以禮
固有罪矣然罪之在莊公者獨可恕乎盖其于
朝不知反正于幣不知正始而皆以非禮處之
===
則其他可知已正名定罪公盖其尤歟此所以
不免公子牙慶父之及也傳曰爲國以禮公其
未之思乎
宋華元出奔晉宋華元自晉歸于宋〔成公十五年〕
張瓛
同考試官學正鄭 批 元之出入獨正人皆
知之而能援據故實分析明白者甚少此作鋪叙嚴
整而文氣雅健迥異衆作信非老筆不能實錄之

宋華元出奔晉，宋華元自晉歸于宋。〔成公十五年〕

translation_en:
…Although the presentation of those baskets displayed exceptional ceremonial honors, it confounded the distinctions between husband and wife. Arbitrarily altering established precedents, they debased the ceremonial propriety of the women of the ruling lineage; devising new rules, they sought to please the ruler’s wife. Though they called this a ceremonial audience, it would have been better to hold no audience at all. Alas! That husband and wife have distinct roles is an ancient maxim. Had Lu exercised self-restraint according to this principle, how could the calamity of the hen crowing have arisen? This, too, is why the Spring and Autumn Annals censures it. Thus, in both instances the auspicious rites were mishandled, and in both instances the Spring and Autumn Annals offers censure. How sternly the Sage’s brush treats Xiao and Lu! Still, the Lord of Xiao’s court audience at Gu and the lineage women’s use of silk gifts were certainly culpable when judged by ritual. But can Duke Zhuang’s own culpability alone be excused? In the matter of the audience, he did not know to restore what was correct; in the matter of the silk gifts, he did not know to establish correctness at the outset. Since he handled both matters contrary to ritual, his other conduct can readily be inferred. In rectifying names and determining guilt, was the duke not perhaps the chief offender? This is why he could not escape the ensuing troubles involving Prince Ya and Qingfu. The Commentary says: “Govern a state through ritual.” Had the duke never considered this?
“Hua Yuan of Song fled to Jin; Hua Yuan of Song returned from Jin to Song.” 〔Fifteenth year of Duke Cheng〕
Zhang Huan.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: Everyone knows that Yuan’s departure and return were uniquely proper, but very few can adduce historical precedents and analyze the matter clearly. This composition’s exposition is disciplined and orderly, while its literary expression is elegant and vigorous, markedly different from the other compositions. Truly, only a seasoned writer could achieve this. We have faithfully transcribed it …

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以式來學
考試官左中允劉批典則可觀
考試官侍講學士吳批敘事嚴整無遺
春秋特予外臣一以其去國之正一以其復國
之正盖華元奔晉歸宋得去就之正也春秋詞
繁不殺以予之也宜哉何則華元宋之右師也
任有獨尊職爲至重固宜效股肱之力保世禄
之榮矣今自宋奔晉自晉歸宋其去就有若可
疑者春秋兩以爲正而予之者何哉盖以去國
===
言若元晅之奔晉宋辰之奔陳或以出而愬君
或以出而脅上未見其正者也元之奔豈晅辰
倫哉盖其時身爲右師而君臣之訓則所司也
惡桓氏之汰驕顧在我無可制之權耻公室之
卑弱責在官有賴寵之咎以是而奔固亦有謀
於其間者使其懷禄固寵重於此行吾知幾不
能見而噬臍之悔何以免之是其奔也非避患
也固爲國耳不然何奔未越境而魚府憂桓氏
之隕魚石有河上之追耶此元之奔所以爲正

以式來學。
考試官左中允劉批：典則可觀。
考試官侍講學士吳批：敘事嚴整無遺。
春秋特予外臣，一以其去國之正，一以其復國之正。盖華元奔晉歸宋，得去就之正也，春秋詞繁不殺以予之也，宜哉！何則？華元，宋之右師也，任有獨尊，職爲至重，固宜效股肱之力，保世禄之榮矣。今自宋奔晉，自晉歸宋，其去就有若可疑者，春秋兩以爲正而予之者，何哉？盖以去國言，若元晅之奔晉、宋辰之奔陳，或以出而愬君，或以出而脅上，未見其正者也。元之奔，豈晅、辰倫哉？盖其時身爲右師，而君臣之訓則所司也。惡桓氏之汰驕，顧在我無可制之權；耻公室之卑弱，責在官有賴寵之咎。以是而奔，固亦有謀於其間者。使其懷禄固寵，重於此行，吾知幾不能見，而噬臍之悔，何以免之？是其奔也，非避患也，固爲國耳。不然，何奔未越境，而魚府憂桓氏之隕，魚石有河上之追耶？此元之奔所以爲正
translation_en:
…to provide a model for future students.
Examiner Liu, Left Mentor, comments: Its adherence to classical standards is admirable.
Examiner Wu, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: The narration is rigorous and orderly, with nothing omitted.
The Spring and Autumn Annals accords special approval to a minister of another state: first for the rectitude of his departure from his state, and second for the rectitude of his return. Hua Yuan’s flight to Jin and return to Song exemplified the proper course in leaving office and resuming it. How fitting that the Spring and Autumn Annals should express its approval through full wording, without abbreviation! Why is this so? Hua Yuan was Song’s Commander of the Right. His charge was uniquely exalted, and his office carried the gravest responsibilities. He should certainly have exerted himself as his ruler’s trusted support and preserved the honor of his hereditary emoluments. Yet he fled from Song to Jin and returned from Jin to Song, making his departure and return appear questionable. Why does the Spring and Autumn Annals deem both proper and approve them?
Consider departure from one’s state. Yuan Xuan’s [?] flight to Jin and Song Chen’s flight to Chen were instances of men leaving either to bring accusations against their ruler or to intimidate their sovereign. No rectitude is evident in these acts. Could Hua Yuan’s flight belong in the same category as those of Xuan [?] and Chen? At that time, as Commander of the Right, he was responsible for upholding the principles governing ruler and minister. He abhorred the Huan clan’s extravagance and arrogance, yet lacked the authority to restrain it. He felt shame at the ruling house’s humiliation and weakness; bearing responsibility by virtue of his office, he would be culpable for merely relying on favor. His flight under these circumstances therefore also had a considered purpose.
Had he cherished his emoluments and clung to favor, hesitating to make this departure, I know that he would have failed to discern the incipient danger. How then could he have escaped the futile remorse of trying to bite his own navel? His flight was thus no attempt to evade trouble: it was undertaken for the state. Otherwise, why, before he had even crossed the border, did Yu Fu fear the Huan clan’s downfall, and why did Yu Shi pursue him to the banks of the Yellow River? This is why Hua Yuan’s flight was proper…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而春秋書奔不省文者顧非所以予之乎以歸
國言若欒盈之入曲沃趙鞅之入晉陽或倚附
而危國或假援以要君未見其正者也元之歸
又豈欒趙匹哉盖其時身之河上而桓氏之族
則甚懼也國人許之討可以無內顧之憂伯主
爲之援可以藉外疆之勢以是而歸必能有爲
於其時者使其趨利避害難於此舉吾知國且
不利而剝膚之災何以救之是其歸也非貪位
也亦爲國耳不然何歸不崇朝而蕩山延頸以
===
就戮魚石竄身以避位耶此元之歸所以爲正
而春秋書歸不省文者又非所以予之乎吁奔
不徒奔必有所謀而後奔歸不徒歸必成所謀
而復歸此元之去就所以有功於國而見予春
秋者耶嗟夫元之忠於其國如此而其先世乃
有如督者何其不倫之甚乎盖古之聖賢皆不
係于世類崇伯殛而禹作司空蔡叔囚而仲爲
卿士亦曷甞世類之論乎然則元也雖不敢上
比禹仲而其制行之美亦足以盖前人之愆以

translation_en: …And when the Spring and Autumn Annals records his flight without abbreviating the wording, is this not a means of commending him? As for returning to one's state, consider Luan Ying's entry into Quwo and Zhao Yang's entry into Jinyang: one relied on partisans and endangered the state; the other borrowed armed support to coerce his ruler. Neither can be regarded as upright. How could Yuan's return be comparable to those of Luan and Zhao? At that time he had gone to the banks of the Yellow River, and the Huan clan was greatly afraid. The people of the state authorized him to punish them, so he need have no anxiety about troubles within; the hegemon supported him, so he could draw upon strength from outside [?]. Returning under these circumstances, he could surely accomplish something at that moment. Had he sought advantage and avoided danger, shrinking from this undertaking, I know that the state would have suffered; how could he then have averted a calamity that cut to the very skin? Thus his return was not prompted by greed for office: it too was for the state's sake. Otherwise, why, before even a morning had passed after his return, did Dang Shan [?] stretch out his neck to receive execution, while Yu Shi fled, relinquishing his position? This is why Yuan's return was upright. And when the Spring and Autumn Annals records his return without abbreviating the wording, is this not again a means of commending him? Ah! His flight was no mere flight: he first formed a plan and only then fled. His return was no mere return: he returned determined to carry out his plan. Is this not why Yuan's withdrawal and return rendered service to the state and earned him commendation in the Spring and Autumn Annals? Alas! Yuan was so loyal to his state, yet among his ancestors there was someone like Du. How utterly unlike they were! The sages and worthies of antiquity were never bound by the character of their lineage. The Earl of Chong was put to death, yet Yu became Minister of Works; Cai Shu was imprisoned, yet Zhong became a minister. When were such men ever judged by their lineage? Thus, although we would not venture to rank Yuan alongside Yu and Zhong, the excellence of his conduct was sufficient to efface his forebear's wrongdoing. By…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
末世論之元其僅見者歟
禮記
唯丘之聞諸萇弘亦若吾子之言是也
陳節
同考試官學正周批作此題者於唯是二
字殊欠發明是篇宛然寫出當時孔子答賓牟賈口
氣盖傑作也
考試官左中允劉批文有思致
考試官侍講學士吳批精確過人
===
聖人然時人之論樂有徵於所聞不謬於所見
盖武樂之失傳也久矣曽謂武王有貪商之志
而形諸樂者有不可揜哉昔吾夫子因賓牟賈
論武樂之聲而然其言如此謂夫樂必發于聲
音而被之器也雖有時而或渝樂必通乎倫理

…Judged by the standards of later ages, was Yuan not a rare example indeed?

Record of Rites
“Yes, what I, Qiu, heard from Chang Hong was also just as you have said.”
Chen Jie

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: Those who write on this topic generally fall far short of elucidating the two words “yes” and “so.” This essay vividly reproduces the very tone in which Confucius answered Binmou Jia at the time. It is truly an outstanding composition.
Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Assistant Adviser: The composition displays thoughtful subtlety.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Expositor-in-waiting: Its precision surpasses that of others.

The sage affirmed his contemporary’s discussion of music: it was corroborated by what he had heard and did not conflict with what he had observed.

The music of the Wu dance had long ceased to be correctly transmitted. Could it really be said that King Wu harbored a desire to seize Shang, and that this found expression in the music in a way that could not be concealed? In former times, when Binmou Jia discussed the sounds of the Wu music, our Master affirmed his words in this manner. His meaning was this: music must issue in sounds and tones and be played upon instruments, and these may sometimes undergo alteration. Yet music must also accord with ethical relationships and remain imprinted in people’s minds; it does not simply vanish with the passage of time. Errors have been inherited and falsehoods perpetuated; the fault lies in its transmission by the responsible officials. I certainly do not doubt you. The age is distant and its people are gone; the explanations contradict the ancient practice of the former kings. How could you be deceiving me? Chang Hong serves our Zhou dynasty. By examining sounds he understands tones, and by examining tones he understands music. At the royal court he must surely have received instruction in this tradition. As for me, Qiu…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
訪于萇弘知聲以言音知音以言樂其於大武
亦嘗有所聞矣論固多端而貪聲之說徵諸吾
子若其口出何彼此之有間乎聞雖已舊而失
傳之云驗于今日言猶在耳何先後之或殊乎
是非出於偶同實其理之不可易者爾何則孟
津一會翕然諸侯之服從人心如此可不順乎
而樂以象成自紀其順人之實于何而貪也牧
野一陳凜然上帝之臨女天命如此敢不應乎
而功成作樂自本其應天之休于何而謬也苟
===
謂有司之傳為不失邪是武樂真有貪商之聲
於志為已荒何精明神武之足尚謂武樂之作
為信然邪是武王果有富殷之意於德為已愧
何布昭聖武之有光今惟理是據而不拘于聲
律之誣卓然其見足祛千古之惑非深知聖人
者不能也惟心是揆而有得于英華之妙確乎
其論不出一己之私非善言武樂者不及也謂
之曰是不其然矣乎吁賓牟賈因論武樂而見
許於夫子如此亦可與言樂者矣大抵周德既

於志爲已荒何精明神武之足尚謂武樂之作
爲信然邪是武王果有富殷之意於德爲已愧
何布昭聖武之有光令惟理是據而不拘于聲
律之誣卓然其見足袪千古之惑非深知聖人
者不能也惟心是揆而有得于英華之妙確乎
其論不出一己之私非善言武樂者不及也謂
之曰是不其然矣乎吁賓牟賈因論武樂而見
許於夫子如此亦可與言樂者矣大抵周德既
punctuated:
訪于萇弘，知聲以言音，知音以言樂，其於大武，亦嘗有所聞矣。論固多端，而貪聲之說，徵諸吾子，若其口出，何彼此之有間乎？聞雖已舊，而失傳之云，驗于今日，言猶在耳，何先後之或殊乎？是非出於偶同，實其理之不可易者爾。何則？孟津一會，翕然諸侯之服從，人心如此，可不順乎？而樂以象成，自紀其順人之實，于何而貪也？牧野一陳，凜然上帝之臨女，天命如此，敢不應乎？而功成作樂，自本其應天之休，于何而謬也？苟謂有司之傳為不失邪，是武樂真有貪商之聲，於志為已荒，何精明神武之足尚？謂武樂之作為信然邪，是武王果有富殷之意，於德為已愧，何布昭聖武之有光？今惟理是據，而不拘于聲律之誣，卓然其見，足祛千古之惑，非深知聖人者不能也。惟心是揆，而有得于英華之妙，確乎其論，不出一己之私，非善言武樂者不及也。謂之曰是，不其然矣乎？
吁！賓牟賈因論武樂而見許於夫子如此，亦可與言樂者矣。大抵周德既
translation_en:
…visited Chang Hong. Understanding sounds, I could discuss their musical organization; understanding their musical organization, I could discuss ritual music. Concerning the Great Martial Dance, too, I had heard something. Our discussions certainly ranged over many matters, yet when I checked his account of the sounds of greed against yours, your words seemed to come from his very mouth. How could there be any discrepancy between the two? Although I heard him long ago, his assertion that the music had been incorrectly transmitted is borne out today. His words still ring in my ears: how could the earlier and later accounts differ? This agreement is no mere coincidence; it arises from a principle that cannot be altered.
Why is this so? At the assembly at Mengjin, the feudal lords unanimously submitted. With the people's hearts thus inclined, could King Wu fail to follow them? Music represents accomplished deeds: it naturally records the truth of his compliance with the people's wishes. Where, then, was there greed? At the battle array at Muye, the Lord on High stood awesomely over you. With Heaven's mandate thus manifest, could you dare fail to respond? When the achievement was complete and music was made, it naturally took as its basis the glory of responding to Heaven. Where, then, was there error?
If one maintains that the responsible officials transmitted it without error, then the Martial Dance music truly contains sounds of covetousness toward Shang. His intentions would already have gone astray: what would remain worthy of esteem in his keen discernment and divinely inspired martial prowess? If one maintains that the Martial Dance music was indeed composed in this way, then King Wu really intended to enrich himself with Yin's wealth. His virtue would already have been compromised: what glory would there be in the far-reaching manifestation of his sagely martial prowess?
Now you take principle alone as your basis, refusing to be constrained by the false evidence of musical sounds and pitches. Your outstanding insight suffices to dispel the doubts of a thousand ages; only someone who deeply understands the sage could accomplish this. You judge solely by his heart and grasp the subtlety of its finest expression. Your argument is firm and does not arise from merely personal bias; only someone skilled in discussing the Martial Dance music could attain this. Was it not fitting, then, to pronounce your words correct?
Ah! Binmou Jia received such approval from the Master through his discussion of the Martial Dance music. He, too, was someone with whom music could be discussed. In general, once the virtue of Zhou had already…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
衰音樂廢缺雖樂之始終節奏世亦鮮能知者
觀夫子之語魯太師可推也武樂之聲淫及商
何足怪乎夫子適周訪于萇弘而嘆周之所以
王與周公所以聖者猶所謂不圖爲樂之至於
斯也其得於武樂盖已深矣至是與賓牟賈論
樂反復問難致辨於得失之間誠欲復古樂以
興周而時君無足以語此者徒以考定其說爲
萬世詔也噫
民不求其所欲而得之謂之信
===

translation_en:
…declined, music fell into neglect and became incomplete. Even the beginnings, endings, and rhythmic divisions of musical performance were understood by few in the world, as we can infer from the Master's remarks to the Grand Music Master of Lu. What wonder, then, that the sounds of the Wu music had strayed into the music of Shang? The Master went to Zhou and consulted Chang Hong. He marveled at what had made Zhou's rulers kings and the Duke of Zhou a sage, much as when he said, “I never imagined that music could attain such heights.” His understanding of the Wu music was already profound. Now, discussing music with Binmou Jia, he repeatedly questioned and challenged him, carefully distinguishing what was right from what was wrong. He truly wished to restore ancient music and thereby revive Zhou, but no ruler of his time was worthy of discussing this with him. He could only examine and establish its explanation, leaving instruction for all ages. Alas!

“When the people obtain what they desire without asking for it, this is called trustworthiness.”

Wang Ji

Its author is someone with whom one can discuss trustworthiness.”

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Assistant Inquisitor: “This is beyond the reach of an immature writer.”

Comment by Examiner Wu, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: “Rich, full, and delightful.”

What makes trustworthiness precious is that fulfillment comes without an agreement. Now, if the people naturally obtain everything they desire, how great such trustworthiness is! title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
夫民生不能無欲有欲不能無求欲而必求則
非出於得已求而後得則已愧於自然其何以
爲信耶是故民孰不有身歟有身則有欲衣焉
食焉爲一身之謀者咸欲其裕民孰不有家歟
有家則有欲仰焉俯焉爲一家之計者皆欲其
周今未嘗以身求也而人爲之自足君臣之際
判然其不相干未嘗以家求也而家爲之自給
形跡之間邈然其不相涉飽其食煖其衣免於
凍餒之憂孰是與謀而願無不償乎安其居樂
===
其業遠於流離之患孰是與處而欲無不遂乎
如此豈不謂之信矣哉何則下以是求上以是
應憧憧往來無復忠厚之風偽孰加焉此有所
施彼有所報紛紛交易適成偷薄之習誠何在
焉若其無求自得是知民匪我不能以身而裕
其身者固吾所也於其求奚俟有欲自遂是知
民匪我不能以家而周其家者固吾分也於其
得奚庸意氣潜孚起居自爾其無恙猶天地至
誠無息而萬物以生也精神黙契耕鑿自爾其

punctuated: 夫民生不能無欲，有欲不能無求。欲而必求，則非出於得已；求而後得，則已愧於自然，其何以爲信耶？是故民孰不有身歟？有身則有欲，衣焉，食焉，爲一身之謀者咸欲其裕。民孰不有家歟？有家則有欲，仰焉，俯焉，爲一家之計者皆欲其周。今未嘗以身求也，而人爲之自足，君臣之際，判然其不相干；未嘗以家求也，而家爲之自給，形跡之間，邈然其不相涉。飽其食，煖其衣，免於凍餒之憂，孰是與謀而願無不償乎？安其居，樂其業，遠於流離之患，孰是與處而欲無不遂乎？如此，豈不謂之信矣哉？何則？下以是求，上以是應，憧憧往來，無復忠厚之風，偽孰加焉？此有所施，彼有所報，紛紛交易，適成偷薄之習，誠何在焉？若其無求自得，是知民匪我不能以身，而裕其身者固吾所也，於其求奚俟？有欲自遂，是知民匪我不能以家，而周其家者固吾分也，於其得奚庸？意氣潜孚，起居自爾其無恙，猶天地至誠無息而萬物以生也；精神黙契，耕鑿自爾其
translation_en:
…People in their lives cannot be without desires, and having desires, they cannot be without requests. If desire necessarily requires asking, this is not something they can avoid; if they obtain something only after asking, it already falls short of what occurs spontaneously. How could this constitute trustworthiness? Who among the people does not have a person to sustain? Having a person to sustain entails desires—for clothing and for food—and all who plan for their own maintenance wish for abundance. Who among the people does not have a family? Having a family entails desires—to support elders above and dependants below—and all who plan for their household wish for adequate provision. Yet here, without ever asking for their own maintenance, people have enough of themselves; ruler and subject remain distinctly apart, without making demands upon one another. Without ever asking for their families, their households have sufficient provision of themselves; in outward dealings, the two remain remote, without involvement with one another. They eat their fill, dress warmly, and escape the worry of freezing and starvation. Who has planned this with them, that none of their wishes goes unfulfilled? They dwell securely, delight in their occupations, and remain far from the affliction of displacement. Who has arranged this with them, that none of their desires goes unsatisfied? Can this not be called trustworthiness?

Why is this so? If those below make requests and those above respond accordingly, there is anxious coming and going, with none of the spirit of loyalty and generosity remaining. What could exceed this in artifice? If one party bestows something and the other repays it, the bustle of exchange merely fosters habits of meanness and insincerity. Where is sincerity in this? When people obtain what they need spontaneously, without asking, it is because the ruler understands that without him they cannot maintain themselves. Providing amply for their persons is indeed his proper charge [?]; why wait for their requests? When their desires are spontaneously fulfilled, it is because he understands that without him they cannot maintain their families. Providing fully for their families is indeed his duty; what need is there to concern himself with their obtaining it [?]? Their intentions and feelings accord unseen, and the people naturally go about their daily lives unharmed, just as Heaven and Earth, through unceasing perfect sincerity, bring the myriad things to life. Their spirits accord silently, and in ploughing their fields and digging their wells, they naturally…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
莫如猶四時有常不易而品彙以成也身者自
身忘其所以爲身一實德之流通爾彼有言能
踐而人益之者曾是以爲信乎家者自家忘其
所以爲家一帝力之何有爾彼久要不忘而家
賜之者信其可語此乎吁欲之得也不出於求
德之施也不責其報古之所謂信者有如此哉
大抵凡求者皆生於不足而得者不必其有餘
以是爲信固已末矣其未信者可勝計哉聖人
