李沆以科甲被遇，事關軍國，必訪裁處，而四方水旱，日以奏聞，中外利害，一切報罷，有以得大臣之體。盖沆少而好學，器識宏遠，詔書應制，文理稱旨，而節用愛人、使民以時，體驗於論語者爲尤切也。不然，則其同列稱爲聖人、當時號曰聖相者，果何謂邪？
若宋神宗銳意太平，謙諮治道，而王安石歡同魚水，驟遷端揆，正當日進讜
translation_en:
…sound principles, thereby responding to the emperor’s virtuous intentions. Why, then, did he make false claims about floods and droughts to cloak his wickedness, and feign frugality to further his deceit, have Zhongshu transferred to Jiaodong, and bring Zhufu to execution, yet do nothing whatsoever to check the emperor’s craving for grandeur and achievement and his reckless pursuit of warfare? Was his professional study of the Spring and Autumn Annals, and his summons to office for literary learning, merely a means of pandering to the age and winning favor?
Zhao Pu won recognition while the emperor was still a prince. In matters great and small, the emperor consulted him for decisions. By advancing sound proposals and rejecting unsound ones, laying aside arms and cultivating civil government, he helped establish the guiding principles of a dynasty. In his youth he had learned administrative business and originally possessed little scholarly learning; in his later years, however, he read constantly, never putting down his books. When called upon to settle major deliberations, he sought his decisions in written texts. His understanding of the Analects was especially profound. Otherwise, what could he have meant when he said of himself, “I have perused the canonical writings and gained some knowledge of the words of the ancients”?
Li Hang received imperial favor through success in the examinations. Whenever affairs concerned the military or the state, the emperor invariably sought his judgment. He reported daily on floods and droughts throughout the realm, while proposals concerning benefits and harms at court and in the provinces were all rejected. In this he embodied the proper bearing of a great minister. From his youth, Hang loved learning and possessed broad capacity and far-reaching discernment. In drafting edicts and composing writings at imperial command, his expression and reasoning satisfied the emperor. He was especially diligent in putting into practice the Analects’ teachings to economize in expenditure, care for the people, and employ their labor at the proper seasons. Otherwise, what did it mean that his colleagues called him a sage and his contemporaries styled him the “sage chief councilor”?
When Emperor Shenzong of the Song set his heart on bringing about peace and humbly sought advice on government, Wang Anshi enjoyed a harmonious relationship with him, like that of fish and water, and rapidly rose to become chief councilor. He ought then to have offered forthright …

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
猷以答殊遇可也柰何變舊章而作新法
斥忠直而進小人始以萬言之書終以三
不足之說使羣姦得志毒流四海人皆爲
諱言則其以文章節行爲高以道德經濟
爲任者豈非欺世盜名之捷徑乎抑嘗因
是而爲之說資稟得之天學力養之人二
者可兼有而不可偏廢也有天資而不輔
之以學雖其建立事功倉卒有濟而規模
疎略無以爲經遠之圖有學術而不本之
===
以正雖其志節衒露若可有爲而聲聞過
情不可責以實用此絳侯博陸不免身家
之及而平津荆國之誤人家國不淺也孔
子以天縱之聖猶好古敏以求之顏淵以
生知之亞至於欲罷不能然則天資之美
者豈可恃而不學其爲學者又可不以孔
顏爲法邪
第五問 劉楷

punctuated:
猷，以答殊遇可也。柰何變舊章而作新法，斥忠直而進小人，始以萬言之書，終以三不足之說，使羣姦得志，毒流四海，人皆爲諱言？則其以文章節行爲高，以道德經濟爲任者，豈非欺世盜名之捷徑乎？抑嘗因是而爲之說：資稟得之天，學力養之人，二者可兼有而不可偏廢也。有天資而不輔之以學，雖其建立事功，倉卒有濟，而規模疎略，無以爲經遠之圖；有學術而不本之以正，雖其志節衒露，若可有爲，而聲聞過情，不可責以實用。此絳侯、博陸不免身家之及，而平津、荆國之誤人家國不淺也。孔子以天縱之聖，猶好古，敏以求之；顏淵以生知之亞，至於欲罷不能。然則天資之美者，豈可恃而不學？其爲學者，又可不以孔、顏爲法邪？

第五問，劉楷。
translation_en:
…counsels, thereby repaying the exceptional favor he received: this would have been fitting. Why, then, did he alter the established institutions and introduce new laws, reject the loyal and upright and advance petty men, beginning with a memorial of ten thousand words and ending with the doctrine of the “three things that need not be heeded”? He enabled a host of wicked men to achieve their ambitions, spread harm throughout the realm, and made everyone afraid to speak of it. Were his claims to esteem literary accomplishment and moral integrity, and to take morality and statecraft as his responsibility, not merely a shortcut to deceiving the world and stealing a reputation?

Reflecting on this, I have ventured to offer the following explanation. Natural endowments are received from Heaven; the strength acquired through learning is cultivated by human effort. Both may be possessed together, and neither should be neglected. If someone has natural ability but does not supplement it with learning, he may accomplish deeds and meet an urgent crisis, yet his plans will be sketchy and provide no basis for governing with the distant future in view. If someone possesses learning but does not ground it in rectitude, he may conspicuously display ambition and integrity and appear capable of achievement, yet his reputation will exceed the reality, and practical service cannot be expected of him. This is why the Marquis of Jiang and the Marquis of Bolu could not escape calamities extending to themselves and their families, while the Marquis of Pingjin and the Duke of Jing brought no small harm upon others’ families and states.

Confucius, though a sage endowed by Heaven, still loved antiquity and diligently sought knowledge of it. Yan Yuan, though second only to those born with knowledge, reached the point where he could not desist even if he wished. How, then, can those with fine natural gifts rely on them and neglect learning? And how can those who pursue learning fail to take Confucius and Yan Yuan as their models?

Fifth question. Liu Kai.

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官學正鄭批時務策正欲觀士子
用世之學此卷於西山先生所謂四事十害者條析
無遺末復說出時弊頗切經生知此殆有用之學也
他日效用慎毋忘斯言
考試官左中允劉批四事十害發自長沙西山
經濟之學見諸行事者也是篇條答無遺又有發西山
所未發者盖嘗以經濟究心也佳士佳士
考試官侍講學士吳批政經數語有關治道非細
此文忠公所望於天下後世者惜少能舉行之耳是策
能歷道之識之高才之贍而痛恤民隱之意溢於言表
===
其殆諳練世故而有槩於中者乎
嘗謂司民社者必先有愛民之心而後有
惠民之政盖心主乎中則惠民之政無不
舉政舉於外則愛民之心有所施司民社
者果能相與如是而斯民有不受福者乎
是道也其惟古之良吏以之而今之有司
所當取法也盖嘗聞之有司者斯民父母
斯民者有司赤子故詩有民之父母之稱

同考試官學正鄭批：時務策，正欲觀士子用世之學。此卷於西山先生所謂四事十害者，條析無遺，末復說出時弊，頗切。經生知此，殆有用之學也。他日效用，慎毋忘斯言。

考試官左中允劉批：四事十害發自長沙，西山經濟之學見諸行事者也。是篇條答無遺，又有發西山所未發者，盖嘗以經濟究心也。佳士！佳士！

考試官侍講學士吳批：《政經》數語，有關治道非細。此文忠公所望於天下後世者，惜少能舉行之耳。是策能歷道之，識之高，才之贍，而痛恤民隱之意溢於言表，其殆諳練世故而有槩於中者乎？

嘗謂司民社者，必先有愛民之心，而後有惠民之政。盖心主乎中，則惠民之政無不舉；政舉於外，則愛民之心有所施。司民社者果能相與如是，而斯民有不受福者乎？是道也，其惟古之良吏以之，而今之有司所當取法也。盖嘗聞之，有司者，斯民父母；斯民者，有司赤子。故《詩》有民之父母之稱。
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, School Instructor: Policy questions on current affairs are intended precisely to reveal candidates’ learning for practical service in the world. This paper analyzes, item by item and without omission, what Master Xishan called the four matters and ten harms. At the end it also identifies present abuses, with considerable pertinence. A student of the Classics who understands these things surely possesses useful learning. When you enter service in the future, take care never to forget these words.

Comment by Examiner Liu, Left Companion of the Heir Apparent: The four matters and ten harms originated with Changsha; they represent Xishan’s learning in statecraft manifested in practical affairs. This essay answers each point without omission and also develops points that Xishan himself did not develop. The writer must have devoted serious thought to statecraft. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Comment by Examiner Wu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: These few statements in the Classic of Governance (Zhengjing) have no small bearing on the way of governing. This is what Lord Wenzhong hoped would be realized throughout the realm and in later generations; regrettably, few have been able to put it into practice. This policy essay discusses them all in succession. Its insight is lofty, its intellectual resources abundant, and its profound concern for the people’s hidden suffering overflows the words themselves. Surely its author is versed in worldly affairs and possesses an earnest resolve within?

I have often maintained that those responsible for the people and the altars of the soil must first have a heart that loves the people before they can implement policies that benefit them. When this heart governs within, no policy beneficial to the people will go unimplemented; when such policies are carried out externally, the heart that loves the people finds an outlet. If those responsible for the people and the altars of the soil could indeed all act in this way, could any of the people fail to receive blessings? This is surely the way followed by the good officials of antiquity, which the officials of today ought to take as their model. I have heard it said that officials are the people’s parents, and the people are the officials’ infant children. Thus the Book of Odes uses the expression “the people’s father and mother” …

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
書有如保赤子之說正此謂耳夫今之人
民即昔之人民也今之土地即昔之土地
也然昔號富饒而今多窮困之家昔稱沃
壤而今多荒蕪之嘆何相去若是殊哉噫
我知其故矣蓋
朝廷設官本以為民而有司入官鮮能為
國因之以天時告災之頻加之以潢池弄兵
之慘安望地不荒蕪而民不窮困也哉然
則如之何而可無亦責之今日有司乎蓋
===
大而受一方之寄則有藩臬藩臬各有僚
屬焉小而受一郡一州一邑之寄則有守
令守令亦各有僚屬焉是皆謂之有司而
繫斯民休戚者也而可以弗加之意乎愚
嘗讀西山先生之書而得所以治民之法
矣蓋西山帥長沙時嘗勸其僚屬勉四事
而去十害今其言固在豈非後人之龜鑑
哉其所謂律己以廉也撫民以仁也存心
以公也蒞事以勤也此之謂四事豈不以

朝廷設官本以爲民而有司入官鮮能爲
國因之以天時旱災之頻加之以潢池弄兵
之慘安望地不荒蕪而民不窮困也哉然
則如之何而可無亦責之今日有司乎蓋
===
大而受一方之寄則有藩臬藩臬各有寮
屬焉小而受一郡一州一邑之寄則有守
令守令亦各有僚屬焉是皆謂之有司而
繫斯民休戚者也而可以弗加之意乎愚
嘗讀西山先生之書而得所以治民之法
矣蓋西山帥長沙時嘗勸其僚屬勉四事
而去十害今其言固在豈非後人之龜鑑
哉其所謂律己以廉也撫民以仁也存心
以公也蒞事以勤也此之謂四事豈不以
punctuated:
《書》有如保赤子之說，正此謂耳。夫今之人民，即昔之人民也；今之土地，即昔之土地也。然昔號富饒，而今多窮困之家；昔稱沃壤，而今多荒蕪之嘆。何相去若是殊哉？噫！我知其故矣。蓋朝廷設官，本以為民，而有司入官，鮮能為國。因之以天時告災之頻，加之以潢池弄兵之慘，安望地不荒蕪而民不窮困也哉？然則如之何而可？無亦責之今日有司乎？蓋大而受一方之寄，則有藩臬，藩臬各有僚屬焉；小而受一郡一州一邑之寄，則有守令，守令亦各有僚屬焉。是皆謂之有司，而繫斯民休戚者也，而可以弗加之意乎？
愚嘗讀西山先生之書，而得所以治民之法矣。蓋西山帥長沙時，嘗勸其僚屬勉四事而去十害。今其言固在，豈非後人之龜鑑哉？其所謂律己以廉也，撫民以仁也，存心以公也，蒞事以勤也，此之謂四事，豈不以
translation_en:
…and the Book of Documents speaks of caring for the people “as if protecting a newborn child”: this is precisely what it means. The people today are the same as those of old; the land today is the same as that of old. Yet where once there was reputed abundance, there are now many impoverished households; where once the soil was praised as fertile, there are now many laments over abandoned fields. Why is the difference so great? Alas! I know the reason. The court establishes offices for the people’s sake, but few officials, upon entering office, can serve the state’s interests. With natural calamities occurring repeatedly, compounded by the horrors of armed rebellion, how can one hope that the land will not lie waste and the people will not be impoverished? What, then, should be done? Should we not hold today’s officials responsible? At the higher level, those entrusted with an entire region include the provincial administration commissioners and surveillance commissioners, each with their subordinate officials. At the lower level, those entrusted with a prefecture, department, or county include prefects and magistrates, who likewise each have subordinate officials. All these are called the responsible authorities, and upon them depend the well-being and suffering of the people. How can they fail to give this their attention?
I have read the writings of Master Xishan and found in them a method for governing the people. When Xishan governed Changsha, he urged his subordinates to strive in four matters and eliminate ten harmful practices. His words still survive today: are they not a mirror and guide for later generations? What he called the four matters were these: discipline oneself with incorruptibility, nurture the people with benevolence, maintain impartiality in one’s intentions, and attend to affairs with diligence. Would one not regard these as…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
爲美政而在所當勉者乎所謂斷獄不公
也聽訟不審也淹延囚繫也慘酷用刑也
泛濫追呼也招引告訐也重疊催稅也科
罰取財也縱吏下鄉也低價買物也此之
謂十害豈不以爲弊政而在所當去者乎
四事切於身心十害切於時弊西山雖爲
當時而言殆若爲今日而發有民社者聞
之能不惕然而興憮然而嘆者乎然以數
者言之則又以四事爲本必先勉其四事
===
而後可以去其十害未有不勉四事而十
害可去者也吾見今之爲有司者其廉仁
公勤以愛民爲心者固多有之然亦有苞
苴入門而乏懸魚之操則持身不得爲廉
暴怒臨民而立吞𧉻之威則撫民不得爲
仁以媚竈之爲能嗤運甓之爲拙則又未
見其存心蒞事之公且勤也夫四事且未
能勉敢望其爲民去害哉抑十害之中則
尤有甚者夫刑獄死生繫干法而今也斷

translation_en:
…as good governance that one ought to strive for? What he called judging criminal cases unfairly, hearing lawsuits without careful scrutiny, prolonging imprisonment, inflicting cruel punishments, issuing excessive summonses and demands for appearance, encouraging accusatory denunciations, repeatedly pressing for tax payments, imposing fines to extract wealth, allowing clerks to descend upon the countryside, and buying goods at low prices—these are the ten harms. Should they not be regarded as abuses of government that ought to be eliminated? The four duties bear directly upon one's person and mind; the ten harms bear directly upon the abuses of the age. Although Xishan spoke for his own time, his words seem almost to have been uttered for today. Can those entrusted with governing a community hear them without rising in alarm and sighing in dismay?

Yet among these matters, the four duties are fundamental. One must first strive to fulfill the four duties before one can eliminate the ten harms. Never have the ten harms been eliminated without striving to fulfill the four duties. Among officials today, I see many who are incorruptible, benevolent, impartial, and diligent, and who take love for the people to heart. Yet there are also those whose doors admit bribes and who lack the integrity exemplified by hanging up a gift of fish to refuse it; their personal conduct cannot be called incorruptible. Those who confront the people in violent anger and establish a terrifying power to devour them [?] cannot be called benevolent in caring for the people. Those who regard currying favor with the powerful as ability and mock the discipline of carrying bricks as foolishness likewise show neither impartiality nor diligence in their intentions and conduct of affairs. If they cannot even strive to fulfill the four duties, how dare we hope that they will eliminate harms for the people?

Moreover, among the ten harms, some are especially grave. In punishments and criminal proceedings, life and death depend upon the law; yet today, in judging…

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之不公用之慘酷者每枉
國法而恣焉則民命死於屠伯之手者多矣
財物多寡出於民而今也科罰取之低價
買之者雖招物議而罔顧則民利入於貪
夫之懷者亦多矣斯人也而可使之在民
上哉嗚呼爾俸爾祿民膏民脂下民易虐
上天難欺吾恐宋人戒石之銘未免爲官
府之文具也盍思
朝廷所以責成我者何如小民所以仰望我
===
者何如而我乃如是哉要當南面臨民之
時動以西山所言爲法首勉其四事以端
一身之本繼去其十害以除一時之弊又
當上與下而相孚彼與此而交勸爲長吏
者必以情達於下而不偃然以自尊爲僚
屬者必以情達於上而不退然以自處勉
所當勉如聖門之尊五美去所當去如聖
門之屏四惡至究其本則又在先有是愛
民之心然後可耳如是則庶幾所謂窮困

punctuated: 之不公，用之慘酷者，每枉國法而恣焉，則民命死於屠伯之手者多矣。財物多寡出於民，而今也科罰取之、低價買之者，雖招物議而罔顧，則民利入於貪夫之懷者亦多矣。斯人也，而可使之在民上哉？嗚呼！爾俸爾祿，民膏民脂；下民易虐，上天難欺。吾恐宋人戒石之銘，未免爲官府之文具也。盍思朝廷所以責成我者何如，小民所以仰望我者何如，而我乃如是哉？要當南面臨民之時，動以西山所言爲法，首勉其四事，以端一身之本；繼去其十害，以除一時之弊。又當上與下而相孚，彼與此而交勸。爲長吏者，必以情達於下，而不偃然以自尊；爲僚屬者，必以情達於上，而不退然以自處。勉所當勉，如聖門之尊五美；去所當去，如聖門之屏四惡。至究其本，則又在先有是愛民之心，然後可耳。如是，則庶幾所謂窮困
translation_en:
…those who adjudicate them unjustly and apply punishments with cruelty repeatedly pervert the laws of the state and act without restraint. Thus many of the common people lose their lives at the hands of these butchers. Wealth and goods, in whatever quantity, come from the people. Yet those who now seize them through fines or purchase them at low prices disregard the public criticism they provoke. Thus much of the people's wealth also passes into the pockets of the greedy. Can such men be allowed to stand above the people?

Alas! “Your salary and your stipend are the people's fat and marrow. The common people are easy to oppress; Heaven above is hard to deceive.” I fear that this admonitory stone inscription of the Song has become merely an empty formality in government offices. Why do we not reflect on what the court expects us to accomplish and what the common people look to us for? How, then, can we behave like this?

Whenever we face south to govern the people, we must take Xishan's words as our standard in every action. First, we must strive to practice his four duties, thereby setting right the foundation of our own conduct; next, we must eliminate his ten harms, thereby removing the abuses of our time. Superiors and subordinates must also trust one another, each encouraging the other. Chief officials must communicate sincerely with those below them, rather than arrogantly exalting themselves; subordinate officials must communicate sincerely with those above them, rather than withdrawing into passivity. We must strive at what deserves our efforts, as the school of the Sage honors the five excellent qualities; we must eliminate what ought to be eliminated, as the school of the Sage rejects the four evils. Yet, tracing this to its root, we must first possess this heart that loves the people; only then can it be done. In this way, we may approach what is meant by the saying, “Those in poverty and distress…”

title: 正德八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者轉為富饒荒蕪者轉為沃壤上有以副
朝廷責成之意下有以慰斯民仰望之私而
天下美政至是成矣假令古之良吏如龔
黃卓魯者為今有司亦不過端治本清弊
源如西山所云者而已安有反古道拂人
情為斯民病哉方今
明天子在上視民如傷所以責成天下有司者
甚至而監臨有司者又有撫按諸憲臣焉
有司四事之能勉與否十害之能去與否
===
公論昭然自不可掩則歲首述職陟勸黜
懲固自有在愚生應有司而來姑因明問
論及之耳豈敢妄曰某也賢某也否以自
取出位之罪哉

punctuated:
者轉為富饒，荒蕪者轉為沃壤，上有以副朝廷責成之意，下有以慰斯民仰望之私，而天下美政至是成矣。假令古之良吏如龔黃卓魯者為今有司，亦不過端治本、清弊源，如西山所云者而已，安有反古道、拂人情，為斯民病哉？
方今明天子在上，視民如傷，所以責成天下有司者甚至，而監臨有司者又有撫按諸憲臣焉。有司四事之能勉與否，十害之能去與否，公論昭然，自不可掩，則歲首述職，陟勸黜懲，固自有在。愚生應有司而來，姑因明問論及之耳，豈敢妄曰某也賢、某也否，以自取出位之罪哉？
translation_en:
…those in poverty become prosperous, and wastelands become fertile fields. Above, this would fulfill the court’s intention in holding officials responsible for results; below, it would satisfy the hopes cherished by the people. Thus would good government throughout the realm be achieved. Suppose that worthy officials of antiquity such as Gong, Huang, Zhuo, and Lu served as today’s responsible officials: they too would do no more than set right the foundations of government and clear away the sources of abuses, as Xishan advocated. How could they contravene the ancient Way, disregard human feelings, and bring suffering upon the people?
Today the enlightened Son of Heaven reigns above, caring for the people as though they were injured. He is most exacting in holding the responsible officials throughout the realm accountable for results. Moreover, grand coordinators and regional inspectors, all censorial officials, oversee them. Whether the responsible officials diligently attend to the four duties, and whether they eliminate the ten harmful practices, is manifest in public judgment and cannot be concealed. Thus, when they report on their service at the beginning of the year, there is assuredly a basis for promotion to encourage them and dismissal to punish them. This humble student has come in response to the responsible officials’ summons and has merely ventured to discuss these matters in response to your discerning question. How would I dare rashly to pronounce this person worthy and that person unworthy, thereby incurring the offense of overstepping my station?

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In autumn of the eighth year of Zhengde, the guiyou year (1513), the time arrived for the Provincial Examinations throughout the realm. In the provinces, provincial officials conduct them according to established practice and, once the proceedings are complete, submit the records to the throne. Only in the two capitals do the prefectural officials, when the time approaches, request the appointment of Examiners, whom His Majesty specially appoints, thereby showing the importance he attaches to the metropolitan regions. Thus we, your servants Yipeng and Long, received the command to preside over the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination.

Having taken leave of His Majesty and arrived at the examination compound, we found that the candidates had already gathered in great numbers. The officials serving in the examination and the requisite artisans had each been assigned to their respective sections and made preparations in advance. All provisions, regulations, and indispensable safeguards for the examination compound were fully and systematically in place. We were therefore able to devote ourselves wholeheartedly to evaluating the papers, seeking thereby to repay the imperial trust. 惟古之用人也，自鄉學論秀而升之為選士，自司徒論秀而升之為俊士，又自大樂正論秀而升之為進士，然後爵祿有加焉。今之士，養於學校，拔于科目，雖其制若有不同，至以漸論選而致諸用，猶夫意也。夫士而謂之秀，以其
translation_en:
…as prescribed, we recorded their names together with the finest of their compositions, to submit them to the imperial repository and circulate them throughout the realm. Your servant then respectfully took up the record and read it, privately exclaiming: “Has the abundance of talent within the metropolitan region reached such heights! Does this not make especially clear the depth of the nurturing influence of our imperial ancestors’ moral transformation, and the manifest and substantial results of His Majesty’s reverence for Confucian learning and esteem for the Way!” With a reverent bow, I have respectfully composed this preface on the closing leaves.
Considering how men were appointed to service in antiquity: the outstanding were assessed in the local schools and promoted to become ‘selected scholars’; they were then assessed by the Minister of Education and promoted to become ‘outstanding scholars’; and they were further assessed by the Grand Director of Music and promoted to become ‘advanced scholars.’ Only then were ranks and emoluments conferred upon them. Today, scholars are nurtured in schools and selected through the examinations. Although the institutions may seem different, the underlying intention remains the same: to assess and select men by stages and bring them into service. 農之種穀也始生為苗吐華為
秀成穀為實士之種學敬遜時
敏足以使人望而畏之則苗之
勃然而興也涵養既深駸駸乎
積中發外之盛乃較其藝而賓
興其尤者則苗之秀拔蔚然有
===
華以向于成也進而不已益深
益盛足乎己而可以及人於是
策名委質用之以治天下則穀
之充然既實穫之以為食也孔
子曰苗而不秀者有矣夫秀而
不實者有矣夫苗斯秀焉不秀

translation_en: …because their talents and accomplishments stand out among their peers, much as grain plants put forth blossoms. When a farmer sows grain, its first growth is called the seedling; its flowering is called blossoming; and its formation of grain is called bearing fruit. When scholars cultivate learning, showing reverence and humility and applying themselves diligently at the proper times, so that others regard them with awe, they are like seedlings springing up vigorously. Once their cultivation has deepened, and what has accumulated within increasingly flourishes in outward expression, their accomplishments are assessed and the outstanding among them are honored as guests and recommended for advancement. This is like grain plants rising above the rest and flowering luxuriantly as they approach maturity. Advancing without cease, they grow ever deeper and more flourishing in their attainments, becoming sufficient in themselves and able to benefit others. They then have their names enrolled in service and pledge their allegiance, and are employed to govern the realm. This is like grain that has filled out and borne fruit, ready to be harvested for food. Confucius said: “There are seedlings that never blossom! There are blossoms that never bear fruit!” Seedlings should blossom; if they do not, it is as though there were no seedlings. translation_en:
…having put forth ears. Thus the farmer worries that his hundred mu of land may remain untilled; he labors diligently throughout the year and rests only when he has obtained grain to eat. The scholar worries that he has not attained the Way; he feels that each day affords insufficient time and rests only when his learning is complete and suited to practical use. There is a further point: the farmer seeks not merely grain, but prizes an abundant yield; the scholar seeks not merely accomplishment, but prizes great accomplishment. Where these aims are not fully realized, much often depends on the setting in which one is placed. Fields adjoining the city walls are to the farmer what the capital, the foremost seat of moral instruction, is to the scholar: nothing takes precedence over these settings in seeking abundance and greatness. Is this not because fertile soil is well suited to planting and readily rewards labor, while the transforming influence of imperial virtue reaches the capital first and permeates it deeply?

秀於此者歛華就實兆成豐穰
厥賦固當上上非他壤可比于

徒以一第之榮自晝昧其遠且
大者甘蹈先聖之戒秀而不實
挍種無功曾荑稗之不如何取
於秀何貴於美種何羨於負郭

已憂者將不在此乎敢以一日
punctuated: 畿甸之内，古之取粟與米于是焉在。視天下猶負郭之田，其温之麥、成周之禾，有厚望者乎？則夫秀於此者，歛華就實，兆成豐穰，厥賦固當上上，非他壤可比。于以使斯民含哺鼓腹，謳詠太平，稱我聖天子安養元元之意，顧不偉與？苟徒以一第之榮自畫，昧其遠且大者，甘蹈先聖之戒，秀而不實，投種無功，曾荑稗之不如，何取於秀？何貴於美種？何羨於負郭之田之良？主司以取士不得為已憂者，將不在此乎？敢以一日
translation_en:
…within the capital region lay the lands from which grain and rice were collected in antiquity. In relation to the realm, this region is like fields adjoining a city’s walls. Should we not have high expectations for its wheat of Wen and its grain of Chengzhou? Those who flourish here should therefore gather in their blossoms and bring forth fruit, promising a plentiful harvest. Their yield should certainly rank in the highest grade, beyond comparison with other lands. Thereby the people may eat their fill and pat their bellies, singing of supreme peace, fulfilling our sagely Son of Heaven’s intention to bring tranquility and sustenance to the common people. Would this not be magnificent?

If, however, they limit themselves to the glory of passing a single examination, remain blind to greater and more distant aims, and willingly incur the ancient sage’s warning against flowering without bearing fruit, then the sowing will have accomplished nothing: they will be inferior even to weeds and barnyard grass. What value would there be in their flowering? What worth in fine seed? What cause to admire the excellence of fields adjoining the city walls? Would this not be precisely the concern of those presiding over the selection of scholars, who worry about failing to obtain worthy men [?]? I venture, on the strength of a single day…
